Grumbling cleaves to him in all the departments of life; when he is well he grumbles at the cook, and when he is ill he grumbles at the doctor and nurse. He. grumbles in his amusements, and he grumbles in his devotion; at the theatre he grumbles at the players, and at church he grumbles at the parson. He cannot for the life of hien enjoy a (lay's pleasure without grumbling. He grumbles at his enemies, and he grumbles at his friends. He grumbles at all the animal creation—at horses when he rides on them, at dogs when he shoots with them, at birds when he misses them, at pigs when they squeak, at. asses when they bray, at geese when they cackle, and at peacocks when they scream. He is always -on the looktout for something to grumble at • he reads the newspapers that t e may grumble at public affairs; his eyes are always open ts look for abomi- nations; he is always pricking up his ears so as to detect any discords, and snuffing up the air to find stinks. Can you insult an Englishman more than by te ling him he has nothing to grumble at! Can you by any possibility inflict a deeper injury upon him by convinciug him that he has no occasion to grumble? Cut his throat and he wid forget it, pick his pockets and he will forget it; but deprive him of his privilege of grumbling, you more than kill him—you expatriate him. But the beauty of it is, you cannot inflict this injury on him; you - 'cannot by all the logic ever invented, or by all the argument that ever was uttered, convince an Eng- lishman that he has nothing to grumble at; be- cause if you were to do so he would grumble at you as long as he lived for disturbing his old associa- tions. Grumbling is a pleasure which we all enjoy more or less, but none, or but few, enjoy it in the perfection and completeness of which it is capab e. If we were to take a little more pains, we should thfa that, havieg no occasion to grumble, we should have cause to grumble at everything. Rut we grow insensible to a great many annoyances, and accustomed to a great many evils and think nothing of them. Waist a tremendous noise there is in the city of carts; coaches, drays, waggons, barrel organs, fishwomen and all manner of abominations, of which they in the city take scarcely any notice at all. Hoeft badly are all matters in government and admit:lets:Won conducted. What very bed bread do bakers make! What very bad meat do the butcleets ,kill In a word, what is there in the whole conipaz-s of existence that is good! What is tacre in the human character that is as it should he? Are e not justified in grumbling at everything that is in heaven above or in the earth beneath, or in the waters under the earth? In fate e gentle reader, is the world formed or gov- erned half so well as you or I could form or govern it? ligowerrsa.s ENERGY.—rne energy of action in Brownine's a ork has eieunted for much in the appeal to his contemporaries. Energy tells at all times, but in a century remarkable for its vigour, in ceaseless unrest, seeking outlets for its life in every direction, excited by its more constant and direct consciousness of its daily life throughout the world, and also better acquainted with the history of the past, filled with great popular movements and wide reaching philanthropy and sympathy, a poet who infuses hia work with vitality and seems to prize it for its own sake breathes the air of the times. It is said that the purest artistic pleasure lies in contemplation ; in action there is p:eaaure of another kind, more strenuous. A poet who sets forth the energy of life appeals to this latter sensi- bility, aroused through sympathy with the doing of a deed, rather than to the former, which involves disinterestedness and disengagement of the mind. Browning himself, in many exculpatory verses, sets forth his claim to the virtue of strength; he is ever praising force for its own sake, in the vein of Carlyle; he likes to exhibit it in others at its high- est pitch. Our own age sympathises with this spirit, and finds it more native to itself than the mood of contemplation, which is the condition of a more ideal art. Browning, however, has rein- forced even this powerful attraction by presenting life not only with great vital force, but upon the broadest scale. He works in the whole field of history, brings his reading in forgotten books to bear, and crowds the \stage with a marvellously diverse gathering of great and obscure men, of artists and musicians, of Jew, Arab, and Greek, of real and imaginary characters; and thus he has satisfied the intelligent curiosity of his readers, playing on the past of the rgece's history, and seeking to 'reconstruct it. He has dealt with the life of man in this varied way, in all ages, in all moods of the mind, and has added to his observa- tion a mass of reflsetion whiCh keeps curiosity itself alive and supports it. Ile is possibly as much obliged to the intellect of his readers, to their appetite for knowledge, as to their poetical sense, in a large portion of his writings: —Atlantic Motahly. DANCING SS/M.S.—The dancing snakes of India are well known; and some of thepeople who kept them one day paid us a visit. They seated them- selves on the floor, produced a snake out of a bag, and a rough kind of music, sang in a monotonous tone, and occasionally clapped their hands. The charmed snake raised itself about half its length from the grcund, and seemed to keep time to the music by the motion cf the body and head. The instant the music ceased, it sank clown, and the man thrust it into the bag, and produced another, which was in like manner charmed. The Psalmist doubtless referred to these reptiles when he men- tions the "deaf adder refusing to hear the voice of the charmer, charm he Lever so wisely." The observation, I am aware, is not new, but the sight of the reptiles rendered it peculiarly striking.— Two Ytars at Sea ly Jane Roberts. THE hair in all ages has been an endless topic for the declamation of the moralist, and the favourite object of fashion. If the beau monde wore their hair luxuriant, or their wig enormous, the preachers, as in Charles ll.'s reign, instantly were seen in the pulpit with their hair cut shorter, and their sermon longer in consequence; respect was, however, paid by the world to the size of the wig, in spite of the hair-cutter in the pulpit. IT seems, Johnson observes in his life of Sir Thomas Browne, to have been in all ages the pride of art to show how it could exalt the low and amplify the little. To this ambition perhaps we owe the Frogs of Homer; the Gnat and the Bees of Virgil; the butterfly of Spenser; the Shadow of Wowerus : and the Quincunx of Browne.

By the death of the Rev. Father Henry James Coleridge, S.J., which has just taken place at the chief novitiate of the Jesuit order at Manresa, , Roehampton, the Catholic Church in England loses one of its most able and distinguished writers in he field of theelegical and philosophical literature, and one of its most cultivated ecelesiasti,...s. Father Coleridge, who was at the time of his death in his seventy-first year, was the elder brother of the Lord Glief Justice of England.having joined the Catholic Church many years since, after leaving Trinity College, Oxford, to which he passed from Eton, and took his degree with first-class honours. He after- wards joined the Society of Jesus, and was well known in London during the period of his residence (some time as rector) at the famous Jesuit Church at Farm-et., where hi a scholarly attainments and his genial and polished manners gained him a wide , circle of friends, who will receive the news of his ,1 death with deep regret. A contributor of the lead- ing high-elrus reviews of the day, Father Cole- ' ridge was also tho author of a vast number of works on religious subjects, and was just previous to his death engaged on a " Life of Christ." Lately be was occupied in the training sal education of the novices of the order at Manresa.

Of the various wedding couples who have been married lately, Lord and Lady Grosvenor are spend- ing their honeymoon at Eaton Hall. Mr. Chetwynd and the Baroness von Alvenslebein have gone to Parts. Captain and Mrs. Fox-Pitt are at Rushmore, Wiltshire, the seat of General and the Bon. Mrs. Pitt-Rivers. Sir George and Lady Baden-Powell have gone to Beaulieu Lodge in the New Forest, which has been lent them by the Hon. John and Lady Cecil Scott Montagu. Mr. and Mrs. John Harford (the latter being the dauglater of the late Mr. Raikes, sometime Postmastei-General) have started for Italy. Mr. and Mrs. Stuart Montagu Samuel are vow at Monte Carlo. Sir James and Lady Fergusson have arrived at Kilkerran. Mr. Hugh and Lady Mary Morrison are now at Bridgend Islay. Captain, and Mrs. Ronald Lane (the former being assistant military secretary at the Horse Guards) have started for the Continent:-

Lord Craven, whose marriage at Grace Church, New York, on Tuesday, to Miss Cornelia Bradley- Martin, is the international match of the year, says of himself that he is rich in cash and richer in lands, but richest in aunts. There are five of these ladies —ell, with one exception, well-known and power- ful leaders of the London social world. Cue of them is the Countess or Cadogan, whose port ege he,is anti who gave him the jewel-studded amber cigarette holder with which the Earl of Craven is wont to smoke perfumed tobacco at West-end clubs. His lordship's second aunt is Elizabeth, Countess of Wilton, celebrated for her devotion to the turf, and particularly to the hunting fields in the vicinage of Melton Mowbray. A third is the popular and lovely Countess of Coventry, wife of the ex-master! of her Majesty's Buckhounds. She was a member of the memorable party at Tanby Croft which bred the baccarat scandal. Lady Emily Van de Weyer is another. She is the wife of a former Belgian Minister in London, a great favourite of the Queen, and often entertains her Majesty at afternoon tea at her cottage near Windsor. Yet another is Lady Evelyn, mother of the bankrupt Marquess of Ailes- bury, who married Miss Dolly Tester, of music-hall renown. Lady Evelyn, after the death of the late Marquess of Ailesbury, married Captain. Coventry, cousin of the present Earl of Coventry, and, after a divorce from him, married Captain Riddell, of the 16th Lancers. She resides in Scotland.

The Bradley-Martins were not born in the purple. They fought their way into New. York society, vihich they astonished by their recklessness and even royal extravagance. The family Game from the head waters of Hudson River. Mrs. Bradley- Martin's father was Isaac Sherman, who, though he began life as a cooper. died a railway king. He left his daughter—the pretty and vivacious Mrs. Brad- ley-Martin—ten millions ot dollars. Before a singe season had passed New York society began to recog- nise in her a new force and in her dinners and lun- cheons a new departure. In the winter of 1889-90 Mrs. Bradley-Martin was selected as one of three distinguished women to receive guests at the new year's ball held in the Metropolitan Opera House. She stood by the side of Mrs. William A•tor, the acknowledged head of New York society. This func- tion fixed her social position in the States, and in securing as a husband for her daughter the heir to a peerage which dates to the days of Charles IL the child of the mcdest old cooper of Troy will cap the climax of a social career which has not been want- ing in tact or dash on either side of the Atlantic. Tuesday's function was emphatically a children's wedding. The earl is a mere boy,and Miss Cornelia is a shrinking bud of sixteen.

Mrs. Lewis and Mrs. Gibson, the scholarly sister who have made the wonderful discovery at the convent at Mount Sinai of a new Syriac version of the Gospels, are well known in Cambridge Univer- sity circles. The former lady is the widow of the Rev. S. S. Lewis, late Fellow of Corpus Christi,Cam- bridge, whose sudden death during a railway jour- ney in the summer of 1891,evoked much widespread sympathy. Mrs. Gibson and her sister have for many years been inseparable, and when Mr. Lewis, who was a profound antiquarian, took his erudite bride to what he was wont to call his "little hat on the hill off the Trumpington-road," Mrs. Gibson also became a member of the household. Their re- searches covered all branches of Oriental classics, gicing them a wide reputation as bas bleus of the deepest dye.

Mr. Lewis had a very Singular personality. 113 was nearing middle age when he took his degree, and he was by no means an old man when he died, but in the interim his labors among the manu- scripts and ancient volumes belonging to his college, of wi.iclr he was librarian, had placed him on a platform among the bookworms where he had very few peers. His acts of kindness to those less wealthy students who came under his notice were numerous and ever unostentatious, and the service in Corpus Chapel on the occasion of his funeral was one of the most impressive that the university town has known.

Sir James Lyall, who has just been elected a member of the Atheumum Club in recognition of. his distinguished public services, has an inex- haustible capacity for bard work, and that after thirty-four yearb' residence in one of the most try- ing climates in the world he should come back to England full of energy and activity is in itself a tribute to his force of character. From 18.58,when he entered the Bengal Civil service, until 1883, when he was appointed resident,- of My sore and C'iief Commissioner of Coorg, Sir James (then plain Mr,) Lyall was actively engaged in revenue and settlement work at Lahore and other towna in the Ptinjab ; and his nomination to the Lieutenant- -0 overnorsh ip of the district of the " Five Rivers" in the Jubilee Year therefore gave unusual satis- faction. Sir James, like his brother Sir Alfred Lyall, is brimful of information respecting the antiquities of India; but the tastes of the two men do not lay precisely in the same direction, Sir James being less poetic than practical.

Lamb and Veal.

Lamb and veal are meats which do not require to be hung any length of time, as they are so tender that it is not necessary to soften the fibres by keeping. A piece of lamb is in prime condition for cooking' within forty- eight hours after it is killed. One of the daintiest ways to cook tender lamb chops is to bread them. Trim the Chops carefully, flatten them, season with salt and pep- per on both sides, dip them in egg,then in bread crumbs and immerse then in boiling hot fat for about four minu- tes. Drain them on brown paper and serve them with either tomato sauce or with Espagnole sauce to which half a dozen chopped mushrooms and a wineglass of Madeira have been added. This may be garnished with heart- shaped pieces of bread fried brown and spread with a little pate de lois gras. The lamb chops may also be arranged in a circle around a mound of green peas, a puree of string beans or mashed potatoes browned in the oven.

Cheap Health. Since the athletic girl has become so dominant a figure in the feminine world, and fragility has grown a re- proach rather than a charm, the treatises multiply on all hygienic matters, and volumes are set forth withoat number to tell every woman what she shall do to be saved from all ills that flesh is heir to. The woman with the interesting paler, the violet-shadowed eyes, and the willow-wana torm, who fainted if one said " 800 ! "to-her, and solved all sentimental difficulties with a brain fever, has given place to a buxom lassie, whose cheeks are red as the dawn, wi,th brown, muscu- lai hands that stop runaway horses, rescue helpless bairns from mad dogs, and amid a wreck of matter and crash of worlds would never feel a tremor of her steel- strung nerves. And this magnificent person is all the product of athletics and athletics, and yet again athle- tics. Ride on horleback, say the lecturers on this sub- ject, play tennis, swim, fence, practice ins gymnasium, take cold baths, live in the open air. And those who follow their advice attain the staltvart loveliness of Atalanta and Hyppolita, bring forth rosy sons and daughters, and are as the pillars of their husband's houses.— Good Health.

div.head: DIED WHILE IN PRAYER.
div.p: DIED WHILE IN PRAYER.

" Another man teas found in a kneeling posture, his face buried ia his handies if he had died in prayer." I clip this pathetic sentence from an account ot the St. Etienne coal mine disaster which occurred in France, in December, 1891. The fire had been smouldering for years in a remote part of the mind, but its further advance had been stopped by barriers. Yet they proved insufficient at last, and the terrible fire-damp exploded, scattering death throughout the avioe. Such incidents are too well-known in England to need further explana- tion or comment.

Has it ever struck you that the interior of the human• body is like the interior of a coal mine ? Well, it is. All its operations go on in solitude and darkness. Gases are engendered in it that are jtist as dangerous as fire-damp. Generally they—yet hold on, let's have the little story first.

It's about a woman. In fact, It's front her, too, and is sure to interest somebody ; may be you. She says that a long run of time, from childhood to years after her marriage, she never knew what illness was ; that is, so as to remember it, or tO`have it make a mark on her, as we may say. But mighty few folks manage to escape the old slave driver altogether. Nor did she. "It was in the summer of 1890," she says, "when I began to feel bad. My appetite was poor, and what I did eat gave me great pain arid distress. My food seemed to lie like lead ; and after every meal, no matter bow simple the food was, I ha l the most excruciating pain you can imagine. I had a nagging, thudding, pain at my chest, and through to my shoulders, that was very hard to bear. So bad was it that I thought something (perhaps a tumour) was growing within me. As soen as ever food entered my stomach I used to say, " It is begin- ning,' meaning the gnawing pain. "I took all kinds of things for relief and applied mustard plasters to the chest, but nothing did me any good. After a time I dared not take a proper meal: I was afraid to eat, and got very thin and weak. It was as much as I could do to go about my house *ork. In October ef this year (1891) Mrs. James Mercer, of 176, High Street, Langton, recommended me to try Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and 1 got a. bottle and com- menced to take it. After a few doses I felt relief. My food agreed with me, and by the time I had taken cue large bottle all the pain had left me, and I now feel as well as ever I ditl."—Yours truly (signed), Mrs. ELIZA- BETH WRIGHT. 12, King Street, Hanley, Staffordshire, November 19th, 1891.

You ask me what the sad fate of the miners has to do with the case of Mrs. Wright. I'll tell you in half a minute. This lady says she was taken ill in the sum- mer of 1890. New, do you suppose the illness and the cause of the illness curie up at the same time? By, no means. Cause first, effect afterwards—that's the order, always. And, see here! A cause may be at work for weeks or years before you notice any results ; and until you do notice results, you don't know there's aught gone wrong. Isn't that so. ? The miners, to be sure, knew there was a fire in the mine. Bht it was fenced -)ff from them and they thought they were safe. The barriers leaked, and death griped them in a twinkling of an eye.

The bcaly is like a mine, as I have said. Disease and death are caused by the action of poisonous gases and acids inside of it. They all start from the stomach and then creep into every part ; sometimes fast, sometimes Blow. In some acute diseases very fag, The doctors often call gout an "explosion "of uric Mid. The sottrce of all these deadly things is indigestion and dyspepsia. Slight symetons first, then the more terrible and alarm. tag. Watch the way it comes on. This was Mrs. Wright's ailment. She suffered fifteen months before she found out what the matter was and what to do. Gracious, mercy ! if we only knew the sort of things that go on in our bodies we'd understand that it's about as dangerous to work in a kitchen as in a coal mine.

div.head: NETTLES AND DANDELIONS.
div.p: NETTLES AND DANDELIONS.

It is not without some reason,says M.A., in the "Vegetarian," that our grandmothers called into requisition the dose of brimstone and i treacle at the time when winter first gave place to tspring. Nowadays, happily we are able to avoid the evils which result from spending the winter months without green foods by a more extended cultivation and importation of fruits, vegetables, salads, and a more extensive use of them in the commu- nity. The worst period, however, is still the last month just before the fresh greens come in, and it is at this period that a valuable vegetable is to be found springing up in every sheltered hedgerow,and bit of waste land in the country. I -refer to the common stinging nettle. Nettles are very valuable for their anti-scorbutic proper- ties, and if the tender tops be cut off, well washed and boiled, a dish will be ready quite equal in many respects to spinach. F3r those who like them more elaborately prepared they may be passed, after boiling, through a sieve and then beaten up with cream. In order to gt the special value of the soluble salts they contain, the water in which they are boiled should be used as a basis for soup, or when boiling it may be poured on to a little oatmeal. and so eaten in the Scotch form of nettle brose. Nettles come at a time when hardly anything else is in season, and I have again and again gathered a basketful from some sheltered hedgebank long before any of the garden greens had put in an appearance. Onlv the young and tender tops should be snipped off, and if an old glove be worn and a pair of scissors be used no stings need feared. An important point to my mind with regard to nettles and other " wild " vege- tables is that they are not spoiled by that heavy dosing with a plethora of manure which is so generally given to garden vegetables which are being grown by profes- sionals for market.

I have lately had another important vegetable brought tq my notice, and this is the common dandelion (for- merly called Taraxacunt dens leonis ,but now more usually Tarasacunt officinale.) A dish of this was prepared by taking the young leaves before the flower buds had ap- peared, washing them, boiling them, draining them, and then mashing them up with a little milk and serving on toast. It was a delightfully pleasant dish with quite enough flavour of bitter about it, but not too much to make it unpleasant. For those who find the bitter a little too strong the dandelion should after boiling and draining be mashed up with plainly boiled rice and a little oil. This vegetable is a capital tonic, and its wide use in spring time would ruin the sale of Clarke's Famous Blood Mixture.

"If he means her well," Mrs. Quillet had said to herself, "I ought-not to take advantage of him. His friends would be angr'y, and they weirld'havc reason to be. Miss Gwen cannot be his wife. And if he means her ill; why she is best kept out of his way. I'll not tell her. He's acted false in going off without a word as he did, and false once false a:ways.Pl Hardening her heart against the handsome, pleading young fellow, she sent him away, and forebore to tell Gwen that be had returned to Lonernoor to see her. In the course of another week Gwen had, through the exertions of her kind friends, obtained two music.pupils, both within easy walking distance of NorthumberlAnd- terrace.

The money obtained for these lessons sufficed to pay her board, which she insisted on doing. Tee Myners expostulated with her, refusing to receive payment from her,' but finally yielded. The SUM elle paid assisted materially to lighten the expenses of the establishment, and the Ilyners lost some- thing of their careworn look. One morning Gwen went out as usual to give one of her lessens directly after breakfast. She had a long wall; before her. The day was lowering and chilly, and she was proceeding briskly. She gave her lesson, finishing in time for her pupil to proceed to her day school, and then hurried notnewards. She had gone but a few streets, and was in tile act of putting up her umbrella, when sbe met Clfutton Orkney face to face. There was no chance of escape. He had seen and recognised her. Yet without a-word to him Gwen hurried on.

He turned and walked beside her, his face glow- ing with great joy. If this isn't the strangest thing I ever knew !" he ejaculated. "I have searched everywhere for you, Miss Gwen,' and here I stumble upon you in the oddest way. I was just thinking of you. It seems incredible that in this great town, with its millions of inhabitautt, I should meet you of all ethers in a morning walk." The girl did not answer. The sight of him had given her an unpleasant shock, and she was think- ing now of sothe plan to escape him. "Miss Gwen,' exclaimed her suitor, "why don't you speak to me? Do you blame me for my father s enmity of you? Where are you staying in London ?'

" Mr. Orkney," said the girl, regarding him now sternly, her proud • young face full of haughty aversion, "I am earning my own living. I have left Lonemoor and its associations for ever. I never want to steak to you again. If you have one spark of manliness you will leave me. The young man's face flushed.. "Mire Gwen," he exclaimed, "have you never forgiven me for my insult t* you that day upon the moor? I have reper.t.ed titterly. I love you, and I offer you honourable marriage. I will Work for you shiet i you from all cares--' " You have my answer, sir." "Miss Gwen, why are you EO cruel to me? I ant prepared to cast off my relations for your sake. I , de,n't blame you for resenting their treatment of you." " Will you leave me, sir ?" Young Orkney began to look vindictive. , "I suppose you think youpg• Chilton is a better match for you?' he sneered.- " Fle is the son of a viscount, while lam the son of a land bailiff.' But let me tell you, Miss Gwen, .he never meant to marry you. He amused himself With you for a few weeks, and then went away in sear..h of newer game." Gwert's eyes flashed fire. Her face, pale as death, shone with her passionate anger. She was not a meek soul to bear insult without resentment, and she cried out, her voice low hut strong— " Will you have the goodness to relieve me of your hateful presence?" "No, I won't", he answered, bluntly. . "I am determined to marry you, Gwen. I sea L! follow you to your home and find were you live, I'll per- secute you until you will be glad to marry me. I'll find out if you are teacning, and I'll get you out of your situation. I'll slander you, if you force me to, till no decent roof can be found to shelter you, and you will be glad to accept the shelter of my name! I swear I'll do all this. You are to te my wife, you understand, and all your refusals 'are struggles will not avail you. Even fate conopircs to help you. See how I met you this morning. You can't escape me now I" • "We 'll see if I can't!" said Gwen, salting her thin lips together. "I don't intend to sublult ts the little plan you have laid out. I don't Mt end to be slandered and driven out of a situation and made to marry yon. Once more will you leave me?" "Once more. I won't !" •

"But which we may be the happier for not know- ing," said Mr. Myner, gravely. "it any person exists who knows the secret, he is not likely to betray it now, after keeping it seventeen years. I think, my dear and Miss Gwen, that in reference to the secret we maylipply an old adage, 'Let sleeping dogs lie l' Your mother, Miss Gwen, 1,..s lain for seventeen years in a dishonoured grave. Had any one lived who could have lifted that cloud front-off her name, I believe be would have done it I Had ay one lived whe lied an interest in her child I believe he would have sworn it."

"You are iight, Thomas," said Mrs. Elyner, "and I agree with Gwen that the advertisement must have come from Mr. Claxton Orkney. The Quillets refused him Gwen's address, and he uses this means to find it. He may have put in the notice since he meet her and she escaped from him yesterday." "It was probably sent into the newspaper office the day before," said Mr. Myner, who had advertised for pupils, and knew how the art of advertising was conducted. "You have to wait two days for an Insertion of a notice in the Times. Like you, I am persuaded that T. T.' represents Mr. Claxton Orkney, my dear. It will be best not to reply to the advertisement."
"I shall not answer it," said Gwen. "I shall remain safely hidden under my new name of Miss Myner, and leave him to continue the search at his leisure."

And so the advertisement, by means of which the wily Maltese valet of Lord Darkwood hoped to dis- cover Gwen, was tossed aside, and Mr. Tomas° Tecino, the brother of Pietro, waited and watched in vain in his home at "No. 37, Blank-street, Soho- square," like a spider in its web, for the coming of the young lady who was expected to make his brother's fortune.
Now," said Myner, taking up his newspaper again, we will read the advertisement winch attracted my attention. It seems an appeal directly to Miss Gwen. Listen!" He read as follows:

Governess Companion.—Wanted, a lady not over twenty years of age, refined, thoroughly well- bred, and versed in all the modern aeccmplishments with a thorough knowledge of the English branches, and of music. To one capable o instructing a young lady of fifteen, whose education has been neglected, and who is impatient of all restraint, a liberal salary will be paid, and a good home offered. —Apply to Mr. Sutton,' &o."_ - - - _ .
TL?scwas the advertisement of Lord Darkwood. A singular fatality it was that had brought it under G.ven's notice.

"It is plain that the advertiser does not want a strict teacher, but a young girl who will instruct by example as well as bywords," said Mrs. Myner. " A good home, a liberal salary, with but one pupil, pro- mises well; but one pupil like the one mentioned here can be very troublesome. What do you think of it, Gwen ? " "I should like to apply for the situation," replied Gwen. "I think I could win the young lady's heart. lam not much older than she, fresh from school, and can certainly be a 'companion,' if not a governess." _ _

- "It will do no harm to apply to Mr. Sutton," said Mr. Myner. "Miss Gwen will certainly be safer in a home than in giving lessons to day pupils, and being obliged to pass through the streets daily ; and if the place doesn't suit, Miss Gwen has a home here, and can return to us at any moment." . _
It was decided that Gwen should send her cation to Mr. Sutton, and she sat down at a little Writing table and wrote it at once. When it 'liras finished she submitted it to her friends.

Her letter was simple and straightforward,written in an exquisitely neat and delicate penmanship. She stated that she wag English, under twenty years of age, that she had been educated partly in England, partly in Paris, that she was competent to fulfil the duties demanded of a "governess-com- panion;' and that she desired a good home rather than a large salary. She had no experience in. teaching, being fresh from school. She had referred Mr. Sutton to the Rev. Thomas Myner, and sub- scribed her name as Marian Pilyper.

"'A very good letter," said Mrs. Myner. "Mr. Sutton will rereive a great many to-clay. Thomas, this had better be posted at once." "I will postit myself," said the curate. "I shall not be wanted in the schoolroom until the next hour." He hurried out with the missive to the nearest pillar box. . As Mrs. Myner had surmised, Mr: Sutton, the family lawyer of the Darkwoods, received a great many applications; but, by a singular chili:ice. he selected the letter of our heroine.

He Called that evening at NartfilllllbertUL,; ',Fst - race and asked to sec .Miss Myncr. •. Tb lawyer, after a few questions, reqiiss cid her to favour him with a little music. She emitptierl and. then sang an operatic air, and the lawyer, ei irred in his iuniost soul by the pdwer and aion of tier voice, by its exquisite - sweetness, tenderness anti depth, wondered that she did net glitl On the stage. " She holds a-fortune in that Slender throat, ' bC thought. "Lord Dark wood Would certainly. her pleased with her." ••• The lawyer expreee.ed,his satisfaction and delight to Mr. and Mrs. Myner at Gweu's musieal p'erforin-' ances, and said— " I am empowered to engage a lady, Mr. Myner,- without reference to my principal. Her pupa will: be the Lady GeorgiasCharteris, of D &who/ m e Castle,' Salop. The situation is likely to prove difficult, the Lady Georgina having been greatly neglected, as was stated in the advertisement. In view of. the difficulties, Lord Darkwood, the father of Lady Georgina, expressly ,desires me to state that the- ' governess-companion ' will be allowed a handsome Suite of rdoins, the partial attendance of a maid, and a salary of a hundred guineas a year, to be paid quarterly." ".The terms are certainly very liberal," said Mrs. Mynri.. . _ . _ _ _

, "Ii Mtn Myner concludes to accept the situation which I now oiler her," said Mr. Sutton," "she will be treated as the equal of the Lady Georgina, will drive with her, will walk with her, and dine with her. The servants will be instructed to treat her with the same respect as that accorded to Lord DarkwoodAlaughter. Miss Myner will need be a companion to Lady Georgina in every respect, and to instruct her in all branches, solid and orna- mental, that belong to the education of young women of the present day. Persuasion rather than authority will be required in the management of the Lady Georgina.' "I accept the offer' Mr. Sutton, subject to the approval of my friends," said Gwen gravely. "J will do my best to satisfy Lord Darkwood and tc benefit his daughter." "When do you wish Miss Myner to go to Shrop- shire 7" inquired Mr. Myner. "Tomorrow, if possible, then as soon as con- venient, sir."

, "I can go to-morrow," 'told Gwen, "In regard to references, sir," said Mr. Myner, "I will 'vouch for Miss Myuer, and I will give you the names of half a dozen gentlemen, including the rector I lately assisted, who will speak for me.' He wrote the hall dozen names and addresses on a card and pve It to Mr. Sutton, who placed it in his note book.

The lawyer then gave Gwen minute instructions for reaching Dunholm Castle, and wrote out for her a letter of introduction which she was to deliver in person to Lord Darkwocxl. "I shall telegraph to 'lsis lordship in the morn- ing that you arc upon the way, Miss Myner," he Said. "Mr. Myner, • you need have no anxieties about your young relative. She will find a real home at Danholni Castle.''
" I wiii send an orderly servant to attend her U far as Shrewsbury," said Mrs. 2,lyner. aon't quite approve of young girls treivelling entirely ' alone."

div.head: TALE OF LONEMOOR.
div.p: A TALE OF LONEMOOR.
CHAPTER XXV.
AN ADVENTURE.
What was to be done with Gwen?

• That was the question which the Myners had ;mitt themselves to consider; but it was by no means easy Ili solution. Gwen was reso'ute in her intention to earn her own living.: She was versed in all fashionable accomplishments: knew thorougnly several lan- guages, was a fine mus:cian, a charming vocalist, and though she was too modest to acknowledge all this even to herself, she yet felt herself capable. of instructing others. She avowed her desire to become a governess. . . .

'‘` Or a companion to an elderly lady," suggested Mrs. Myner, wlio knew from experience many of the hardships of a governess's life. "Or you might stay with us and give music lessons, dear." "We shall see what can be done," said Mr Myner: " There is no haste, M arian. Miss Winter can make us a visit, and we will judge •whaL is best to be done, and wait for opportunities. Let us have patience." And so the matter remained in abeyance. Daring the next few days Gwen visited with her old friend, assisted a little in the school, and arrived at thin conclasin that she was not really needed in the house, thakthe staff of teachers was complete without further addition, and that she must look elseidiere for employment, whatever her kind friends might say to the contrary. She began to search the advertising columns of the newspapers, answering several advertisements for governesses ; but her application was never rewarded with an answer.
Her friends begged her to continue to be patient, and themselves soueht a situation for her. They could find none which they deemed suitable for her.

At the end of a week, Gwen received a letter from Mrs. Quillet, in response to one whial she had written announcing her safe arrival. The Lonemoor housekeeper wrote coldly, and confined herself to the narration of events. She said that young Mr. Orkney had been over to Lonemoor, and had begged Gwen's address. It being refused, be had declared that he knew she had gone to London, and that he was going thither the next day. And in his angor at Mrs. Quillet's refusal to gratify his curiosity, he had sworn an oath that he would find Gwendoline Winter if she were in England, even if he had to employ a, detective to search her out. -4. I can't help thinking, Miss Gwen," the house- keeper continued, "that he will find you. Ho is a bold, bad man. Ho has set his heartippon you, and means to have you. lam very uneasy. Now you know, Miss Gwen, that you have no right to the name of Winter • couldn t you exchange it for some other? You will be safer under another name."

Gwen showed the letter to Mrs. Myner. "I agree with Mrs. Quillet," said her friend, thoughtfully. "You see, dear, if you should get musiepupils, or a situation as governess, this Orkney might find you out and bring some sort of ecandal upon you. You cannot be troubled with his pursuit. Mrs. Quillet says truly you have no actual right to the name of Winter. Let me give you my own name. I am too poor to make you any other present, little Gwen. •When•you begin your AO lifa let it be as MTss Marian Myner." _ _ _ . .
- Mr. Myner, on being appealed to approved this ides, and Gwen became thenceforth Miss Marian Myner, although she was still called Gwen by 'her two friends.

"It was thoughtful of Mrs. Quillet to send your letter under cover to me," remarked Mrs. Myrna. ""I he Peniatone postmaster cannot betray your address under the most artful questioning. And wherever you may be, little Gwm, you can send letters to the Quillets under cover to me. Let the old life he cut off by a great Wall." It will have been ivAiced that the Lonemoor housekeeper made 'no mention of Mr. Chilton's visit to her the day after Gwen's departure. Yet he had returned to Lonemoor at the time stated, and had made every effort to discover Gwen a address. The housekeeper had refused to give it to him. She believed that he loved"the girl sin- cerely, but she had reflected upon the folly of unequal marriages, and had decided in her own mind that it would not be right to allow him, the son of a peer, to marry a name!ess girl. Such a marriage might result in a double misery. She refused utterly to contribute to such a deplorable result. '

Urwen's keen eyes had espied a policeman in the I distance. She walked on slowly, the villain at her side, believing that she had given up the contest ; but when thd girl drew near, enough to the officer of the layr,-libe hatted, saying in her clear low voice. which was quite calm— "Will you protect me, sir! This man has insulted me, and threatens to follow me to my home.," The officer regarded the pair narrowly. Owen was a lady—that fact was apparent at a glance. Bet the bailiff's son was as manifestly her social inferior. His flushed, coarse face, and somewhat. flashy attire, proclaimed him as belonging to another order of beings. "Loox here, young man," said the policeman, "this won't do, molesting of young ladie3 in the public street. Pass on, miss, I'll see to this person." Young Orkney protested that he knew the young lady, that he was her lover, and that they ha.l quarrelled. It required the expenditure of a soirereign, delivered to the officer in the most secret Wanner, to induce that guardian of the law io accept his statement and release his grip upon his arm. But when he did so Gwen had disappeared. Orkney ran up -the street. There was no trace of her. She had completely vanished. In truth, she had turned the nearest corner, had signalled an empty passing eab, and was on her way to Northumberland-terrace more than a mile distant.
He had found her only to lose her. "I'll haunt the vicinity of the place where I met her this morning," he resolved. "11l search high and low for her; and I'll make her pay for her scorn I"
Gwen reached home, dismissed the cab, and hurried into the presence of her friends. She hastened to tell them of her adventure.
I shall not dare go to that neighboarhood again to give lessons I" she exclaimed. "I am afraid of that man. He is terrible l''

Mrs. Myner sighed. "You ought to have a permanent situation, Miss Gwen," said Mr. Myner. "It would be safer and better. We will begin to search the newspapets again for advertisements. Something may present itself in that way." "And in the meantime she must give up this pupil," said Mrs. Myner, "the man will haunt that neighbourhood believing her to belong there. If we find no advertisement that promises well, we will advertise after a few days for you, dear." The, next morning after breakfast, as the three sat In the little parlour studying the advertise- ments, Mr. Myner exclaimed— " Here's the very situation for you, Miss Gwen, if we can secure it. Hear this--"
Mrs. Myner interrupted with a little cry. "Why here's an advertisement for Miss Gwen- doline Winter. What can it mean ? Hear this r
CHAPTER XXVL A PRESENTIMENT.
Mrs. Myner hastened to read to her husband and her guest, in a quick, excited voice, the following notice—

"Information wanted of Miss Gsvendoline Winter, wbo left Yorkshire recently for London. If Miss Winter will communicate with T. T., No. 37, Biank- street, Soho-square, she will learn something greatly to her advantage."

- . - Mrs. Mvner dropped V3e newspaper into her lap and looked inquiringly at her companions. "What do you suppose that means ? " she demanded_ " Information wanted '—by whom 7 " "By borne one, evidently, who could not obtain it , in Yorkshire," said Mr. Myner, "By some one whom the Quillets distrusted and. refused to answer."

" I hal a fancy," said the curate's wife, diap- pointedly, "that the advertisement Might be from, some person who knows the secret of Gwen's parent- age." "If that were so," said Mr. Myner, "why have they not come forward before 7" "They must, have obtained that informatio,, from renistone or Loncreoor," said Gwen. "If that person who advertised is honest and means me no harm, the Quillets would have given my address. They would gladly be relieved of all responsibility in ref,ard to me, could they find some one to take it."
"Miss Gwen is right," said Mr. Myner. "I think the notice was written by Mr. (Paxton Orkney," said Gwen. "This advertisemeat is a clever little trap to catch me."

Mr. Mynei concurred in this opinion. "I hoped it might have some bearing upon that secret wh:ch seems so impenetrable," said Mrs Myner, slghing. "Some o, e must hold the clue to that secret. hem° oYte knows what we would give so much to know—"

Brilliant as the weather has been, the well-known treacherous character .of the English Spring should !hake you careful in the matter of - clothing. Happily, there is such variety in the colourjzi and texture of woollen fabrics that, while keeping, to warm materials, you can still appear in gowns and mantles suggestive of the season, yet calcu- lated to protect from ohild. Some of the new, Spring gowns are charming. For a girl, a simple walking costume is made in fawn-coloured fine cloth, trimmed with green velvet; there are two bands of velvet round the skirt, one round the • edge, the other just below the knee. The collar and waistband of the short bodice are of velvet, as are the f all sleeves; the pretty little lircular cape for out-of-door wear being of the same cloth, with •velvekedged double shoulder frills; and the hat is •of fawn and green straw, trimmed with velvet and ostrich feathers to match, these being set to fall over the front of the hat, where the brim is much raised. This costume in any two really good combinations of colour looks very well.

A pretty hat is of brown or any other colour •straw with the rim underneath bordered with an applique of cream lace run through with gold thread, the same lace ornamenting the brown ribbon, which in conjunction with ostrich tips forms the trimming. Another emlrt little hat in a similiar style is made of black fancy straw, with the inevitable coloured edge to the brim, and the trimming consists of a baud of pink velvet with narrow iridescent edge round the crown, terminat- ing in a small bow in front; two black ostrich plumes in front, and a third arranged to rest on the hair at the back. .

I understand that capes are not to have it quite all their own way, for though these will enjoy a large amount of popularity, it is one they will share with the short jacket. The smartest of jackets will be made quite tight-iitting, with the basques rather full. An elegant style which, how- ever, made it first appeam.nce last year, is cut in an Eton shape in the tront, with a full basque as the back and a belt round the waist, which heads tjae basque in the front, bringing it under the Eton fronts to fasten over a blouse. This I have met in drab cloth with the revers faced with black satin and the belt of gold galoon studded with jet, and extremely nice it would look worn over a skirt to match with blouse or skirt of any description. I expect fronts will somewhat take the place of blouses for the next few weeks, for under our coat sleeves you will not want the huge puffed 'sleeves of the blouse, and so that you have an open coat you only need display some pretty and attractive garment from neck to waist.

A very simple but dressy little blouse i 3 merety a plain short blouse trimmed in zouave fashion back and front, and with frilled epaulettes over the sleeves. Although this looks tolerably plain at first sight, yet it is a charming style, and becoming to full figures, for it does not increase the size as do frills and broad revers. For the crossed blouse, to fasten at the back, allow four yards and a-half of silk, or five yards if the sleeves are pouffed, or five-and-a-half if ends come round to the front, and the sleeves have added pouffs. These measurements are estimated for the blouse cut the reverse way—viz., with selvedge top and bottom. Double-width er3pon is more economical as three yards will make a nice blouse, with the longer ends and very full pouffed sleeves.

I often wonder how it is that, as a rule, very little apace is devoted to the subject of boys clothes when fashions for children are under dis- cussion? Certainly girls' frocks are more interest- ing, and can be made at home with the happiest results, while the attempt to turn out wearable boys' clothes at home is usually attended by utter failure. Happily, however, there are so many cheap and good suits to be obtained that there is no need for mater-familias to worry concerning the expense of school outfits, and thoroughly well-made and serviceable suits of every description, a par- ticularly pretty one buing a neat sailor suit of blue and white serge or washing, cotton. A new short mantle I saw recently was of green' velvet, striped with jet galon —that le, the galon was laid on, the velvet giving the striped effect. It had no sleeves, but merely side openings, through which the arms passed, these elite being hidden by long loose ends of black satin ribbon. It was cut with a thick ruched collar, which stood out from the neck like an old-fashioned ruffle, and was lined with green shot silk. Bengaline silk was used for a new vimite, which fitted the figure, and there were deep epaulette capes of guipure falling over the shoulders, and long, stole like ends of silk.
Yours very sincerely, '.. JENNIE.

An Apple Salad. For the basis use solid tart apples, pared and cut into small bits. With this mix an equal quantity of celery, out in nits of the same size. After thoroughly mixing, dress them in the salad bowl with a simple mayonnaise made as follows : luto the yoke of one egz, previously beaten, drop a, sufficient quantity of salad oil, slowly making a thick cream, which should then be thinned to the proper consistency by vinegar, added as carefully. Add pepper and salt to taste, and the mayonnaise is ready to dress the salad.

Pearl Barley Pudding. Put i lb. pearl barley into 3 pints of water and boil gently f,r two hours ; add half teaspoonful of salt and 3 tablespoonfuls of sugar, and pour it into a 'pie dish. Pare and cut up two large apples, stir these into the pudding, and bake for an hour. Serve with sweet sauce —Another recipe :—Soak two ounces pearl barley in cold water for twelve hours, then drain the water away; put the barley into a pudding dish ; mix 5 ounces sugar with it, then one quart of milk ; sprinkle a little nut.

div.head: BOTTLEMAKERS' STRIKE.
div.p: THE BOTTLEMAKERS' STRIKE.
LOSS OF .£25,000 IN WAGES. NO COMPROMISE IN ST. HELENS.

Information was received in St. Helens 'on. Tues- day that the conference between the Yorkshire glass bottle manufacturers and representatives of the strike hands, at Wakefield, terminated without any terms being agreed upon, so that the dispute, in Yorkshire continues as before. This comes as a disappointment to St. Helens,. where about 600 bottle hands have entered upon the tenth week of the strike, and where hopes were entertained that if Yorkshire effected a settlement, Lancashire would immediately follow. We believe we are correct in stating that during the stoppage in St. Helens about £25,000 has been paid leAs in wages. The effect of this upon trade has been keenly felt. Bottle hands are a class of men who get " good money," and who spend it freely, and the reduction of, say, £20,000 among tradesmen is a most serious matter. In place of the 50s or COs a week, whole families are struggling to exist on lOs and 12s strike money, and this has reduced the exchequer of the Glass Bottle Makers' Trade Protection Association by something like £3,000. Meanwhile the foreigner is reaping a rich harvest, and the warehouses of the Lan- cashire manufacturers are being gradually but surely- , ; depleted. The Continental agents in Liverpool and IManchester are, it is said, doing a thriving business, land are supplying orders for bottles which ought to be , made in St. Helens. The foreign manufacturers are $o busy that orders must take their turn, and frequently there are considerable delays in delivery. Mr. William Ashall, one of the Lancashire delegates to the men's national cotaference, states that the Yorkshire manufacturers had offered the men either a 3s.reduction on the wages and nothing off overwork, or the 1892 wages with a reduction of 10 per cent. off overwork. A ballot was taken, and the votes counted at a meeting of the Yorkshire Emergency Committee. The result was that 1,400 voted against submitting to any of the mas- ters' proposals, and there were none in favour of submit- ting to a reduction on the 1892 irates. The national conference afterwards met, at wbich delegates from Yorkshire, Lancashire, Sunderland, Seaham Harbour, Glasgow, Bristol,Brierley Dill, and Dublin were present. Mr. Wheater (yorkshire) presided. The reports of the districts were received,and the Yorkshire representatives were instructed to demand the 1892 rates and conditions. At the meeting of masters' and men's representatives which followed, these proposals were submitted, with the result that nothing could be agreed upon The St. Helens men still appear determined to resist anY reduction, and a telegram was sent on Tuesday to the conference as Wakefield, stating that the Lancashire dis- trict would oubmit to no compromise. An appeal is to be issued for support. In it attentiol is called to the victory of the Dublin bottlemakers, an to the fact that Yorkshire and Lancashire are deter-' mined also to win. It is also stated that the Lancashiorne masters havo resorted to the importation of fore', bottles,3o,ooo gross of which have been shipped to Liv tr pool alone. In order to frustrate these designs, _lice- National Conference has decided to send delegates Continent and all the principal seaport towns in the United Kingdom,to get the moral and pecuniary support of all trades unionists. Seamen,firemen,dock laboure rs and all engaged in the transmission of these foreiga bottles are to be asked to retuse to handle them. to tsi

div.head: DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT RUNCORN.

About midnight on Friday last week, the manu- factory of the Highfield Tanning Co., Runcorn, was discovered to be on fire by a fiatman named Thomas Sheen, of 5 Lyon-st., as he was passing along the canal, and after he had aroused James Randall, who resided in a cottage forming a portion of the block of buildings, information was conveyed to the police station and the fire bell rang. With commend- able promptitude, the brigade in command of deputy- superintendent W. Wright was on the spot with the reel at 12.20 but unfortunately the water was shut off from the mains and the hydrants. As quickly as pos- sible the brigade returned for the fire engine and with some difficulty brought it to the scene of conflagration. By this time the fire had obtained a strong hold and the whole length of the building, between 70 and 80 yards. was in flames, and to prevent the destruction of the place was beyond the bounds of possibility. The fire- men therefore directed their attention to saving the ad- joining works of the Australian Alum Company, and in this they were successful. They were enabled to obtain a plentiful supply of water from the canal. There was also saved a considerable portion of the limehouse. About one o'clock Mr. R. Posnett, the manager, des- patched a messenger on one of Mr. Yarwood's horses for the Warrington Fire Brigade, which arrived at three o'clock an hour after receiving warning and did good service. The building being principally of wood and oil and other inflammable substances bone stored there, the flames occasionally reached a great height, and the heat was terfific. The brigades poured water on the ruins of the buildings until noon on Saturday, when the Warrington Brigade returned home, and the local fire- men, continued to play on the smouldering mass until night. The damage is estbnated at between £25,000 and £30,000. The stock included a large quantity of finished leather as well as between 30,000 and 40,000 hides in course of preparation; the former was totally destroyed and the latter were much damaged. The books, which were In one of Milner'ssafes, were found to be uninjured. Mr. Randall's furniture valued at £5O was totally destroyed, and the joiners at the works have lost their tools. The destruction of the tannery throws eighty 'nen out of employment, but the directors Messrs. Parker, Walker and Seige, have decided that the pre- mises shall be reconstructed as speedily as possible. The damage is to a great extent covered by insurance.

ACCOUNTS IN HALFPENNY WRAPPERS.

A tradesman has issued the following circular : " Gentlemen—Please notice that next time you send me any invoice or statement of accounts whatever under halfpenny envelopes, my account will he at once closed, as I consider our country post-office officials know quite enough of trade matters without this free education,and to say the least of it, I consider it a cheese-paring way of transacting business, and if a client's account is not worth A penny stamp, its not worth retaining."
HOW OLD SOLDIERS FARE ON THE CONTINENT.

4 Parliamentary paper has just been issued describing what is done by the European Powers to provide for the employment of discharged soldiers. In Austria- Hungary nearly 60,000 Government posts are avail- able for old soldiers. In France 500 descriptions of appointments are reserved for retired sub-officers. In Germany 92,345 places under Government are reserved for soldiers who have served twelve years with a good character. Moreover, a well-conducted soldier or sailor who passes into the reserve after three years' service is always sure to obtain employment, and it is a common thing to read in advertisements for men, "Must have been a soldier." In the Italian War Office and Admiralty all the available posts, in number 2,602, are exclusively reserved for soldiers and sailors. In other public Offices 4,645, or one-half of the available appointments, are reserved for soldiers and sailors, and on the railways 1,700, or one-third of the available posts. a EDUCATION AT ASIITON-IN- MAKERFIELD.

FREE PLACES TO BE PROVIDED. From an answer given by the Vice-President of the Council in the House of Commons on Thursday evening, the Education Department intends to use its power to provide means of free education in the Ashton-in-Maker- field district. Mr. Woods complained that a child who had not brought the fee had been refused admission to St. Luke's Mission School, Stubshaw Cross. Mr. Acland explained that this schcol retained the right of charging fees underthe Act of 1891, and the managers had acted within their right. The child's parent now for the first time made application to the Department for free educa- tion for her, and the Department would at once proceed to take steps prescribed by the Act to provide a free place for her. Until, however, such free place was pro- vided, the parent was still obliged to send the child to school and to pay the fee.

div.head: MR. BRITNNER, M,P., AND THE HOME
div.p: MR. BRITNNER, M,P., AND THE HOME
IIILE BILL.
A SMART REPLY TO PRIMROSE DAMES.

The Primrose League habitations comprised in the Northwich Parliamentary Division recently forwarded a resolution to Mr. Brunner recording their strong con- demnation of the Home Rule Bill, and" the subjugation of the propertied and industrial minority to the majority guided by agitators and unscrupulous leaders." To this Mr. Brunner has forwarded the following reply to Miss A. i"). Turner, hon. secretary of the Northwich Divi- sional Council Primrose League, through his private secretary lam desired by Mr. Brunner to acknow• ledge the receipt of the resolution you have forwarded him from the Northwich Divisional Council of the Prim- rose League, setting forward inter alia the danger of civil war following the passing of the Home Rule Bill. Mr. Brunner condemns and deplores, as must all Loyal- ists, the actions of agitators and Anarchists, academic or otherwise' who would endeavour to dissuade the people of Ireland from loyal submission to the law."

div.head: DOW4-ER DU-CHESS'S CONTEMPT.
div.p: THE DOW4-ER DU-CHESS'S CONTEMPT.

ILLNESS OF HER GRACE. INTERESTING BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCH. A Windsor correspondent telegraphed on Thursday that her Grace the Dowager Duchess of Sutherland still keeps her bed and cannot be moved consequently she was unable to surrender for arrest on Thursday having been ordered to prison for six weekit for contempt of court.

THE DOWAGER DUCHESS'S CAREER. Just thirty years ago the Prince of Wales took the honorary degree of D.C.L. at Oxford. Mr. Disraeli, wh.4 was already for years D.C.L., was present, and dur- ing his visit stayed at St. Giles's, at the house of the Public Orator, the Rev. Richard Mitchell, afterwards Principal of Hertford College, who was the father of the Duchess Dowager, then a striking-looking girl, of whom the statesman took much notice, and whose brothers were as distinguished in athletics as they were in the schools. In course of time Miss Mitchell married a Captain Blair, and the marriage was as happy as that of most people, until the captain took to the cup that cheers and inebriates. The Duke of Sutherland, a married man with a charming wife (herself Countess 0 Cromartie in her own right) and a grown-up family—one of whom married Mr. Henry Chaplin, after having given hopes to the Marquis of Hastings—met Mrs. Blair, and became fascinated with her. In consequence of what came to his ears, truly or falsely, Captain Blair blew out his brains, and soon after his widow accompanied the duke to the far East in a long voyage, during which the lady declined at one port to receive some of tfte duke's friends, gentlemen well-known in society, was herself not recognised at any port till Siam was reaaied, and at Bangkok a palace was put at his grace's disposal. Here she dismissed the young doctor who had been engaged by the duke, and who haa to bring an action before he could recover, the money due to him. Soon after the duke's return, accompanied by Mrs. Blair, to England, the duchess died in November, 1888, and then the pair were married in Florida, four- teen weeks after the first wife's death. On their re- appearance in England some of the old retainers left the ducal service, and the farmers near Dunrobin Castle got into the black books of his grace because their wives would not recognise the new duchess. His grace died on September 22 last, leaving all that he could possibly control to his widow and her daughter by her first husband.

THE EX
I WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, for the official year, was held on Wed— nesday morning at the Town Hall. There were present Messrs. R. Heaton, Ryland, W. Gill, Muir, J. Houghton, Clarke, Turton, Aukland, Ratcliffe, A. J. Jolley, Davies, Fairclough, Smith, Dobson, Swin. ton, Owen, W. Houghton, Hibbert, Hill, A. Jolley, Mather, Pilling, Dignum, Balharry, Shaw, Langton, Kilshaw, Dr. Patterson, Rey. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. El. Ward (master), and H. M. Mines (superintendent of Padiate schools).• APPOINTMENT OP CHAIRMAN. The CLERK was voted to the chair pro tern ; the first business tieing the election of a chairman for the ensuing year.—Mr.R.HEAToR had great pleasure in proposing Mr., Wm .Houghton as chairman .Mr. Houghton was wellkno wn he thought, and the motion required no recommenda- tion from him. Every member could not but be aware of the very able manner in which Mr. Houghton had dis- charged his duties as guardian.—Mr. A. J. JOLLEY seconded the motion.—Mr. Dobson proposed as an amendment the election of Mr. George Ratcliffe.—M.. James HILL seconded the amendment, and said that Mr. Ratcliffe had been chairman of the House Committee during the past year, and he had made a capital chair- man. He thought that Mr. Ratcliffe was unfairly dealt with last year. He had been vice-chairman for two years and he ought therefore to be promoted to the Chairman this year. He respected Mr. Houghton but at the same time.he thought Mr. Ratcliffe bad the prior claim to the office. (Hear, hear.)—On a vote being , taken Mr. Ratcliffe was elected by 13 votes to eight for Mr. Houghton.
VICE-CHAIRMEN. After a considerable amount of discussion, Mr. R. Heaton was elected senior vice:chairman, and Mr. Wm. Houghton junior vice-chairman. COMMITTEES. _

The memberS of the various committees were all re- elected with the exception of four on the Asylums visiting committee. Messrs. Beaton, W.Houghten' Ratcliffe and Shaw gave way for members who had not yet visited any of the Asylums. The chairman and vice-chairman weie appointed, with the clerk, representatives of the Board at Poor Law Conferences. _

- ATTENDANCE OF MEMBERS. The following list of the attendances of members was submitted. The first figures are for Board meetings and the second for the Committee meetings :-Fair• dough 17, 7; Humphries 11, 12; Smith 21, 35; Balharry 23, 19; Turton 20, 33; Swinton 5, 23; A. Jolley 26, 89; Pilling 26, 64; Clarke 22, 49; Hibbert 12, 39; Ratcliffe 22, 01; Wright 5,3; Dr. Patterson 2,3; Dignum 17, 22; J. Eloughton 15, 36; Rev. G. F. Roberts 16, 17; Kilshaw 3, 5 ; Owen 7,6; Warburton 3,1; Mather 16, 4; William Houghton 26, 67; Aukland 21, 49; Davies 23, 57; Dob- son 15, 10; Gill 19, 3; Heaton 24, 32; Hill 22, 54; A. J. Jolley 25, 87; Longton 16, 22; Muir 22, 45; Shaw 25, 58. SCHOOL COMMITTEE. The children were reported to be generally healthy. The results of the examination of the schools at Padgate were to hand, and showed that 89 per cent. of the scholars had passed, and the inspector's report was generally favourable. At the last meeting of the Schools Committee a vote of thanks was passed to Mr. William Houghton for his services as chairman during the past year, and also to the superintendent and matron, Mr. and Mrs. Mines for their services, and their courtesy to the Committee during the year. The minutes were passed unanimously. House COMMITTEE. At the last meeting of this Committee votes of thanks were passed to Messrs. Ratcliffe and Davies for their iBervic2s as chairman and vice-chairman respectively Iduring the past year. CARE OF LUNATICS. On the question of the keeping of lunatics at asylums, Mr. DAVIES said that some of the lunatics charged on the Warrington Union might be brought back to the Work- house. He believed that with proper treatment they could take care of them, and room could be found for worse cases from the Union. He could never understand why harmless lunatics should be allowed to remain at the asylum at their expease.-Tke CLERK said that he was going to Rainhill in a few days, and would like the Board to nominate two members to accompany him to see if they could arrange to take away the harmless cases in exchange for others.-The Chairman and Mr. Davies were chosen, on the motion of MT. W.BOUGHTON. -Mr. PILLING moved that the lunatics te sent to the Workhouse, and that a nurse be got until the time of their removal.-Mr. Was. HououTois seconded. Mr. Devies, in supporting, said that the Board ought not to saddle the relieving officers with the responsibility of looking after lunatics. There ought to be some one, whose business it was to take charge of them.-The motion was carried.

CLERK'S REPORT. The anon, in giving his report for the past year, said that the Union had been very successful in its disputed cases for removal of paupers, and they had had only one case of litigation during the year. Only three paupers had become chargeable upon the Union from other Unions. The saving effected from the cost of mainten- ance of paupers and lunatics from which they had es- caped by these removals,would amount to almost £l,OOOl per year. They had also succeeded in getting all their lunatics in Rsinhill, and thus escaped the expense of private saylums.—Mr.A.J.Jozzny proposed,and Mr.Baz- HARRY seconded, a vote of thanks to the Clerk for his services VS the Union, and Mr.RATCLIFFE, in supporting, said that they were greatly indebted to the Clerk for his valuable services. He was the means of saving the Union thousands of pounds. The motion was passed unanimously, and the CLERK in replying, said that there was no Union of ita size which could show such results as the Warrington Union in the number of removals or recoveries. TEM HIRING OF CABS. Mr. A. JOLLEY caned attention to the way in which the cabs for Union purposes were hired, complaining that only two firms had supplied them. Mr. Ward pro- mised to consider the matter, and the proceedings of the Board terminated. SONG.

THE LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY. SIR GEORGE FINDLAY'S SUCCESSOR. The "Manchester Guardian" hears that an official announcement will shortly be made that Mr. Frederick Harrison has been appointed general manager of the London and North-Western Railway Company, in suc- cession to the late Sir George Findlay. Mr. Harrison has for a considerablo number of years held the post of assistant general manager, and has all through the lengthened and laborious inquiries into the question of railway rates and charges had the conducting of the case on the part of his company.
