THE P.S.A. AT WYCLIFFE.

On Sunday afternoon a large gathering of men assem- bled at the Pleasant Sunday afternoon meeting in Wycliffe Church. The movement seenas to have " caught on" in Warrington, as evidenced by the increased atten- dance at each meeting. The membership still goes up, nearly 500 members having been enrolled, and the pro- moters are in hopes of reaching 1,000. The services are kept up to the motto they were commenced with— Brief, Bright, Brotherly." The services commence punctually at three o'clock and conclude at four. The singing of hymns is heartily taken part in by the men, led by a good choir under the leadership of Mr. W. H. Wallington. The benevolent fund for the relief of the mgn who may be in needy circumstances, is largely con- tributed to. A temperance pledge book has been placed in the institute and some have already attached their names. A tea meeting has been arranged for Monday next when the chair will be taken by Mr. T. Morris, F.G.S. The speakers on Sunday were Mr, John Fair- dough, J.P. (chairman), and Mr. Booth (St. Helens). The chairman gave some excellent advice to those pre- sent. Mr. Boath considered tbe Christian churches had been too stiff and cold to the working-men, and had failed to reach as it ought, the masses of the people, and he considered the P.S.A. movement one that was wanted. Miss N. Picton was the soloist. The organ was presided over by Mr. W. H. Payton. MUSICAL, SERVICES AT ST. ANN'S.

In this church on Sunday special musical services were teld, with full orchestral accompaniments, by a band and choir of 50 conducted by Mr. Percy Randall. A solo was given by Miss B. Rigbey, a duet was also rendered by the Misses Taylor, and the "Gloria in Excelsis " waa given with very good effect by Miss A. Randall. The pulpit was occupied by the Rev. Morley Stevenson. There was a good congregation, and the collection was a satisfactory one. UNITARIANISM. At the Unitarian Chapel, Cairo-st.,on Sunday evening, the Rev. W. H. Drummond, pastor, delivered a sermon on "Our faith ; what it stands for." There was a very large congregation. Taking for his text "Good tidings of great joy," he said he was net fond of controversial sermons ; they seemed often to have so little food for the soul in them, and his sympathy with what was best in all the churches was too keen to make of him a good theological advocate. The Unitarians had no creed, for they had learned that the Word of God was too vast and the human conscience too sacred for any bond of that kind, but they had great truths committed to them as a holy trust, precious te them as the sacraments of his church to,the Catholic ; and though fidelity to them might not win for them popular applause, it was the only condition of their religion becoming a joy to them and a help to their brother man. When he cast his eye over the various forms of contemporary religious Would saw how some men were still trying to walk in the old narrow paths, and knew nothing of the strength and gladness which the great new thoughts of God and re- velation and progress were bringing into life ; when he saw others struggling with the fetters which the past had forged for them, drinking timidly at the new wells of inspiration, trying to twist the words of their ancient creeds into meaning things of which their authors never dreamed, and in their public Ksseinblies assuming that a common mantle of orthodoxy could be made to cover the rigid champions of a worn-out creed, and the men of the larger message and the fuller hope ; when he saw the crowds of men and women in the busy centres of population untouched by the current forms of Christian- ity, to whom a doctrine of the priesthood or sacramental grace or Biblical inspiration meant simply nothing, with souls all unfed because religion bad never seemed simple. I natural, human enough for them to care for it, then he felt anew the privilege and joy of speaking from that free pulpit, where there need be uo suspicion of compro- mise, no shuffling with words or pouring of new wine Into old wine skins, but a clear outspoken message con- cerning God and His love and the true nobleness of Christian living for thinking minds and hungry hearbs to-day. The keynote of th-6 Unitarian faith' was the belief in the spirituality of God. This was a truth which no Christian would ever think of denying, but it made a great deal of difference whether it was the one complete, satisfying .thought which embraced every other, or was held simply as one among many beliefs which only have a distant connection with it,and to their church it was in a sense the only truth, for it was the source from which all their affirmations sprang. To believe in the spirituality of God was to believe that he was ever present, ever living and ever revealing his love to the universe,that the human soul could come into his presence without a mediator or help of any natural symbol, tor God himself was nearer than anything else could be. It was to believe that they had the witness of his existence, his law, and his love to-day, as sorely as it was present with prophets and saints of old, and to rely no longer on miracles or ancient Bible records as the foundation of their trust. It was to believe in the adorable unity of God, not, as some opponents maintained, as a cheap mathematical formplat but as the highest thought they could have of him in harmony at once with the keenest demands of the intellect, and the deepest religious ex- perience. Their second distinctive principle was their attitude toward Christianity. It was said by same people that they were opponents of Christianity because they refused to subscribe to the deity of Jesus Christ, but there were signs that there was an awakening to the fact that to be a Christian was not to wear a party badge, but to possess a spirit of justice and purity to God and man, to be conformed to the likeness of Christ. They also believed in liberty to think on all subjects connected with religion and themselves, and not to be compelled by a sad necessity to employ words they did not quite believe, and to make mental reservation in the holiest acts of worship. THE REV. T. ROSS AND THE RECTOR.

On Sunday evening, at the Bold-st. Wesleyan Chapel, Warrington, before a large congregation, the Rev. T. Ross made a rejoinder to the Rector's " instruction" relative to the creed of the Wesleyan denomination. He ead they as Methodiets ob- jected strongly to the 'sacerdotal teaching that bad pervaded the whole series. The setting forth tf. doctrine as held by Nonconformists in many in- stances had been nothing more or less than a cari- cature, and they thought it was far more satisfac- tory to look into the teaching of Scripture than to pin their faith to what was said by the " Fathers "or even the " Holy Catholic Church." In connection with each deliverance the Rector had shown a kindly spirit,

and they failed to see how the instructions cOulct en: gender bitterness ; and yet they thought no satisfactory end would be attained. Sacrament i and ordinances had been so uplifted that the question as to where the Rector tended was no longer left an open one. In his last ad- dress on the "Holy Catholic Church," he said, with regard tl ritualistic practices, "I have endeavoured to lead the congregation on gently and quietly." Whither? and to what? He could answer these questions. Re was leading them gently and quietly—doubtless unwit- tingly—from St. Elphin's to St. Mary's; from the truth as it was in Jesus to Roman Catholicism. And yet the Rector concluded his series by saying "No one who is thoroughly instructed in the faith once for all delivered to the Saints could become a Romanist or a Nonconfor- mist." The only inference was that those who did leave the Anglican Church were not thorogighly in- strlicted in the faith. The Rector's misresenta.- dons as they affected Methodism would be dealt with in the May Issue of their own "Church Record." Mr. Ross also dealt With the subject of re- generation. On thia point there was no doubt as to what the Rector taught, and it was avowedly and definitely" Baptldinal regeneration." According to the Rector's teaching many of the vagabonds in England to-day having been baptised at church were regenerated men, which on the face of it bespoke ridiculousness. The Rector said "admission into the Holy Catholic Church is by baptism." So it might be into St. Elphin's, but baptism was not the way into the Kingdom of God. A present-day popular clergyman had said " We must guard against that mechanical view of baptism which I am sorry to say obtains in our own Church, and which has been ona great cause of spiritual death within our Church." Nicodemus thought the way to life was through the gate of knowledge. The Rector and many other High Church clergymen said the way to life was through the ordinances. The Rector said they grieved that Nonconformist ministers should administer the sacrament, but what should they say of so-cal Jed minis- ters of Christ. 011 !it was pitiful and sad that with the open Scriptures men should still listen to the Church and be thus deluded and in their turn delude others (vide 1 . _
Cor. ill. 11-16). Flow could this change be effected ? The only' answer was by the Holy Ghost. " Except a man be born of water and the spirit he cannot enter the Kingdom of God."
ACTION-FOR, FILSE IMP RISO N M ENT.
DAMAGES FOR A Si'. HELENS COLLIER.

At St. Helens Countir Court, on Wednesday, the action for false imprisonment and malicious pro- secution of Newton v. London and North-Western Railway Company was heard by his Honour Judge Shand. Mr. H. L. Riley (St. Helens) appeared for plaintiff, and Mr. F. M. Preston (instructed by Mr. Penne) defended. Mr. Riley said this was an action brought by a collier named Joseph Newton, residing at 41, Watery-lane, Sutton, St. Helens, against the London and North- Western Railway Company and a man named William John White, who was in the employ of the company as a sort of detective or officer specially charged with look- ing after the affairs of the company in detecting tres- passers, &c. On the 21st September last, plaintiff alleged that White, acting on behalf of the company, arrested him at Sutton Moss, and in so doing assaulted him, and afterwards falsely imprisoned him in a railway van. He was taken to Widnes and locked up in a cell for a night, and on the following morning was brought before a magistrate (Mr. John Burchall), and cherged with having unlawfully and wilfully obstructed White in the execution of his duty, and the case was dis- missed. The facts of the case were that on the 21st September, plaintiff had been working at the Bold Col- liery, and he, with several other men, was crossing Sutton Moss (which is a tract of land lying between St. Helens Junction Station and Collins Green) on his way home. The defendant White, accompanied by a county police officer was expecting to find some trespassers on the railway. Plaintiff and Pds friends passed the railway where the two officers were. One man, whom the plain- tiff did aot know, he believed jeered,laughed,or taunted the officials. The man undoubtedly thought that they had come to catch someone, and had not done it, and jeered at them in a good-humoured way. White seemed to have come to the conclusion that Newton was the man who had" booed "at him. He came off the line. and said to the plaintiff, " What are you shouting at ?" Plaintiff replied." We were not shouting." White then said, "I'll knock you up and down the Moss if you take me for a fool." Be then cot over the fence, and two I men named William and John Seddon ran away. To add to White's irritation, as he was getting over the fence he fell into some dirty water into the ditch. He then went to Newton and got hold of him by the nose, screwed it round and made it bleed. Newton was carry- ing a pick, and White took this off him and threatened to strike him with it. Newton was then handcuffed, and pulled through the fence on to the railway line. The officers stopped the first luggage train, and Newton was put into a van and taken to Sutton Oak. He was then transferred to a railway carriage, and taken to Widnes and locked up. This was done just as he was wringing wet through from his hard day's work in the coal pit, and reeardless of the question of personal con- venience. The news of his being locked up reached his home, and a solicitor was engaged for, when he was brought before the magistrates. Evidence in corroboration having been given, Mi. Preston called Detective William John White, who said that on the 21st September he was stationed as detective at St. Helene station. On that day he, in company with Con- stable Forster, went to Bold Heath to watch for tres- passers. There had been numerous complaints of trespassing between Bold signal-box and St. Helens Junction Station. They were walking along the Moss side of the railway, off the line. They had taken several names and addresses, and while getting on the line over the fence he distinctly saw Newton and several others getting on the line from the opposite side. As soon as they saw witness they turned back, walked along to the bridge, and crossed over by the bridge. When they were coming along witness was going towards them and plaintiff remarked, " Yes, there the are. If either of them comes near me, I'll push this pick through him." He did not say anything to them until he got ever the fence. The two Seddons then ran away, and there was only witness and Newton together. He asked him for his name and address, and he began to use bad language and refused. The Seddons were about fifty yards away and shouted, " Don't give him the name." Witness told him that he would have to have it, whereupon New- ton raised his pick, which was without a shaft, and struck at him. He put his left hand up, and received a severe blow. Witness closed in with Newton, who delib- erately pushed the point of the pick into the palm of his hand. Forster then asked for his name, but he again refuted, and White asked the constable to take him into custody. The handcuffs were put on him, and he was taken in a goods van to St. Helens Junction. At this point the fence had been broken down by trespassers previously, and was very low. No violence whatever was used in getting over the fence. Pollee Constable William Forster said plaintiff refused his name and address. There was no dragging through the fence. A signalman spoke to trespassing being very frequent on the line. Mr. Preston then addressed the jury. He would re- mind the jury that this case was brought by the Miners' Union, in order to try in some way to establish a right of way over this line ; but they must bear in mind that this was not a genuine case where a man was bringing the action himself of his own motive. He was supported ' by the union for some indirect motive not brought before them. _

Mr. Riley said it was a source of satisfaction to think that a poor man who was a member of the union was not left single-handed to light a great corporation like the London and North-Western Railway Company when they took the law into their own hands. The evidence was overwhelming that Newton had not on that day trespassed, and White had no reason to go to him. He hoped the jury would consider this was a case for exem- plary damages. His Honour pointed out that the onus of proving the false arrest, &c., lay upon the plaintiff, and if the jury had considerable doubt as to which story was the cor- rect one, it was their duty to find in favour of the defen- dants. The jury found a verdict for plaintiff, and awarded him £5 damages, costs to follow.

LONGEVITY.

A complimentary dinner has just been given by the Royal Meteorological Society to Mr. Henry ?algal, F.R.A.S., in celebration of his 92nd birthday and of the completion of 40 years service as treasurer. The Presi- dent (Dr. C. Theodore Williams), in proposing the toast of the evening, gave some interesting particulars of the Perigal family, tracing their history back to some time before the Norman Conquest, It appears that the family have been remarkable for longevity. Mr. Pen- gal's father who was 99± years of age when he died, was one of 13 children, nine of whom attained respectively, their 64th, 67th, 77th, 80th, 88th, 90th, 94th, 97th, and 100th year, the last five averages 93 years 100 days. Their' father and mother died in 1824, the former being nearly 90 and the latter upwards of 80 years of age. Mr. Henry Perigal was the eldest sf six children,one of whem lived , to th% age of 85.; and the youngest,Mr.Frederick Perigal, now in his 82nd year, was present at the dinner. Mr.' ! Perigal briefly responded to the tnast,thanking the com- pany for their congratulations and kind wishes. r!

HOURS QUESTION.
DEPUTATION TO MR. GLADSTONE.

A deput;lio-n-rsentir-tg-t-1;11-1-iie-r-s'-i;tional Union of Northumberland and Durham waited upon Mr. Glad- stone on Wednesday to lay before him their views respecting the Eight Hours Bill. Mr, John Wilson, M.P.. ,and others stated that they represented the majority of the miners in the Union, and they were against State interference with the hours of adult labour. Working time had already been materially shortened by trade union effort and by arrangement between employers and employed, and they thought they were able in themselves to secure whatever other cdncessions might be reasonable in the matter. In the course of his reply Mr. Gladstone expressed satisfaction ac the arrange- ments which the men represented by the deputation had been able to make by agreement with their employers, for he confessed that he regarded that method of settl- ing differences as the normal one. After asking ques- tions as to the means taken in districts other than Durham and Northumberland to ascertain the extent of the difference of opinion existing amohg miners as to the desirability of an eight-hour day, Mr. Gladstone went on to say, in dealing with the case of those who were favourable to the measure, that there were some admissions to be made. There was first the admission that eight hours underground was long enough for any human being to work, and then they could evi- dently allege a very large amount of miners' opinion on their side. Supposing,he asked, an Eight Hours Bill had to be dealt with, aid the deputation think their district would desire or think it practicable to be exempted from it? If what they called local option could be made ap- plicableto different mining districts, it might be a solu- tion of some of the difficulties of the case. Mr. Wilson remarked that the matter had not been considered in that aspect, and added that he thought Northumberland and Durham would favourably consider a proposal of the kind. Mr. Gladstone further said it was conceivable that different bodies of miners might find it expedient to give some consideration to that question. At present they were at a deadlock. Parliament would, he was sure, endeavour to deal with the difficulties of these cases honestly, and, though it might not be able to solve them all, would treat the matter in a spirit which would , meet with approval.

div.head: -AN EXPRESSION OF REGREt.
div.p: -AN EXPRESSION OF REGREt.

A national conference of Scottish miners' representa- tives was held on Thursday,in Glasgow,Mr. R. C.Robert- ion presiding. It was reported that in several districts trade had slightly improved. In all the districts the men were in favour of the reorganization of Scotland. Mr. Weir (Fifeshire) drew attention to the statement made by Mr. Gladstone on Wednesday to the deputation who waited upon him from Durham and Nr4rthumberland re- lative to the Eight flours Bill for miners. Many delegates expressed the feeling that the position of affairs was either ignored by or withheld from Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Robert Smellie (Lsrkhall) moved, and Mr. Robertson seconded:—

"That this conference observes -with regret :the un- founded and incorrect statements made by Mr. Glad- stone regarding the attitue.e of the Scottish miners to the Eight Hours Bill, more espeeially as by statement, ballot, and petitions to the House.of Commons 99 per cent of the miners of this country declared in favour of the principle of the pill." _ .
- Copies of the resolution are to be sent to tar. Gladstone and the members of the Cabinet.

:At the Executive Committee meeting of the Miners' Federation of Great Britain at Bristol yesterday, 'a reso- lution was adopted expressing regret at the position taken up on Wednesday by the Premier re,!ardieg adult labour, minorities, local option, and the eight hours question. The meeting declared that ibe Premier had taken sides with the minority against the majority, and was likely to oppose the Eight Hours Bill. The meeting also passed a vote of condolence with the sufferers by the Pontypridd disaster, and decided to urge the Dean Forest miners to resist a reduction of wages.

div.head: OVER. THE ATLANTIU.
div.p: OVER. THE ATLANTIU.
BY MIL W. H. BUTLER.

" Alt aboard ?" " All aboard sir !" "Ship the gangway." In obedience to the captain's order the gangway was speedily hauled in, the sails as quickly adjusted, and at 3.10 p.m. Thursday, the 26th of January, the "Catalonia " began to move very slowly and cautiously out of Alexandria Dock. The ' branch dock in which we lay was crowded with vessels of different sizes; and it was no easy matter to prevent the apparently certain pulveris- ation of sundry coal barges against the granite walls. However, by dint of much skill on the vessel, and quite as much off, the passage on the whole was at last safely accomplished. But the clocks of the city were striking five before we found ourselves in the river with our faces turned in expectation towards the setting sun. And a beautiful sunset it was. Such a mingling and har- monizing of soft and gracefnl tints at once the despair of the artist and the delight of the simple lover of nature. Lovely ground tones of faint fawn and yet fainter green ; deep orange bands with crimson fringes. Above the darker colours of the night.. Below, the tremulous movement ot the water—the wild waters—touched into magnifi- cence by the far-off glory. Our first evening aboard was spent pleasantly enough. A fine moonlight night; and we—my wife and myself along with Mrs. Murphy—seated right aft over the propeller watching the lights of the old country as one by one they were left behind. The water was quite calm and the future held no terror for us. At nine o'clock we went below and having partaken of a little Supper—biscuit, cheese, and tea—returned to our room. It was situated nearly amidships ; contained two sleeping berths, and a lounge, carpeted throughout and well fitted with all necessary adjuncts, including electric light and steam for warming. I noticed with satisfac- tion that we were quite near a large ventilator. Un- doubtedly it was one of the best rooms on the boat. • Friday, January 27th. Fine morning. Rose 7.15 ; on deck for a short time and then to breakfast—tea anti steak. On deck all morning, had a conversation with the chief engineer, Mr. Jas. Stewart—a kindly hearted Scotchman. Wrote postcard home and gave them to Mr. Gore the pilot to post them when put asbore at Queenstown. We reached this famous Irish port at 1.15 p.m. The Cunard tender came alongside with mail passengers—chiefly steerage—and fresh 'provisions, and- in forty minutes we were under steam again. Roche's Point was passed at 2.15 p.m., then came the Fastnet and after that the mighty, broad, heaving Atlantic. The breeze freshened considerably and soon the vessel began to roll heavily; this with a pretty constant pitching simply turned us inside out. Neither tea nor slipper were required, the remainder of the day being spent in a very unpleasant frame of mind. Confined to our room we were at full liberty to meditate on the frailty of man and the pitilessness of Nature. Run for the day 223 miles. _ _ _ _

..... __. Saturday, January 28th: Still unwell. Very little food. No reading. How remorseless the elements ! They seem to be determined to shake every atom of nourishment eut of one. Rolling from port to starboard pitching from stens to stern ;no rest, no ease. Run for ,he day 258 miles. Sunday, January 29th: The ex- periences of to-day similar to yesterday's. Little or nothing to eat. Weather worse if anything. No divine service to-day. Mrs. Butler and myself had the church service together in the evening. We passed a Wilson Liner this morning' bound from London to New York. Restless night. Everything on legs in our room and moving about all night. Run per day 226. Monday, January 30 : Weather still very bad. Dreadfully unpleasant day. Run 210 miles. Tuesday, January 31 :—Weather still dreadful. No solid nourishment at all. On deck fora short interval. No reading. No writing. Subject of profound medita- tion—The helplessness and extreme insignificance of man. Run to-day-252. Wednesday, February Ist: No improvement in the weather nor in us for that matter. Living on soup. Shall be thoroughly glad when we set foot again on land. Run fee day-182. Thursday, February"2nd : Weather just as bad as ever. Rose at seven o'clock, both feeling slightly better. Had a little food brought Into our cabin. The order of the day is :—Breakfast 7.30 and 8 o'clock; dinner 12 and 12.30; tea 5 and 5.30 p.m.; supper 8 p.m. to 9 p.m. The " Servia " which left Liverpool on Saturday last. passed us at 11 o'clock this morning pitching heavily. The crew of the "Catalonia " pitied the people aboard of her ; they say that the "Catalonia" is the best sea-going boat in the Cunard fleet. Run for the day-195 miles. Friday, February 3rd: Weather as before, but we are on the improve. Long chat with Mr. Stewart this morn- ing. Am coming to myself again, being much in- 1 terested in the changing temperature of the sea water.' The temperature of the Mersey on the day we left web - F 434; it has already poised thrOugh the following gra- dations :—F 45, 47,50, 52, 534, 52, 54, 58, 50, 44. The water increased in temperature the first eight days out, and then fell very considerably and will continue so to do until Boston is reached. It better tune for eating to-day. Run for the day-195 miles. Saturday, Feb. 4th : Nothing special to-day. The weather is worse than ever. Run for the day-182 miles. Sunday, Feb. 4th: Rose 7.30. The for'ard part of the ship is covered with ice and the.wind very cold. To divine service in the saloon, the prayers being read by the captain. After the name of the Queen came His Excellence the Presi- dent of the United States. Enjoyed the service very much. Quiet day. We are becoming accustomed to the motion of the vessel. I have analysed the effects of its motions and with the following result :—Rolling, that is movement of the vessel from port to starboard, effects mostly the stomach. Pitching or movement from stem to stern effects the head. The quicker the boat and other things being equal the more she pitches. I found that lying with my feet in the direction the vessel was going was the only way of overcoming those unpleasant sensations. Run for the day-183 miles. Monday, February Eth : Much ice for'ard. On deck a good deal to-day. Nothing else of importance to-day. Run for the day-216 miles. Tuesday, February 7th: BO vft'ether again. Au alteration in the colour of the 1 ocean is now noticeable. Run for the day-258 miles. Wednesday, February Bth: Weather better. Expect a rod run. Very cold for'ard, six degrees below freezing, e-lth icicles hanging from the rigging, and the decks coveret.4 With frozen water. A groat shout about 6.30 p.m. heraldeel the appearatMe of No. 7 pilet boat on the horizon. AnclioNl off kostoe Light at 10.30 p.m. Everybody packing till and in a State of wildest excite- ment.y Oth i Land on both sides of Thursday, Fe bruil* A us—a most pleasant sight. At eight o'clock the U.S. C doctor came aboard. The U.S. , ommissioner also came aboard sli.,rtly afterwards and cros's-examined everyone as to ways and means. He asked me Whether I could read and write. About 9.30 the Catalonia 7 Managed to dock. But what a dock! A little narrow pass-,ege down which the Catalonia was pushed by three tue'beats. Received letter from Rev. Joseph Ellison inviting us- to rest a few days at his house. The luggage was soon ouf and quite as soon through the custom's. I then gave it over to a transfer agent, with instructions to forward at once to the Boston and Albany R. IL Depot. (A railway station is always called a depot here). We were now free and on land again with splendid health and in good spirits. The first thing I did after forwarding a telegram to Mr. Ellison was to enter a hairdresser's establishment. Hair cut and shave cost me forty cents (1 eent-1 halfpenny). We then tool: the East Boston ferry over to the city, and having entered an electric car presently found ourselves at the Boston and Albany Depot. Greendale where Mr. Ellison resides is about three miles out of Wercester, and this latter city is forty miles from Boston. The Worcester train left-at one o'clock, and the fare was a dollar each. We arrived about three o'clock, and were delighted to see the smil- ing face of our friend Mr. Ellison. " Never mind your baggage." said he, " you have the check, I presume." I answered in the affirmative. " Well come along then, no occasion for you to look after your baggage in this country. They have a splendid baggage system !" We left Mrs. Butler in the waiting room, and together we strolled round the city, he pointing out to me, with evident pride, the points of interest. We returned in time for the 3-50 Greendale train, and in a few minutes found ourselves at the beautifully situ- ated New England village. It did not take us long to arrive at the Manse which was an elegantly built wooden detached villa. We were quite charmed with it. And it was as nice inside as it was outside. Mrs. Elli- son—Mr. H. Whitham's daughter—welcomed us very warmly and EIViVB had not tasted since hreakfast,quickly made tea for us. The American meals, at any rate in this district, are breakfast, dinner, and supper, the last- named meal taking place from six to seven o'clock. In the evening there was a supper 00 10 connection with Mr. Ellisoe's Church, and we were favoured with an invite. They do not as a rule buy things for their tea meetings, and social affair; here. The ladies make pies and tarts,and ell manner of high class eatables, apd give them for the purpose. A paper serviette—quite a work of art—was given to each person. We spent a very pleasant evening, ending our way home about ten o'clock. On Friday I went to Boston. and was there all day. On Saturday I was taken by Mr. Ellisen and a friend, over the chemical laboratories of an immense and splen- didly fitted up Technical Institute in the City of Worces- ter. From the roofs magnificent view of the surround- ing country was obtained. Sunday, my first Sunday in America, preached from Mr. Ellison's pulpit from the words" And when he came to himself." Mr. H. Whitham and family present. Mr. wialiam, Mr. Ellison, and myself had a walk over the hills. During the afternoon we discussed several matters one of which Mr. Whitham mentions (" Examiner " just to hand). . From my diary I find that the chief sub- ject ol our conversation was" the populatiorequeetion— ire its more American aspect." I Kind remembrances to all my friends. . , ' 296, Plainfield-st., Olneyville, R.I. ,

CURIOUS LOTION BY AN AUDITOR.

lata THE POWER OF DIRECTORS. .At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before Judge Shand, James M. Idle, of Ormskirk, sued the Mill-lane Mining Company, Rainford, for .£5 for services rendered as auditor. The plaintiff conducted his own case, and Mr. Thoinas defended. From the evidence it appeared that the plaintiff had been auditor to the defendant company for 14 years, and at the general meeting of shareholders in February 1892, he was again re-elected. In November 1892, he was convicted for drunkenness and assault on the police and sentenced to six week's im- prlsonment. At a meeting of the directors the appoint- ment was revoked, the directors considering he was not a fit and proper person to Wit the books. The plaintiff contended that he was appointed at a meeting of share- holders, and a meeting of shareholders would have to be called before the appoittment was revoked —His Honor said that after a person was convicted he could easily understand that he was not worthy to act, but it would be a very wrong thing for a company at a general meet- ing appointed certain persons to particular offices and , then for the directors to revoke the anpointmen% He did not see that the directors had power to dismiis an auditor who had been appointed at a gem:rat meeting Without calling a special general meeting of the share- holders.—Mr. Thomas : That was not done —His - Honour, continuing, said the directors were acting bona-fide and perfectly tight, but he did net think he had power to do it. Thera would be judgmmt fir the plaintiff.

div.head: IIT.PERI2L PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IIT.PERI2L PARLIAMENT.
MONDAY.

In the House of Commons on Monday the Lord Mayor and City Council of Dublin presented at the bar a peti- tion in favour of Horne .Rule. Sir E. Grey informed Mr. F. Stevenson that the Sultan had granted a general amnesty to the Armenians who in various parts of Asia Miter hal been sospected of bAng concerned in the post- ing of seditious placards. Mr. BURNS moved the adjournment of the House for the purpose,of calliig attentitm to the alieged partial conduct of the Hull Board of Guardians in connection with the labour dispute. Mr. ,FOWLER read telegrams which he had received from the Guardians to the effect that they were of opinion that if the men declined to accept work it would not be right to maintain them at the expense of the ratepayers. l'he right lion. .gentle- man said that if there was any infringmenc of the fair position of neutrality in a dispute of this kind and the Local Government Board had the power to interfere they would do so. The motion was by leave with- drawn.
Mr. MUNDELL/I brought in a biL to make provision for the establishment of boards of coneilisti,n and arbitration for labour disputes. The bill was read a first tine.

Tie debate en the Home Rule Rill was resumed by Mr. Gnschen, who spoke at some length on the financial proposals of the measure, and complained that the land question had "eeen loft untouched. Mr. RaTanoNE spoke in support of the Bill and Mr. FORWOOD againrit it. The debate was adjourned on the motion of Lord R. Churchill.
Just before the House adjourned at midnight Sir J. Whitehead obtained leave to bring in a bill on the sub- ject of railway rates and charges, and it was read a first time.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

In the House of Commons, on Tuesday, 'Mr.llryce was further questioned respecting his action in the matter of the Lancashire county magistricy,and Mr.Maclure gave notice that be should take an early ruportunity of cal- ling the attention of the House to the subject. The debate on the Home Rule Bill was resumed by Lord It. Canaciimi, who said that nobody was readier than himself to give the largest local liberties to the Irish people; but between his position on Irish local govern- ment and his position in regard to the proposal to create a powerful and independent Parliament a gulf was fixed which he could never cross. Great Britain on this issue could not give way from the sheer instinct of self-pre- servation. Mr. J. MORLEY addressed the House at a later stage. Referring to references which had been made during the debate to public opinion in the great centres of trade, he said there was no county in which there had been such a growth of feeling in favour of Home Rule since 1858 as there had been in Lancashire which had shown its belief that peace and contentment lay in the conciliation of Ireland. The debate was ad- journed at midnight. WEDNESDAY.

In the House of Commons on %Waneslay Dr. Rstr- Ton resumed the debate on the motion for the second reading of the Home Rule Bill. Mr. JOHN LENG spoke strongly in favour of the retention of the Irish members Mr. W. SeuNDERS could not support the Bill, contending that a property qualification in connection with Home Rule was an anachronism. Mr. H. C. PLUNKETT opposed the bill. Mr. J. BENNETT warmly supported it, remark- ing that the measure meant not only benefit to Ireland but justice to English villages. Mr. W. L. JACKSON ex- pressed the opinion that the ( ffect of the bill would be to increase the friction in every department of Govern- ment. He sometimes thought one of the best things that could happen for Ireland would be the filling up of the Irish Channel, for much of the past difficulty had been clue to the country's isolation, On tbe motion of Mr. SEXTON the debate was adjourned.

The right hon. gentleman assured Mr. 1. The debate on the motion for the second reading of the Home Rule gilf was resumed by Mr. Sexton, who declared that if Protestants were allowed to speak out the Nationalists wouid show a great majority of Ulster in favour of the bill. Saa long as most momentuous ques- tions were reserved to the Imperial Parliament, he asked that the present power of Ireland in that Parliament should remain undiminishoc.i: Mr. CARSON and Colonel SAUNDErZSON spoke in opposition to the bill. The debate was again adjourned. •

div.head: HOW ANTI-HOME RILE PETITIONS ARE GOT UP.
div.p: HOW ANTI-HOME RILE PETITIONS ARE GOT UP.
SINGULAR STATEMENTS.

In the House of Commons, on Thursday Mr. M'Lagan, as Chairman of the Committee On Petitions, informed Mr. Loder that up to and including Wednesday the total number of petitions in favour of the Home le Bill was 15, and the numtier of signatures 3l.—(Laughter.) The number against the measure was 1,861, with 533,700 signatures.—(Opposition cheers.) Mr. Dalziel asked whether the Committee on Petitions were aware that the following communication had beeta sent to the hotel keepers : " Dear Sir,—The Conservative Association are very anxious to have as many sheets of petitions against Home Rule as pozsible. (Ironical cheers.) Will yott help us by signing and getting anyone in the hotel—man, woman, boy, or. girl—b do the same—(derisive laughter)—and return the signed sheets? Your visi- tors in Easter week should be able to fill up several sheets (Laughter.) It makes net difference if such sheets have been signed before.' (Laughter.) The cir- cular, he added, was dated March 28th, 18.93, and signed by Thomas Holland, Mount Epnraim House, Tun- bridge Wells, local Conservative secretary. (Ministerial cheers.)
Mr. Flynn remarked that p titions against Rome Rule had been signed in the names of children in arms. (Laughter.)

Mr. Pemberton added that children in pohlic schools in Ireland had been forced to sign such pAtitions. Could he give information on the subject? kCheers.) The Speaker: If the hon. tnemb4r wilt supplY that information to the Committee they will no doubt investi- gate it to the utmost. (Hear, hear.)

'l7°les to two, to dismiss Mr. and Mrs. ROACH from their service for endeavouring to se- eu e a proper supply of wholesome water for the achools. The Education Department has very rightly branded this outrageous conduct of the Arlington School Board as "improper and unjusti- fiable." The misfortune is, however, so far as the dismissed teachers are concerned, that tho Educ- ation Department has no power to interfere

with the discretion of a School Board in a -matter of this kind. It is in the high- 'st degree desirable that schoolmasters—and for the matter of that all public officers—should be protected from capricious tyranny of this discrip- tion, and the case will, doubtless, strengthen the a...;itation for the establishment of a judicial Court &Ppeal for such dismissals, which are said to be far from iLfrequent.

A sentence of six weeks imprison- 42slIteern- I;t. ment passed upon a DOWAGER DUCHESS—to say nothing of a fine .of £250--is a novelty in the anna's of English law courts. It is enough to make some of the adieners of the "good old times" and the liphtlders of the privileges of our old nobility declare that the country is "going to the dogs. It inost be admitted, however, that if any tesPect is te be paid to courts of law the I)„l3lvAanit DUCHESS OF SUTHERLAND, who 7t'Peara to be of the " arbitrary " type of human- ity, richly deserves her punishment. Her offence was a peculiarly gross kind of "contempt of c aut. The widest publicity has lately been given to the afairad cuttyhat litigation is pending, or, rather, has been entered upon, between the DOWAGER IDRUCHESS and her step-son the present DUKE of iturnizatsaNn. In preparation for this litigation a ge number of documents of the late DUKE have been taken charge of by the legal authorities. The DUCHESS made a special application to the Probate Court to be allowed to see some of these documents and that application was granted as a , favour. The object in view was to select from the Ina" Of Papers certain missives which might be bmitted to both parties to the suit, and iI, they both agreed that the contents were a private nature and not material to the Inattela in dispute these missives were to be with- drawn from the case. In duo course the docu- ments weie unfolded before the Dueness in the Prestnce of certain legal gentlemen. Whilst the lesla•ction was being made the DUCHESS, it is said, 4`,3llberately selected one paper and, before any- ne could interfere, she placed it in the fire where it was burnt. This was an incident which could of course, be overlooked,not even for the sake v4i DowAGER DUCHESS. It is true be afterwards ssi)r°f,essed penitence, and promised to be entirely 174'141 as to the contents of the document which "d been irretrievably destroyed. But this was good enough for the Probate Court nor for th'-no other party to the suit. The DUCTLESS'S story at til° Paper was only a letter containing an ac- count Of tin " unpleasant occurrence" between a stea. ard iWid a maid which bad happened during a quituetit9g excu:sion of the late DUKE, might be s ; but then, on the other hand, it might -;.rsise;)teertue at all' or only partially true, and the might, as a matter of fact, have had a vseir3cal,e'Por tint bearing on tho case. At all events it4NCIS sala JEURE, the presiding judge, was not p,iss the incident over lightly, and he te,:7'egunt bernmiLtedly ordered that the DOWAGER DUCHESS eioBurttEaskED must pay a fine of £250 and be to prison for six weeks. There must snillething distressing in all this to those good People who think that Dukes and Duchesses should be treated like ordinary mortals, but after an it case is not so bad from their point of view t might seem. The JUDGE was almost apologe- tic n giving his sentence, and the DUCHESS was not hauled off to gaol wit h the little ceremony that would have been observed if she bad been, say, a washerwoman. In fact she was not hauled off, to gaol at all, for we are told that she afterwards drove away from the Law Courts in her carriage, accompanied by her solicitor. The DucnEss had listaased her word that sho would surrender—when suited her, we suppose—and therefore the ser- vwi.ces of t um ial court officials had been dispensed The latest news is that the DOWAGER ""lIES3B S tOO ill "to be removed" to goal.

--- - - - PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAZAAR AT WIDNES. This bazaar, held in La eey-st. School last week, rea- lised a total amount of £7O. When in want of a chaate and elegant wedding or birthday present go to PRITCRARD'S. 51, Itighast.—Adrt. VOLUNTEER CHURCH PARADE AT RUNCORN. The annual church parade of the Runcorn co.npanies took place on Sunday, when 60 non-commissioned officers and men under the command of Captain D. Ashton marched to the Parish Church. The other officers present were Captain U. F. Ashton and Lieut. Speakman. The Rev. Canon preached the sermon. If yen want stocky wedding ring go to 51, Rran-sr.,wkoro you will gets present with it.—Advt.

RUNCORN AND DISTRICT TEACHERS' ASSOCIATION. The members of this association have resolved to be- come affiliated to toe Cheshire District Union of Teachers and that the president and vice-president represent the association on the executive committee. The amount raiscd by the members in aid of the National Union of Teachers' Benevolent and Orphanage funds is £5 13s. Greater efforts are to be made in aid of these charities during the coming year. JOSEPH PRITCHARD is prepared te wind and keep is repair, private clocks from 10s. per annum.—Adrt. SYMPATHY TO SICK COMMISSIONERS IT RUNCORN. At a special meeting of Runcorn Commissioners on Monday evening, a resolution was proposed by Mr. Wynne Humphreys, and cordially approved by the Board that a vote of sympathy be tendered to Mr. Leach, and to Mr. Coward in respect of the severe ill- ness from which they are respectively suffering, and ex- pressing the hope that they might soon recover their usual health to enable them to join the members of the Board in their deliberations. Go to PRITCCIARD'S for the best five guinea watch a work- ingman can have.—Adid. A RUNCORN VESSEL Smut. A collision occurred about eight o'clock on Friday evening on the Mersey between the schooner Edith Mary, of Bangor, arid the flat Zoar, of Runcorn. The collision took place in the tilot.ne, and resulted in the sinking of the Zoar, though fortunately no lives were lost, the grew of the vessel reaching New Ferry by means of their small boat. The Edith Mary also received con- siderable damage. Her jibbo.irm, topmast, and rails were smashed. PRITCHARD'S have now stood the test for 50 years, andquality and first-class workmanship are still guaranteed.--Adet.

THE POLISH CARD PARTY. At Widnes Police Court on Monday, Sylvester Oustra, ,1 Pole, of Cromwell-street, was charged on remand with Lyda wildly wounding Charles Jeweller, also a Pole, of 29, Barn-street. The two men were members of a card oar,y, on Saturday night the eighth inst., and after a quantity of ale had been consumed, the prisoner struck the prosecutor on the head with a quart bottle, inflicting a serious wound. The priswner was committed for trial. Jesr:ra PRITCHARD has the best stock of ladies' silver and geld watches in the town.—Advt. ALBERT-NOAD SUNDAY SCHOOL, WIDNES. The anniversary services in connection with the above schools were held on Sunday, when the pulpit was I occupied by the Rev. A. M. Brown (St. Helens). In the afternoon an encouraging address was delivered by the same gentleman to the scholars and teachers. A public meeting was held on Monday evening, when a spirited address was given by the Rev. J. Pullford Williams, of Runcorn. Collections were taken in aid of the school fund. destrig PRITCHARD keeps spectacles to suit all sights frees a shilling a pair.—Adrt. CAMDEN WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. The anniversary services was held in St. Paul's Chapel on Sunday, when the Rev. Joseph Posnett of Leicester, preached morning and evening to large congregations. The choir and scholars rendered several pieces under the leadership of Mr. Samuel Bazley. Mr. W. H. Grice was at the organ. On Monday evening the Rev. Charles Garrett preached to a crowded congregation. It was stared that there were the namta of 630 scholars on the boaks of Camden School and that the expenses reached £6O par annum. The collections realised £42.

On Wednesday night at a meeting at Garston Conservat- ive Club, a letter was read from Mr. J. S. Hilliat, M.P., for the Widnes Division. in which he looked forward confidently to the next election, and said, " nmy opinion we have every cause for encouragement and hope. We have truth and right on our side. We are hampered by no pledges we are not sincerely Jesirous to carry out. The second reading of the Home Rule Bill may indeed be carried by the normal majority, based on Irish votes, but we know now by unmistakable evidence t hat the heart of the country is against it, and sooner or later we shall throw it out!' JOSEPH PRITCHARD. Watchmaker mid Jeweller, ii,Higk- at.. and 4, Bridge-st., Runcera.—ildiet. ALLEGED ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. Henry Reynolds and Mr. P. Speakman, Henry Massey, a young man 17 years of age, was charged with attempt- ing to commit suicide. The prisoner was employed by Mr. Duckett, fishmonger, Church-st., and on Saturday he was seen by a boy to drink some liquid from a: bottle labelled poison, and which was afterwards found to con- tain a liniment of camphorated oil and chloroform. Mr. , Duckett at once sent for a doctor, but in the meantime another youth called " Mickey " had given the prisoner a couple of glasses of milk, which caused him to be very I kick, and when Dr. Robinson arrived he was out of dan- ger.—The prisoner said he took the poison because he was melancholy, and it was stated that he wanted to go to sea.—The Bench remanded him to the Workhouse for seven days, and Mr. Shaw the missionary promised to , try and find him a berth on a ship. Both PRITCHARD'S Shops are under personal supervislon.and , austAmem may rely upon recei ring every attention.—Advt.

ROBBED OF Illa BRAIN sty DRINK. At Widnes Police Court, on Saturday, before Mr. Deacon, a middle-aged man named John Hickey, Dick- son-street, an ex-soldier, was brought up charged with being a wandering lunatic.—P.C. McGuinniss stated that he met tile defendant in Widnes-road on Friday night, acting in a very strange manner, and talking about all sorts of things. He seemed very excited, and was there- fore taken to the police station. Hickey said there were demons in the house where he was staying ; he saw them quite Alainly. He ran out, and twa of them fol- lowed him down the street. He was very frightened, as anyone would be under the circumstances. He had been a soldier, and served in different parts of Africa for a number of years.—P.S. Carter said defendant's landlady told him he had been drinking heavily up to a week ago, and since then had acted strangely.—The prisoner was handed over to Mr. HaIIIpSOII, the relieving officer, to be detained at the Workhouse hospital for 14 days. If you wantyour watch repaired by skilful workmen, take 44 to PRITCHARD'S.—Advt.

----- RAILWAY FATALITY AT DITTOS. On Monday afternoon, Mr. S. Brighouse, count) coroner, held an inquest at the Mill Inn, Ditton, on the body of John Norbury Sum ner,aged 30,0 f s,Chatsworth- at., Edgehill. The cieceased was employed at Ditton Junction Station as a la mpman by the London and North-Western Railway Company, and about half-past six on Saturday evening, after having finished his work, he was hurrying back to the platform to catch a train for Edgehill. He was walking just outside the metals of this main line, and was seen in that dangerous position by the driver of the London express,due out of Lime-st. at 6-15, which was coming along at a speed of about 50 ' miles an hour. The driver whistled, but the deceased, who was running with his head bowed, did not seem to hear, therefore, the driver whistled in a jerky manner. That attracted the attention of the deceased, who, on seeing the engine so near him, appeared to lose his pre- sence of mind, and in trying to get out of the way he jumped right into the track of the train and was killed, his body being frightfully mangled. There was nothing to prevent his stepping away from the engine. A verdict of "Accidental death" was recorded.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 22, 1893.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 22, 1893.
RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY..
During March 1837, books were issued in the lending department. The financial year closed on the 25th March, when there was a balance in hand of £2O 2s. 9d.

FOOTBALL : RUNCORN V. WARRINGTON. We are informed that, owing to the extreme rough- ness exhibited by Warrington in the recent match with Runcorn, the Runcorn Committee have scratched all future engagements with the Warrington club. MR. J. C. MILLER AT RUNCORN. This professor of the art of healing by electricity has delivered a lecture each evening during the past week on electricity as a healing power. Fairly large atten- dances have gathered in Bethesda schoolroom to listen to his dissertations, and many have given testimonials as to the effiacy of his treatment. THE REV. R. MISIKLEJoILN, OF WIDNES has occupied the curacy of ENtuanuel Church, flast7 ings. During his stay in Widnes, Mr. Meiklejohn has made himself highly popular, and he has especially won the goodwill of the younger parishioners by earnestly entering into their games and pastimes. He is a good preacher and an energetic parochial worker.

SPECIAL FOOTBALL MAT= AT RUNCORN. From an advertisement in another column it will he seen that a special match has been arranged to take place on the Ira ell-lane ground, on Tuesday evening in aid of the Volunteer Band. At the conclusion of the game the band will give a concert on the field. It is hoped that the services of the band during the winter will be rewarded by 'a bumper gate.

WEST BANK MISSION Room, WIDNES. With the object of wiping off the debt of £9O on the mission room, a sale of work was commenced on Thurs. da7 afternoon. The proceedings were opened by a short address from the vicar, the Rev. G. H. Garrett, who described the good work accomplished by the mission, and then Mr. Stuart Deacon, B.L,performed the opening ceremony. He said the mission got into touch with many people who did not go to Church, and was worthy of support. PARISH CHURCH BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN. The last meeting of the present session was held on Monday evening, in the Parish Church Schoolroom. There was a crowded and enthusiastic audience. The Farnworth Church Temperance Society Minstrels gave an interesting entertainment, consisting of nigger songs and instrumental solos. The artistes were under the conductorship of Mr. J. W. Davies ; and Miss Hunter acted as accompanist. BURNING FATALITY AT WIDNES. Yesterday Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner, held an inquest at Widnes Accident Hospital on the body of Edzabeth Lawton, aged 10 years, daughter 6f James ! Lawton, of 76, Dock-st., who died on Wednesday from injuries received on the 10th ine, During the absence of her mother from home the deceased set her clothes on fire, and before the house, could be extinguished she was terribly burned about the body, neck, and arms. THE PARISH CHURCH COMMUNICANTS' CLASS, RUNCORN. On Tuesday evening, under the auspices of this class, a pleasant "Social " was held in the National Schools. There was a good attendance of members and friends. The company partook of tea, dispensed by Mrs. Wood, IVlrs. Holden, and Mrs. Shakeshaft. An exceptionally good programme, arranged by Mr. James uittle was gone through by the members of the church choir, Miss Crosby, Miss Rogerson, Miss Tatters, Mr. Price, Miss ' Ainsworth, and Mr. Scott, the latter of whom inter- preted humorous songs to the satisfaction of all present. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD ACCOUNTS. •An adjourned meeting of ratepayers was held in , Bethesda Lecture Hall, on Thursday evening for the purpose of receiving the accounts of the Burial Board for the past year. Mr. S. Walton presided and Mr. W. Sutton, assistant overseer, read the balance sheet which showed that the receipts had been £1,998 61. 31. of altich £l2O had been contributed from the rates, £456 19s. 101. from interment fees and £124 Bs. 3d. from mortgages. The expenditure included £1,050 mortgages paid off salaries and wages £196 135., making and draw- ing Victoria-road (balance of account) £lB4 3s. The certificate of the auditors Messrs. John Littler and J. K. Dis,ges was produced. The balance sheet was adopted unanimously and the proceedings terminated. The complete statement of accounts will be found in our advertising columns. A POLL OF RATEPAYERS AT TIALTON. On Friday evening last week a meeting of ratepayers was held in the Girls' Schoolroom, Halton, for the pur- pose of electing two members on the Burial Board, Rev. G. D. Wray presided. There was a large attendance. The old members, Messrs. John Barrow and George Leatliwood, were nominated, together with Messrs. A. Fryer and J. S. Jeao-adc. A show of hands was taken in the room, with the following result :—George Leath, wood, 35; John Barrow 35; A. Fryer, 21; J. S. Jeacock, 20. A poll was demanded on behalf of Messrs. Fryer and Jeacock, which the Chairman fixed to take place to-day. The old members are Nonconformists, and the two others nominated belong to the Church of England. JOSEPH PRITCHARD, Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, High- at.. and 4, Bridge at., Runcorn.—Advt.

_ RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD: EVENING CLASSES. At the recent examinations held under the auspices of the Lancashire and Cheshire Union of Institutes, 39 students attending these classes voluntarily presented themselves for examination in arithmetic and four in English. The examinations were superintended by Messrs. George Roberts and Peter Davies. The follow- ing are the names of the successful candidates :—Arith- metic, Ist class, D. Catterall, I'. A. Millinger, and Ernest Gleave ; 2nd class, J. W. Gleave, C. Bate, C. Burrows, Frank Burrows, W. Littler, T. Briscoe, T. Curzon,flarold Stnitn, W. H. Hopwood, T. Leach, C. Watson, H. Yates, S. Blundell, J. H. Littlemore, F. Wilkinson, Sidney Wharton, George Reed, Wm. Cook. and.G. H. Marsli. English, 2nd class, Joseph T. Percival, Win. Littler,Wrn. Cook, and Wesley Coventry. A FILTHY WOMAN AT HatEwoon. At Widnes Petv Sessions, on thursday,an old woman, named Minnie Lewis, of Halewood, was charged with sleeping out. Mr. A. Wood, relieving officer,said he had known defendant for 18 months. She formerly lived in a cottage at Halewood,but on account of her dirty habits he had to report the matter to the Rural Sanitary Autho- rity, who had the home cleansed and fumigated. She was at this time getting parish relief, which had since been stopped, as the Guardians did not think she was , capable of taking care of herself and wanted her to go to the Workhouse, but she refused to do so. He could not describe the filthy state her house was in.—Defend- ant said they had turned her out of the house, and her clothes and furniture were still there.—Mr. Wood stated that there was some furniture in the house,but the land- lord bad nailed the doors up and would notlet defendant live there on account of her dirty habits.—The magis- trates granted an order for defendant to be taken to the Workhouse for fourteen days.

WIDNES CASES AT TICE LIVERPOOL COUNTY SESSIONS. On Tuesday, at the Liverpool County Quarter &s- -sines, James Allender (16), Dock-st., Widnes, was in- dicted for having unlawfully wounded his mother, on the 28th of March, by striking her with stones, bricks, and crockery. Although only 16 years of age there were several convictions for stealing against the pri- soner, who on this charge was sent to prison for nine months with hard labour. --Sylvester Oustra, Cromwell- st., Widnes, the Pole who was committed for wounding a fellow countryman whilst playing cards, was sentenced to three months, hard labour.—On Wednesday, at the same court, Patrick ewall, of Widnes, was charged with wounding his sister, Ellen Newall, on the 26th ult., and was sent to gaol for four months with hard labour.— Margaret Boyle, a married woman, who was charged with wounding Thomas Dyas, at Widnes, on the 25th ult., by striking him in the face with a drinking glass and inflicting a serious wound, was bound over in £2O to come up for judgment when called upon.—Thomas Cruise was found not guilty of ass-)ulting an old woman named Ellen Whaller, at a lodging-house in Marsh-st., on the 25th March, and was discharged. FUNERAL OF MR. GROUNDS OF WESTON POINT. On Wednesday afternoon, the remains of Mr. William Grounds, of the Dock Hotel, Weston Point, were interred in the Runcorn Cemetery, the officiating clergyman being the Rev. G. H. Kingston. The deceased gentle- man came into this locality from Rainford 22 years ago. Since Christmas he had been ailing, and he died on Sunday, at the age of 56 years. The funeral was wit- nessed by a large number of persons, and the blinds of the houses were drawn. After the hearse came a carriage containing the five sons of the deceased ; in the second rode his daughter Lily, Mr. F. W. Clark (son-in- law), Master R. Clark (grandson), Mr. James Naylor (brother-in-law), Mr. Thomas Grounds, and Mr. George Myers. In the third carriage were Messrs. W. Shaw (missionary of the Seamen's Institute), H. de Corte, Dunbavin, A. Barker, R. Morris (undertaker), and James Dutton (coffin-maaker). The bearers were members of the Tontine Club, of which the late Mr. Grounds was treasurer. Beautiful floral emblems were forwarded by relatives and friends. The carriages were supplied by ' Messrs. F. and W. Yarwood, Runcorn. The arrange- ments were efficiently carried out by Mr. Morris. RUMOURED WINDFALL FOR .6. S. HELENS JOINER. Rumours have been current in St. Helens that a joiner in the employ of Messrs. Pilkington Brothers, glass manufacturers, St. Helens, had been left a fortune, variously estimated by the gossips at from £l,OOO to £lOO,OOO. From inquiries made it appears that the :joiner in question Is a native of North Lancashire, and that some years ago an uncle went abroad. About a month since news was received that this uncle had died, and bad made the person referred to heir to considerable property. This, it is understood, consists of oil mills in Russia. and some property in the Argentine, but until the estate can be realised no estimate can be formed of its value.

At Dalkeith, on Friday, an interesting wedding took place. John Clark, the bridegroom, was born et the close of the last century, and the bride, whose maiden neme is Young, has seen sixty bummers. 'lbis is the bridegroom's fourth and the bride's second matrimonial venture.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESTONS)ENT.

I met by accident a day or two ago a Lymn acquaintance who informed me of a brave deed done in that village by Mr. Frank Wiswall, chair- man of Runcorn Baena of Guardians, in the course of his professional dutiea as engineer to the Bridge- water canals. Mr. Wiswall was on a flat in the canal at Lymm, a boy fell into the water some dis- tance away, and a medical gentleman who was near jumped in to save bin, but he became exhausted before he had conveyed him to the side and both were in grave danger when Mr. Wiswall leaped in- to the water, encumbered with the whole of his clothing and hoes and swam to their rescue which he safely accomplished. After obtaining, a change of clothing at a house in the neighbourhood, Mr. Wiswall came on to Runcorn. This gallant deed has been kept exceedingly "quiet," but it ought to be made known of what stuff our "chief ruler" is made.

Time will show whether the ratepayers came to a wise decision respecting the purchase of Runcorn Waterworks on Wednesday evening. The general opinion is that they did. On sanitary grounds it is ,to the interests of all that the water supply should be in the hands of the Local Authority, but there can be, as the Chairman put it at the previous meeting, such a thing as paying too dearly for your ! whistle. The price on the first report of the ! auditor seemed a most extravagant one, but the statement presented on Wednesday evening, pre- sented quite another picture, and justified the ac- quirement of the undertaking. But it must not be forgotten that the surplus of £l7O is shown on the assumption that the Board of Commissioners are permitted to defer the repayments of the loan for the first five years, and it is by no means certain that the Local Government Board will permit that in regard to the works which have been in exist- ence for 30 years. If not there will be a charge upon the district rate. Mr. Speakman as an owner of much property, is prepared to make present sacri- fices for the future benefit and prosperity of the dis- trict, and there are no doubt others like him. At the conclusion of the meeting, Mr. Torrie demanded a poll on the question, and on the following morn- ing went to the Town Hall to pay a "deposit " for the purpose, but as the meeting was altogether in- formal, such a course is impossible.

In honouring Mr. Timmis on Tuesday by the pre- sentation of an illuminated address, the Widnes School Board honoured themselves. Not only had Mr. Timmis done yeoman service for the ratepayers as chairman of the Board for twelve years, but he has helped forward education in countless other ways, and his last munificent benefaction will cause his name to be remembered and blessed in centuries to come.

That the Weaver Navigation ought to be a pro- perly elected and representative body, no person would perhaps have the hardihood to deny, and the action of the Runcorn Board of Ouardians in decid- ing to petition the House of Lords to that effect was only doing what was natural and according to the wishes of the ratepayers. The Board could not go the full length Mr.Brunner desired them,and the suggested abolition of exemptions, whenever it is brought forward practically, will rouse the strenu- ous opposition of the farmers on the banks of the IVeaver as they have considerable privileges. It would be interesting to learn why these exemptions were granted in the first instance, for it is nothin g more nor less than Assisting one trade at the expense of others.

The management of the Gilchrist Lectures,which are to be delivered in Runcorn during the coming winter, is to be placed in the hands of a represen- tative committee of fifty; with the Rev. Canon Wood as chairman Ir. J. B. Holland, treasurer ; and Messrs. J. D. Jones and B. Crosby, secretaries.

div.head: WIDNES PRIMROSE LEAGUE.
div.p: WIDNES PRIMROSE LEAGUE.

The annual meeting of the members of the Widnes Habitation of the Primrose League was held in the Conservative Club, on Thursday even- ing. Mr. James White. ruling councillor, presided. Mr. J. S. Gilliat, ALP., sent a telegram expressing regret that he could not be present. Mr. Crawford, hon. see., stated that they had now the following members-12 dames, 6 knights and 155 associates and contended that their member would not have been elected by so large a majority but for the efforts of the League. The following officers were elected :—Ruling coimcilior, Mr. James White; hon. secretary, Mr. J. C. Crawford ' • assistant-secretary, Mr. T. Atherton, junr. ; treasurer, Mrs. Imison ; executive committee, Mr. E. Charles, Mrs. Crawford, Mr. It. Lewis, Mrs. F. Neil, Mr. It. Eastwood, Miss Ilignett, Miss Barlow, Mr. G. H. Davies, Mrs. Grundy, Mrs. Forshaw, Mrs. Edwardson, and Mrs. Rogerson. On the motion of Mr. R. Lewis, seconded by Mr. E. Charles, a resolution protesting against the iniquitous Home Rule Bill was passed.

div.head: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB.

For some months past this club has been tempo- rarily located in Bank Chambers, High-st., and the members have had to endure considerable iuconvek- ience in their social gatherings and business opera- tions. The club, it is now decided, shall be per- manently housed in Union Hall, Regent-street. Mr. Brunner has offered the building on exceedingly generous terms, which the members unhesitatingly accepted. The price is £4OO. It will be necessary to carry out con- siderable alterations to adapt the premises for the pur- poses of the club,and steps are to be taken to have them carried out with the utmost despatch. It is intended to have a billiard room capable of accommodating two full- sized tables, and there will be a newsroom and various conveniences provided.
WIDNES COUNTY COURT.

_ At this Court yesterday before his Honour Judge Shand, Wm. Turton, labourer, Egypt-st., sued Annie Jamieson, pawnbroker. Ann-st., to recover a bed, or £3 the value of it.—Mr. F. J. Poole was for the plaintiff. and Mr. Edmund Bury for the defendant. The plaintiff alleged that she ledged a feather bed with the defend- ant for 153., and reclaimed it in January of this year. When she opened it out at home she found that it was not her bed but one much inferior.—The defence was that Mrs. Jameson was not in the habit of receiving furniture and this was the only bed she had had in pledge during the past four years.—His Honour gave judgment for the defendant. - -

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY.—Before Messrs. H. VV. Deacon, and E. Mather. MISCELLANEOUS. John Winn, Fisher-st. ; James Walsh, Lunt's Heath ; and James Molloy, Gossage-st., were each fined for drunkenness. Ann J. Pickering, Cross-st.; Ann Fearnett, Cross-st. ; and Timothy Mit- chell, Walmsley-st., were bound over for committing breaches of the peace. A WANDERING LUNATIC.—A middle-aged man named Herbert Rudkin, who said he came from Liveroool, was charged with being a wandering lunatic.---P C. Heaton stated that at nine o'clock that morning he went to Lunt's Heath, where he saw the defendant in Mr. Houghton's garden, digging a large hole with a pick and spade, and acting in a very strange manner.—ln answer to Mr. Deacon, Rudkin said he was doing the work for the good of his health. He had been looking for work, but could not get any.—Mr. Wood, relieving officer, said ho would take defendant to the workhouse for 14 days.—Mr. Deacon said it would be better to send him there.—Defendant said he was willing to go any- where he was sent.

JUST SCALES,—Ann Routledge, Mersey-road, was charged with having in her possession a pair of scales which were nine drachms out of balance against the purchaser.—A fine of 53. and 12s. costs was imposed.

div.head: DANITT AND HIS GENEROUS
div.p: DANITT AND HIS GENEROUS
FRIENDS.

Mr. Michael Davitt has been pressed from all sides to take gifts of money to clear off the bill of £l,BOO for the recent election petition. A Nationalist friend has offered him £l,OOO, a lady friend of his wife £5OO, and a large number of smaller offers have been received from working-men who have written to Mtn. But (says a London contemporary) he ii stoutly re3olved never, to take any public money for his private concerns, and to all these offers lie has given a positive refusal.

Ars EAIII3MTOWN FOOTBALL CLUB. On Tuesday evening the playing members of the Earlestown Football club, and the cornmittee.to the number of 30, sat down to a knife and fork tea at the Prince of Wales 'Hotel. The catering was per- formed by Mr. R. Lythgoe, and gave every satisfac- tion, the repast being theroughly enjoyed. Alter the cloth had been removed,the subsequent proceed- ings were presided over by Mr. T. Sickleley, captain and a convivial evening was spent. Songs were given by Messrs. Waddington, Lewis, and Tyrer, and a ventriloquial entertainment was given by Prof. Vistow of Leeds, whose manipulation of a couple of inanimate figures, caused much amuse- ment,

div.head: _RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: _RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The first triennial meeting of Runcorn Guardians was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesda3 Present : the Bev. J. W.N. Tanner, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Rev. J. Hanby, Messrs. Mclntyre, Davenport, , Knowles, Parr, Lewis„Woodward, J. Hall, Pickering, urner,Williams, Heywood, Aaron, Ford, Brandreth, Parkinson, Stokes, W hitley, Horton, Baxter, C.C., S. Taylor, J. W. Baguley, S. Yarwood, T. Handley, D. H. Jones, I'. Lea, A. R. Norman, Jenkins, J. Ashton (clerk), G. Ashton (deputy clerk).

THE CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMAN. The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, as the " father of the Board' proposed the re-election of Mr. Mclntyre as chairman.—Mr. Williams seconded, and the motion was carried unanimously, and Mr. Mclntyre on taking Os chair referred to Mr. Williams' remarks at the Rural Sanitary Authority and said he considered them a hint to the members as well as to himself. He boped the proceedings would be conducted on the same amicable and gentlemanly principles as in the past.—On the motion of Mr. Aaron seconded by Mr. Tanner and sup- ported by Dr. Gristaldi, Mr. Joseph Knowles was elected vice-chairman.--The Chairman extended a hearty wel- come to the new members.

In reply to an inquiry from the Clerk, the Local Government Board stated that the appointment of Chairman and vice-Chairman should he made annually at the first meeting of the Guardians after the fifteenth of April. There should, in the opinion of the Board, be an annual appointment of the Visiting Committee, Assessment Committee, School Attendance Committee and Parochial Committees.

div.head: ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.

Mr. Aaron moved that the four ex-officios—Messrs. C. Reynolds, A. Thomas, LI. Neila and Dr. Steele be re- appointed.—Mr. Pickering moved Mr. Woodhouses in place of Mr. Neild.—Mr. Tanner seconded. The voting was equal-14 each—and the Chairman gave his casting vote for Mr. Neild. The four gentlemen were therefore re-elected. Of the eight elected guardians,Mr. Pickering I proposed Mr. Woodward in the place of Mr. P. Hall, dwelling upon the importance of the district (Kingsley Norley, &c.), that gentleman represented.—Mr. Lewis seconded the motion.—Dr. Gastaldi moved Messrs. H. G. Heywood, E. Aaron, S. Taylor, and T. Handley.—Mr. Ford seconded. The mover pointed out that the impor- tance of the Runcorn and Frodsham districts and the large works there to be assessed.—Mr. Brandreth pro- posed eight members as follows :—Messrs. E. Aaron, H. , E. Heywood. J. Mclntyre, J. Knowles, Thomas Lewis, Samuel Taylor, John Weir, and Thomas Handley.—Mr. Aaron seconded.—Mr. Norman supported the motion in the interests of those who had to pay rates. In future Runcorn would he much affected by the Assessment Committee and Runcorn ought to be strongly repre- sented on the Committee. Toe Ship )anal was ap- proazhing completion, and some people expressed them- selves confident that several new trades and industries would settle in Runcorn district, and it was very im- portant that there should be two representatives on the Committee from that district, so that greater help could be given in the assessment brought before them.—Mr. Woodward as a new member refused to serve on the Committee and nominated Mr. Pickering. It seemed unfair that a rateable value such as theirs should be left out in the cold. There were already four who repre- sented Runcorn and Frodsham.—Mr. Baxter said the Committee should be representative of all the district.— Mr. Williams in supuorting Mr. Brandreth said they would see great development in Runcorn and Prodshain through the Ship Canal. They had already had a law suit in connection with dm Ship Canal, and there would be new, valhations arising every week. lie bad seen a Runcornian viewing land at Frodsham with a view of , building fifty houses.--The Chairman pointed out that formerly there were so many representatives elected from. eaeh district.—Mr. Jenkins said it was men not districts they were electing.—Mr. Taylor pointed out that difficultieshad arisen with the Runcorn assessments and he supported Mr. Brendreth's nroposition which was eventually carried by 21 votes to 6.

div.head: WEAVER TRUeI.
div.p: THE WEAVER TRUeI.

The Clerk read the following letter :-9, Ennismore Gardens, S.W., April 14Lh 1893. Sir,—l tun desired by Mr. Brunner to acknowledge receipt of your communi- cation on behalf of the Runcorn Union of the sth met, to my that he worts that they donor view the matter in quite the same light as he does. Mr. Brunner's best thanks are due to the Board for the kindness and courtesy with which they have formerly treated him even when disagreeing with his proposals. He begs to enclose an amended dralt of petition which he ventures to think will be more acceptable. If the Board should see its wa3 to adopt some such petition he wculd be greatly pleased. Yours faithfully, Colin H. Browning. The petition stated that the Trustees are a self-elected loOdy, with large statutory powers of levying tolls on all goods carried on the river Weaver, but they do not in any way represent either the interests of the trade , which uses the navigation, or the interests of the county as a whole. For many years past a large surplus from the tons has been under the old Weaver Navigation Acts handed over to the county of Chester in relief of the county rate, while there has also been a considerable expenditure by the Trustees in building and endowing churches. The aggregate amount paid to the county of Chester for the ten years 1880 to 1889 inclusive, was £115,000. Your petitioners allege that the constitution of the frustees is anomalous, and the working of the Trust unsathsfactory,and they expressly complain of the constitution of the Trust as being non-representative. Your petitioners humbly pray that in accordance with the recommendation made in the report of the Beard of Trade in 1857, emphasized in that of 1872, your lordships will be pleased to insert in the Bill new pending in your Lordships Right Hon. House Clauses (1). Placing the navigation in the hands of a body fairly representative of the, whole county. (2). Revising the tolls so as to make thon fair and equal and abolishing exemptions therefrom. (3). Providing for a proper audit and publication of accounts.—Mr. Heywood said the clause to which they took strong exception—the abolition of exemptions—was retained.—Mr. Stekes said it Was about the exemptions the great fight would be. The farming community on the banks of the canal had manure and other articles carried fro and they would resist the abolition of exemptions most strongly.—Mr. Brandreth said he would vote for the Weaver being managed by an elected body who could deal with the exemptions.—Mr. Handley suggested that the clause regarding exemptions be struck out and the petition then adopted.—Mr. Norman said he had reason to believe Mr. Brunner was at one with the Board in considering it most important that the Trust should be representative and it did not trouble him if the Board supported the petition that far and no farther.—Mr. Jenkins said at the time the erceptions were made there must undoub:- edly .be good consideration given, and he denounced the tendency to sweep away old reservations.—Mr. Brand- reth moved and Mr. Woodward seconded, that the seal of the Board be attached to a petition to the House of Lords, in favour of placing the navigation of the Weaver in the hands of a body fairly representative of the whole county, and also of a proper audit and publication of the accounts.—Sevehteen members voted for the motion and none against, and it was declared carried.
