div.head: NEW PICTURES FOR TIIE ART GAILERY,
div.p: NEW PICTURES FOR TIIE ART GAILERY,

We understand that the brother of the late Mr. W. Barlow, acting as executor, has very generously offered to the Warrington Museum Committee the whole of the deceased gentleman's fine collection of pictures for public exhibition in the Art Gallery. They will be publicly exhibited for nine months. We believe, too, that the Museum Committee con- template purchasing some of the pictures, if ar- rangements can be made, to add to the permanent collection at the Gallery.

div.head: AFFAIRS OF THE WARRINGTON
div.p: THE AFFAIRS OF THE WARRINGTON
FOOTBALL CLUB..

div.head: AN INTERVIEW WITH MR. J. E. WARREN.
div.p: AN INTERVIEW WITH MR. J. E. WARREN.

Last evening. an "Examiner" reporter called upon Mr. J. E. Warren, secretary of the Warrington Football Club, to have a chat with him respecting the " alleged mobbing " of a referee, and the atti- tude taken by the Runcorn club, in cancelling their fixtures with Warrington. Mr. Warren who is a member of the Lancashire Union Committee attended the meeting ot that body on Thursday evening, when the charges made against the club were considered. In answer to questions by our reporter, Mr. Warren said The charge laid by Mr. Seddon against the club of" mobbing 'him was not a matter which in any way compromised the behaviour of either the players or the officials, it practically concerned the behaviour of just a handful of men who pro- bably had their money on the game." "But the club was suspended from playing the match to-morrow (Saturday) with the Manchester Rangers."

_ " Well, the Club was not exactly susp3nded—it was the ;pound which was suspended ; the club are allowed to play away if they wish. The real object of the action is to punish the spectators. You know this rough behaviour towards referees is becoming very coalmen indeed, and it is desirable that an example should be made of someone—Warring- ton appear in this case to be the unfortu- nate ' someone.' Mr. Seddon in laying the charge entirely exotterated the officials and the players from any blame, and as I explained before, the matter is not in itself so important, but it is neces- sary.to show to spectators in general the necessity of treating the referees in at least a civil manner." "What is your idea of the alleged mobbing, Mr. Warren 2"

" I don't think it was quite so serious as it has been made out. When Mr. Seddon blew his whistle about half-a-dozen fellows rushed towards him. But immediately they did so, all the officials and a very large number of spectators rushed up to his protection. They did this, no doubt., in response to a request made in a circular from the club, asking them at the time of any disturbance to assist the officials. Very naturally, Mr. Seddon would think these people were mobbing

„ "I am told that the Runcorn Club have cancelled their fixtures with you in consequence of alleged rough play.” " Yes, at the meeting last night, Mr. Ashton of the Broughton Rangers, who was the referee in the match between IVarrington and Runcorn laid a charge of "brutally rough play" againstWarrington. Jolley, who had been ordered off the field, was charged individually, but was acquitted and , thoroughly vindicated. From what I can gather, Mr. Ashton's charges were rather unfounded. All our men absolutely protest that they did not show one atom of rougher play than the Runcorn melt. True, there was one of their men injured, Abram, but John Bate of our team was also injured. As far as I can gather, IVarrington's play was sicaply rather vigorous, whilst that of the Runcorn men was not faultless. In cancelling the fixtures, don't think they have dealt with us at all fairly,and onless they at least play off the return fixture for Monday I bepeve they will hear more of it." "In what way?" " Well the fixture I refer to was made in accord- ance with an agreement with us, and it is probable that we shall sue them for loss of "gate" money, &c. This is the letter respecting the agreement:— "November 23rd, 1892. Dear Sir,—We agree to meet Warrington some Thursday in April—we to have .E 7 10s. towards our expenses. Can we ask a favour of your men? On Saturday, December sth, Cheshire play Durham—eight of the nineof our men will be required. It you ate not playing that day we should be glad if you could spare us two three- quarters and Boscow—we are playing Liverpool Old Boys.—Yours truly, J. B. hangshaw." " It has been suggested that Warrington showed spleen." "I don't think they did. We have been on very ' good terms with the Runcorn players for the past two years, until this."
-•____ DII. GORNALL AND THE WARRINGTON
BOAItD OF GUARDIANS.
MIL SHAW'S MOTION REJECTED. LIVELY PROCEEDINGS.
At the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guar- dians, held on Wednesday morning at the Town Ir. Ratcliffe presiding, the Clerk read the fol- lowing motion of which Mr. W. J. Shaw had given notice

`‘ That pursuant to the terms of contract for vaccina- tion dated February 25th, 1891, the Board give to Mr. John Hankinson Gornall twenty-eight days notice in writing of their intention to put an end to the contract --subject to Mr. Gornall having power to apply for re- appointment according to the conditions to be set forth in an advertisement." Mr. SHAW in submitting his motion said that from what lie had gathered since the motion had been put into I print, he felt somewhat annoyed that he had taken the course he had. He could not help but go through with the matter now. He had received a letter from Dr. IGornall in which he pointed out that he had held the office for 21 years. He also said that the course which he was taking was causing him pain and anxiety and a lot of financial suffering. The appointment held by Dr. Gornall tie would point out was terminable at 23 days notice on either side, and therefore if the Guardians felt disposed to end the contract they had a perfect right to do so. He had not one word to say about Dr. Gornall's abilities, but nevertheless, although every satisfaction had bean given, he did not think Dr. Gornall had any right to expect to enjoy the privileges of that Board more than any other officer. Dr. Gornall wanted to know why he should be singled out from any other official; and he theught they were taking an undue advantage of him. He (Mr. Shaw) had a feeling of respect for Dr. Gornall, hut he observed from the tone of his remarks that such a feeling of respect did not exist in Dr. Gor- nail's mind towards him and the members of the Board. He had talked about the matter in town and had called it a Tory trick. Those were remarks which he at least thought Dr. Gomel' Ehauld have kept from the hearing I of the Board. In this ',natter he had acted without per-; sonal or political bias; he had merely endeavoured to I do a duty which devolved upon him as a member of that' Board, and he was Acting without the co-operation of any second person. He considered that it was not right that a medical man should be allowed to come straight from an infectious diseases hospital to a vaccination station. He asked if the members of the Board did not prefer to have their children vaccinated by a private practitioner in preference to Dr. Gornall, who was continually may- ing about in an infectious diseases hospital. There were paupers who would be more willing to suffer the penalties of the law than undergo the operation by Dr. Gornall,and run the risk of the dangers consequent upon coming into contact with him. That was his main reason for moving the motion, but if it was the wish of the Board he woald not go on with the matter any further. He had taken an entirely independent stand upon the matter ; there had been no coaching, no individual had attempted to tempt him ; and no influence of medical men had been brought to bear upon him in bringing the motion for- ward. He hoped that Dr. Gornall would not attribute his action to a reflection upon his abilities, for he believ- ed, as Dr. White had said in a letter, Dr. Gornall's wark 'could not be done any better than it was. The only ground upon which he had taken action was the desire which he had to prevent any possible contraction of disease by poor people from their contact with Dr. Gor- nall, at the vaccination station. Mr. A. JOLLEY secondeo the motion. Mr. PILLING : I ask Mr. Shaw to withdraw that mo- tion. (Bear, hear.l Mr. Suaw : I have told you that if it was the desire of this Board, I will withdraw the motion. Mr. PILLING : I hope I can prevail upon you to with- draw it. Mr. BILL: I hope Mr. Shaw will not withdraw. I have very great pleasure in supporting the abolition of what I consider a great injustice to the medical men of ' the town. Mr. RYLANDS said he hoped Mr. Shaw would withdraw his motion, because he did net see where Mr. Shaw based his reasons for the action. The statement which he made to the effect that there was danger of the spread of infection caused by Dr. Gornall visiting the vaccination stations after attending at the infectious diseases hospital was weak .(Hear,hear.)They were always subject to that; ' medical men in the ordinary course of their duties often visited one patient after attending a person suffering from an infectious disease. He had known several cases where medical men had taken disease into houses ; but it was because they did not take the proper precautions before going there. (Hear, hear.) He would like to point out that Dr. Gornall had been the medical officer for over 20 years ; and that he had given the whole of his time up to public duties,and he had also given up his private practice. (Voicea :—" No, no.") Ile contended that there was no danger out of the common created by the fact that Dr.Gornall as medical officer of health came into contact with people as vaccination officer. He would, therefore, move that the motion of Mr. Shaw be not passed. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY strongly opposed Mr. Shaw's motion. He thought Mr. Shaw's arg,inzent about the danger of Dr. Gornall spreading infection was idle and did not merit consideration. From what he could see of the points adduced by Mr. Shaw against Dr. Gornall, he ' could only arrive at the conclusion that Mr. Shaw was moved by personal animosity. Cries of "Order, order." and Mr. Shaw rose and said: I pretest &pint Mr. Jolley using the term" personal

/animosity." No such feeling has animated me upon this question,and I call for a withdrawal of the chug*. Mr. Mina : Withdraw, please. Mr. HILL. Withdraw at once please. I will not sit hear to hear insults passed. Mr. JOLLEY : I will Oa withdraw. I repeat what I said : that all I could see in the points adduced by Mr. Shaw, only led me to the conclusion that he was prompted mainly by personal animosity. A number of the members rose to their feet and loudly called for a withdrawal, which Mr. Jolley stoutly re- fused to grant. Mr. &raw : I will insist upon the withdrawal of those words.

Mr. MUIR : SO Will I. Mr. JOLLEY (to Mr. Shaw) : Oh, sit down. Mr. SHAW : I Will not sit down sir. Mr. MUIR : You are out of order on thequestion. Mr. JOLLEY : I am not ; and I intend to discuss this question.

The CHAIRMAN : Do withdraw them, Mr. Jolley. Mr. JOLLEY : I absolutely refuse, sir. I will repeat then! if you please. Many of the members thereupon appealed to the Clerk. He said he thought that as the Chairman had called upon Mr. Jolley to withdraw the words" personal animosity "he ought to do so. It was a precedent set by the House of Commons that if any member was ap- pealed to by the Speaker for a withdrawal or an apology he should consent, no matter how much he felt he was in ths right. He hoped that Mr. Jolley would excuse him suggesting that he might see his way clear to fol- low that precedent, for although he might believe what he had said it was a very difficut thing indeed for one man to prove personal animosity against another. (Ap- plause.) Mr. JOLLEY : I do not care anything about what the House of Commons do ; I merely express what the facts before me lead me to think. More cries of " withdraw " were raised and for a con- siderable time the business of the meeting was at a dead lock. Eventually the Chairman, evidently perplexed by the situation, said : " Mr. Jolley, I call upon you—l ap- peal to you—to withdraw those words." Almost the whole of the Board were now upon their feet and the appeal ef the Chairman was followed by a painful pause whilst Mr.Jolley was evidently debating with him- self whether to withdraw or not, at length he said. " Well, as the Chairman has made a personal appeal to me, I will withdraw the words." In further speaking against Mr. Shaw's motion Mr.Jolley said that although Dr. Garnett might b. unpopular amongst some people in the town it was the duty of that Board to merely take a judicial view of the case, and as Dr. Gornall had done his work so admirably he thought they had no right to treat him as suggested. A letter was next read from Mr. Long, in which he spoke against Mr. Shaw's motion and for many reasons said that it was a snost undesirable action. Mr. B. lIRATON said that although to a great extent agreeing with Mr. Shaw, he thought it would be un- wise to issue a 28 days notice, in the face of that fact that there was so much smallpox in the town and Dr. Gornall had worked so hard during the epidemic. He wished to point this out, however, that he considered the office of vaccinator and medical officer to a Union were almost inseparable and that in all the Unions he knew of the medic4l officer who did the hard work was allowed to benefit from the more acceptable and remun- erative duties of vaccination officer. But, still, he did not think it was advisable for the Board to give Dr. Gornall 28 day's notice then, and he would propose that the matter be deferred for 12 months for further consideration. (Hear, hear.) The CLERK explained that when Dr. Gornall retired from the medical officership of the Union there were certain circumstances which rendered Dr. Gornall's ser- vices as vaccination officer very acceptable, and those circumstances still existed.
Mr. Itvrauns seconded Mr. Ileaton's proposition and Mr. IL Owen supported it. It was then put to the vote and carried unanimously.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.

As I expected, Mr. W. J. Shaw's proposal to give Dr. Gornall twenty-eight day's notice of dismissal from the post of public vaccinator did not meet with the approval of the Board of Guardians. Even Mr. Shaw himself seemed rather ashamed at the last moment of the motion of which he had given notice, and he almost asked the Board to invite him to a ithdraw it. This was not done, but the,matter was shelved for all that, for twelve months at least, Mr. Shaw seems to have been reconsidering his arguments. When he first gave notice of the motion his object was—so he said--to give the "younger faculty " a chance of getting some of the" sweetmeats" of office. On Wednesday he appeared to think very little about the " younger faculty's " taste for " sweetmeats ;" be was only afraid that because Dr. Gornall has charge of the infectious diseases hospital he might be the means of spreading disease amongst people he came in contact with in connection with vaccination.

It was quickly pointed out that that is an argu- ment which applies to all doctors and not to Dr. Goma]] alone, Suppose one of the " younger faculty" had been appointed, would Mr. Shaw have made it a condition that he mtv:t keep away from all intec7ious cases ? If he didn't—and no medical man who did not give up private practice could comply with such a condition—what about all the expressed anxiety for the poor people who have to take their children to be vaccinated ? Mr. Shaw reconsidered his first arguments and they disappeared ; and those he used on Wednesday might very easily be improved out of existence by the same process. By this time next year I have no doubt he will have arrived at the conclusion which has already been come to by most people, that for a public body like the Board of Guardians to dismiss an officer who has given over twenty years of thoroughly satisfactory service, without having any ground of complaint, would be an act of disgraceful meanness.

Mr. Shaw and some others seemed to be under the impression that the appointment of public vaccinator is one which expires every year and must be renewed, but that is a mistake. Dr. Gor- nall was appointed in January 1872, and there has been no break and no re-appointment since then, though there was an amendment of terms in 1890 when the vaccination station at Grappenhall was done away with, on the recommendation of Dr. Gornall himself. Mr. Shaw will see, therefore,thst the appointment is not like a publican's license—it does not need to be renewed every year.

-- Some men have an irrepressible longing to see their relatives; and that Thomas Roach is one of those victims to unrestrained affection is clear from the facts which explained his appearance at the Borough Court, on Monday. In the "Merry month of May" Thomas became quite anxious to see his "uncle" ; but how to do it, he didn't know. Pre- sently, a happy thought struck him ; he tip-toed quietly up to the private room of his landlady, qrs. Sheridan,who was also his aunt,and carefully taking up some jewellry, he chuckled to himself and mur- mured " shticks." He had found the way to see his "uncle" ; he went to see how much die jewelery was worth. His accommodating relative said £3 ss. and gave him the money. A. private business matter called Thomas out of town then; and he never would be able to see Mrs. Sheridan any more he thought. But last week he had a desire to see his aunt again, and whilst he was visiting her on Thursday, he was taken to the Mansion House to see some more friends. Mrs. Sheridan was there on Monday, and Thomas not having her jtwelery said he would pay for it; but remarked, "You must give me time." But Mrs. Sheridan might have "given him time," but the Bench, to show her a generous example, said they would give him " time"; they gave him a month at Strange- ways.

Anent the betting raid case which came before the Bnrough Bench on Monday, I might mention that a peep in the books which were produced is absolutely delightful to those who like to see their neigh bour's name coupled with a shady thing. There were no addresses in the books, but some of the - names which appeared were very similar to the names borne by some of the " big pots" of the town. But it's a pity the addresses were not en- tered fully. 'net would, I am sure, have saved some of the expounders sal even the administrators.of the law frr.m the insinuation that they had, in a mild way, contravened the statutes made and pro- vided with regard to betting.

The audience at Bewsey-road Chapel on Wednes— day night, were delighted with the Rev. Mark Guy Pearse's lecture on "Some Old Folks at Home?' His style of speaking is to a large extent tlramatio, and the source of his power in delineuting char— acters was explained by himself during the night. lie said that when sketching a character he placed himself in the position of that person, and spoke aa though he were the person he was speaking about. When he was giving "Old Anthony's account; of his wife's conversion," he gave it in the Cornish dialect, and one could almost imagine that it was old. Anthony himself that was speakiag. There was a. good audience, but it would no doubt have been better, if there had been a difference of price for different parts of the chapel. A shilling ",all round" is rather a de'errent price to many people who do not find shillino s.Wry plentiful com- modity. • SEUUN.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall), Alder- man Francomb. Councillor Roberts, and Mesars F. Monks, W. Pierpoint, and S. Wright. DRUNICENNESS.—EIIen Gandy, in Rose and Crown- street, on Sunday morning, ss. and costs; Margaret Molloy, dismissed. CHIMNEYS ON FIRE.—For this offence, Patrick Mooney and Mark Burke were each fined is. PUGILISTIC NEIGHEOIIRS.—Mary Smith and Mary Broderick were each charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Dallam-lane on the 10th inst. P.C. 47, said that the two women were fighting in Mrs. Smith's house, and witness put Mrs. Broderick out, when Mrs. Smith followed, and the women began fighting again in the street. They were both drunk, and witness locked them up. The magistrates inflicted a fine of ss. and costs.
TUESDAY.—Before Mr. It. Garnett (c. hairman), Mr. E. J.
_ Guest, and Dr. Smith.

TRAVELLING WITHOUT RAILWAY TICRET.—For attempt- ing to travel from Manchester to Liverpool on the Cheshire lines on Monday, without a ticket. William Thompson, a labourer, of Manchester,was fined 40s. and costs or a month's hard labour. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—For this offence, committed on Monday in Parker-street, Thomas Carey was fined ss. including costs or seven day's hard labour. Scaoor.. CASES—The following were brought before the magistrates for neglecting to send their children to school :—William Thompson, 15, Refuge Square, fined 2s. 6d. ; Hannah Mapp, 3; Stanley-street, 2s. 6d. ; Mary Towey. Berry-yard, ss. ; John Bibby, 307, Winwick- road, 2s. 61. ; Ellen Hayes, 15, Egerton-street, 2s. 6i.; John Fiddlers, William-street, ss. Thomas Lusby, 31, Dial-street, adjourned for one month. Frederick Roberts Kean-street, stated that he had no control over his son IJohn, and his son was sent to the Ship "Clio." WEDNESDAY.—A:cIerman Holmes (in the chair), Abler- man J. E. Wright, Messra. John Geddes and John Fairclough. BEOOING.—Thomas Lee, a stranger in the town was charged with begging in Winwick-street at twelve o'clock the pi evious night. He was ordered to leave the town. SLEEPING Our.:-John Smith, WAS charged with sleep- ing in the hay shed of Mr. Williams', in Folly-lane. and doing damage to the hay to the extent of cne Mr. Williams said the prisoner had opened three trusses of hay and made a comfortable bed. Prisoner was sent to gaol for seven days hard labour. THURSDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton (chairman)

6);;;Jilor •Jas.-Fairclough and Captain' Ridgeway. THEFT OF IRON FROM AN IRONWORES.--TWO boys Patrick McNally and Thomas Harris were charged with stealing from the ironworks of Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co., on the 18th inst.. a quantity of scrap iron, valued 3d. Mr. Forshaw who appeared for the Company said that-two employes of the firm, Thomas Jefferson and John Reddish, saw Harris carrying the iron out of the works and stopped him, and he was brought before Mr. Burton, the manager, where he said that the boy. McNally had sent him in the works. On being asked what he did with the iron be stole, Harris said that it was taken to a man in Sankey Bridges who would give a 'penny for it. Confirmatory evidence was given by Thomas Jefferson, John Reddish, and Thomas Burton, the latter further stating that large quantities of iron were taken from the works, and he had beard of one person wno had half a ton stored up on his premises. The magistrates ordered each boy to receive six strokes of the birch rod, and Detective Monaghan was told to inform the county police of the man who received the stolen scrap. DESERTION or FAMILY.—Enoch Jackson was charged with neglecting to maintain his wife and family, and leaving them chargeable on the Union on Feb. 17th. Mr. Shearer proved the case, and prisoner was sentenced to one month's hard labour.
FIIIDAY.—Before Alderman Wright (chairman) and Councillor Roberta.

Trtart or Snons.—George Warburton was charged wit!? stealing from Wm. Hach, 74, Pierpoint-at., on April 17th, a pair of girl's boots valued 85., and Sarah Ellen Warburton was charged with receiving them know- ing them to be stolen.—The Chief Constable said that prisoners were mother and son, and resided at 88, Pier- point-st. The boy George was playing with the children at Finch's house on the night of the above date, and a girl told him to put the shoes under the dresser. Next morning the shoes were missed and suspicion fell upon ' George Warburton. On Wednesday the matter was re- ported to Detective Monaghan, and he found the boots had been pawned at Turistall's pawnshop by the female prisoner for 2s. fid. The prisoners were arrested on 'Thursday night, and when charged with the offence they pleaded guilty. , George Warburton was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod, and Mrs. Warbur- ton was fined 10s. or 14 day's hard labour. MAINTENANCE ORDERS.—Wm. Hands was ordered to is. per,week towards the maintenance of his father; Bernard Hopkins, and John Hopkins, of Newton-le-Wil- lows, were ordered to pay 4s. and 35. per week towards arrears for the maintenance of their mother. INFRINGEMENT OF THE WEIGHTS ANI, MEASURERS Acv. —For infringement of this Act. William Purnis, and Co., Haydock-street, were fined 10. and costs.—Joseph Swinton, Pinners Brow, was charged with committing a fraud in using scales for weighing sugar purporting to berme lb., but which was deficient. The Town Clerk who prosecuted said that defendant was manager of a shop on Pinners Brow. On the 18th inst., Inspector Place visiting the shop saw defendant weighing some sugar. He bought a lb. packet and fouud it to be 14 ozs. There were about 100 packets of sugar in the shop which were made up and Mr. Place weighed several of them and found them to be the same weight. Defend- ant afterwards reweighed them and made them the right weight. The CECUSP he made for having the pac- kets short of weight was that the sugar trade was rather precarious and the price had gone up. Defendant was fined 20s. and costs. Natizzor or Wirz AND FAMILY.—Wm. Chadwick, 7, Edward-st., Sankey Bridges, was charged with deserting his wife and family on the 10th inst. Mary Jane Chad. wick said that her husband left her and went to live with his mother on the 10th inst., and he had refused to give her more than IN. per week to keep her and her child upon. The magistrates made an order for 95. per week, but expressed the hope that they would live together again.

PICKPOCKETS REWARDED.

At the Borough Court, cri Monday, Annie Yates and Wm. 'tats, 37, Scotland-road, licensed hawkers, were charged with steadng the sum of 2.81. in money from Peter Moss, brieksetter's labourer; in the Crown and Sceptreyard, on Saturday night, and also with stealing the sum of 14s. from John Farrar, co the same night. The Chief . Gsostable said the prisoners came into the town on Wedeesgay, and had, beep staying at Daisy's lodeing•house, Scotland-road. Co Saturday night, Mess wa3 drinking a glass of beer in the Currier's Arms,when the female prisoner went in and spoke to hirn,and asked him tostand treat, and afterwards asked him to come outside. Be put the money he had in his hand in his pocket, and the female prisoner immediately put her hand in his pocket and took the money, and r. :n away to the Boar's Head, Town Hill, where the male prisoner was, and the woman cried out "I want you to come cut William, there is a man following me." On Moss corn- ing up, the.male prisoner told him that the woman was his wife and threatened to strike him. The police were informed and Con.tables Evans and Fish apprehended the prisonerS at 930, and charged them with the offence. The other charge of stealing from Farrar,was a stronger case. The woman came up to him in Buttermarket-st., and asked him to stand her a glass of beer. She after- wards put her hand in his pocket, and whilst doing so, the stale priraner cam' up and held his (the complain- ant's) hands behind him. The woman ran away with the money, and the male prisoner struck Farrar several blows and felled him to the ground, and while on the ground the prisoners escaped. After evidence by the Constables and others, the Bench sentenced the female prisoner to one month's hard 'labour on both charges, and the male prisoner one mosth's bard labour on the second charge.

Thomas Roach, a forge labourer, was brought before the bornu,gh magistrates, on Monday, charged with stealing, from the house 0/ Mary Sheridan, a widow, 3, Back Raydock-street, jewellery to the value of £3 Si„ OR the 16th May last year. From the evidence it ap- peared that the prisoner came to Warrington on the 14th May, and lodged with the complainant, hie aunt, until Monday the 16th, when the jewellery was missed, and the prisoner never returned. Information was given to the police, and they ascertained that the prisoner had tried to pledge the articles at Mrs. Tunstalls' pawnshop, but his aoswers not being satisfactory, she refused to take them in. Nothing farther was heard of the prisoner until five o'clock on Sunday when he again called on his aunt. He was arrested by D.S. Monaghan, and in answer to the charge of stealing the articles he said "I took them and add them in Yorkshire. I will pay her for them if .he will only give me time." The magistrates Rave him two Months hard labour. EMBRZZLEMENT DT A CLOTHING CUM COLLECTOR.

George Win. Dixon, was charged at the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, with embezzling and stealing three separate sums of is., kis., and 25., between Feb. 27th and March 13th. Mr. Arthur Browne, who pro- secuted said that prisoner was remanded from Friday, when he was charged with obtaining money under false pretences from Mrs. Shelrnerdine. Prisoner was a col- lector for the Provident Clothing Club, of Bradford, of 'which there was a Warrington branch under the super- intendency of Mr. Knowles. Prisoner had been dis- charged by Mr. Knowles, hut had collected some money after be had been discharged. An examination of the books had been made and it was found that £8 in odd shillings was missieg, hot, the company had resolved only to prosecute for the above sums. Mr. Knowles in- formed the prisoner th4t he would have him locked up, whereupon he fled and went to Newcastle, and the police had to bring him from that place. A letter was sent to prisoner's father asking him to refund the money, but he refused. Prisoner was sentenced 0 two month's bard labour.

div.head: SENT TO " CLIO."
div.p: SENT TO " CLIO."

Leah Briars, William-street, was again brought before the borough magistrates on Wednesday, charged with neglocti lig to send her boy James Edward (13) regularly to school; The case had been remanded from the pre- vious day, in order that the boy might be present, being absent to; doubt in order that he might not be" sent away." The magistrates on the suggestion of Mr. Riley committed the boy to the " Clio " until he was sixteen. On hearing the decision his mother used some not very complimentary language to Mr. Riley. She exclaimed 4' yeu cat you've got nothing else to do, but send little lads away, and don't cry lad for him, he is not worth crying for." . A QUARTER SESSIONS CASE. At the Liverpool County Quarter Sessions, on Tuesday Toni Barber, 21 years of age, described as a labourer, was charged with having stolen at Warrington, on the '2Bth July, a pair of men's trousers, a black cloth vest, two boots and a pawn ticket, the moperty of Daniel Davi.s, end was committed to gaol for three months. The local magistrates on the bench were Col. McCor- quodale, Mr. Comber, and Captain Withington. RIVAL CREDITORS.

At the Warrington Police Court on Friday, Thomas Holbrook and Maggie Ryan wars charged with assault- ing and beating Frank Garrett on the 13th inst. There Was also a cross-summons against Garrett for assaulting and beating Mamas Holbrook and Maggie Ryan, on the -Same date.—Mr. Arthur Browne appeared for Garrett, and Mr. fl. J. Longtan for Holbrook and Ryan.—Mr. Browne said that Garrett was manager far John riarrop, furniture dealer in Bridge-st. Mr. ,Barrop was the largest 'creditor of Messrs. Cohen who kept a place of businass in Rylands-5t., some time ago, and when that place closed, he took over the book debts of Messrs. -Cohen, one of which was a hiring debt against Mrs. Ryan, the female defendant. As she did not pay, an -execution was taken out against her, but when the bailiffs went to execute the warrant, they found that the house was tenanted under the name Maggie Rabbit, who, however, was the same person as Maggio Ryan. On Garrett being informed, he went to the house, and found that the furniture was exactly the same as the hiring debt was for. He accordingly went with the bailiffs to execute the warrant ; -but when they arrived at the louse, they found Mr. Holbrook, who collected the rent for the house,lnside. Mr. Garrett and a bailiff named Faulkner 'went into the house when Holbrook said "You must not take Anything from here. There is some rent owing." , Mr. Garrett, however, trld the bailiffs to do their duty, and he himself took a chair in one bond, and a pan ia the other. While he had these articles in his hands, Mr. Holbrook sois,.4 him by the collar, and tore it open. Garrett drepred the articles in his hands, and got hold 1' of Mr. Holla-oak to defcrid himself, and while he was in ,1 that position ha was struck behind the head by the defendant Ryan. 'They were parted by Faulkner, and the arle:= the house were afterwards taken. Gar- rett, Alfred F whiner, sad Thomas Stone bore out Mr. Browne s statement. —Mr. Langton said that Mr. Garrett was not a bailiff. and had no right to go to the house at all, but should leave it to the bailiffs. Mr. Holbrook had come the same afternoon as the bailiffs and Garrett had maw, to make a distraint for rent. It appears that he and Gerrett got bold of different ends of a table. and both struggled for it, when Garrett sized , Holbrook and knocked him away. Holbrook WAS after- wards 3AS:Sill!,ii in-the entry. Afterwards Garrett .was abonz, to go upstairs, when Mrs Ryan told him he should, not go up bui: 11, pushed her on nine side and went up. Be (Mr. l'.nnutra) contended that Mr. Garrett had no Tight to o into the house at all. Mr. Holbrook, Mrs. an, niunci:,everal other witnesses gave evidence, after •*.l!--:illsthllti the rnagistratrs dismissed the case ordering each • side to pay their own coats.

Robinson, and Joseph Bushill,youths were charged with gaming with cards off York-st., on the Bth inst.—The Superintendent said in consequence of the complaints made with regard to this practice he had been obliged to put men out in plain clothes.—The whole of the defendants had been previously convicted for gaming, and they were each fined ss. and costs or 7 days. A NIIISANCE.—David Watkin,provision dealer,Church- st., was summoned for having the ashpit and rivy of his premises in a detective condition, through being tin- paved.—Mr. Lake, law clerk to the Board of Commis- sioners said Mr. Watkin was willing that an order should be made upon him rtallinq upon him to remedy the nuis- ance within a month.—The defendant said this action I had arisen out of a misunderstanding. The order was made, and defendant paid costs of a guinea. A SHIP CANAL Row.—James Applegate, of The Ruts, Big Field, was summoned for assaulting Thomas Walker, a gatekeeper, at the same place in the employ of Mr. Jackson, contractor.—Mr. Lake appeared for the com- plainant. The complainant's duty was to regulate the traffic to and from the yard and on the afternoon of the 6th inst. the defendant came to the gate with a cartload of furniture. As he had not a "clearance note" from the timekeeper or the cashier, complainant refused to allow him to leave, whereupon the defendant assaulted Wm.—The defendant denied striking the gatekeeper.— The Bench imposed a fine of 10s. and costs £1 Us. 3d. The defendant wore two ribbons and two medals, one of which VMS a Victoria Cross. DRUNEENNESS.—James Ilix, Jno. Coleman, Mathew MeMoban, were each fined ss. and costs for this offence. this season was won by the "Saints," ard the Widnesians were anxious to get (eve!. The home team had a strum contingent, but Widne9 were short of Drummond, Bren- nan, and Barber. Up to the interval the game was a good one, both sets of backs showing smart form, The "Saints" were the first to score, Cross and Little giving Doherty a nice chance which he availed himself of, and play being rushed immediately afterwards to the other end, Clarke sprinted in at the corner. Neither try was converted,and the "Saints" having the advantage of the wind in the second half, had most of. the play, but were only able to score twice by Doherty and Sudlow. Foulkes converted one, and another win for St. Helens was re- corded, the final result being—St. Helens, one goal, two tries ; Widnes, one try. The Saints" were the better combination, all their backs exhibiting excellent form, the passing of Cross and Little and the kicking of Foulkes being very clever. Widnes had a strong set of forwards, bat of the backs only Alford, Clarke, and Wright played good football. Towards the end of the first half the breaking up of a sarummage foundGraliam, of St. Helens, and Gordon. of Widnes, indulging in a wrestling bout, which started in the Westmorland style, hut developed into a match under the Marquis of Queensberry rules. The referee's attention was attracted, and Mr.Beswick promptly ordered both men off the field. It is expected that the matter will be reported to the County Committee.

RUGBY. LANCASHIRE CUP COMPETITION. WARRINGTON V. BROUGHPON RANGERS.

Although the present Rugby season is fast drawing to a close, the interest is maintained in many quarters,and the Broughton Rangers' ground on Saturday was lined by an enthusiastic crowd who had assembled to witness the return match between the above clubs. The general opinion was that Warrington would confirm the result of the first meeting, though not in so decisive a manner, for on that occasion the Rangers were sent home de- feated by a goal and four tries to nil. The Rangers played the four three-quarter system, and had a repre- sentative team, but Warrington were minus the services of that capital half back John Bate, who had not re- covered from an injury received at Runcorn the previous Wednesday. Kicking off against the wind,

Warrington were almost scorers in the first minute, and Hacking was indeed lucky to save at the second time of asking. Campbell got away with a line out, and reached the half way flag, but capital passing by Donohue, Thornily, and Bate again placed the visitors on the aggressive. Bate and Evang at this early stage asserted their superiority, and following some clever passing by this pair, eventually saw the former throw- ing to Barnes and Potts taking up the running, Hacking pulled up the three-quarter on on the verge of scoring. The home forwards again relieved ,and Boscow responded ' well, and his forwards offering a disregard bar the off- side law the homesters took the penalty kick. Barnes responding. Warrington continued to attack, and sev- eral of their passing displays did not fail to elicit cheers. Barnes kicked to Green, who got the oval away well, and mulling by a Warringtonian saw Boscow tested, but he met the opposition well, taking the oval from their feet and directing it to touch near the half-way. Jolley and Turner were conspicuous in some loose play, and then Bate negatived an effort by Ashton, and Barnes and Potts taking up the running, the latter forced the lirst minor. Boscow met the drop-out in true style, but the reply saw Potts tackled, and for the next few minutes the visitors were hard pressed. Davies gallantly came to the rescue, dribbling to the half-way, but the next moment saw a change come over the game for a beautiful passing display, initiated by Wild, and taken up by Chapman and Hacking, saw Ashton racing over for

A Grand Try, which Chapman turned to account. Soon after the restart Ashton again tried to effect the downfall of the home goal with a long drop, but this time the oval went outside, and following this let off came a determined raid by the visitors, ably led by Jolley and Berry in one rush. Ashton supplemented this with another dribble, whilst a penalty kick brought about a permanent attack A mark to Evans was more than equalized by the judicious kicking of Green and Ashton, but Warrington, by the aid of the clever play of their half backs and the unselfish passing of the three-quarters severely har- rassed the home defence. Again relief was forthcoming to the Rangers when Oman led his men to half-may, and here Cleminson and Berry became conspicuous in one tussle on the touch line, the visitor getting the better of the argument. After Bate had travelled past half- way Thorniley got well away from a line out, and pass- ing nicely to Barnes, the latter eventually threw across to Potts from amidst a host of opponents, and this player 1 taking the chance in fine style scored a meritorious try at the corner, a position too difficult for Fair Turner to turn to account. Another pretty run by Bate, from a I pass by Evans, was supplemented by good kicking on the part of Heesom, who so far had had but few chancep. Another pretty spell of passing, started by Bate, and taken up by Evans and Heesom, saw the latter Dropping at Goal, but the shot was wide, and Bate raced up for the try, but a plea for off-side being answered in the affirmative, a scrimmage was ordered ten yards from the line. Another passing movement, taken part in by Bate,Evans Barnes, and Heesorn, terminated in another minor. The same ill-luck attenned dribbles by Randles and Jolley, but after Thorniley and Berry had led to the line, the oval fell into the possession of Bate, who after bluffing his opponents, well gained the second try, no goal being forthcoming from the place. This brought about half time with the score—Warringtcn, two tries ; Broughton Rangers, a goal. On resuming, a spell of monotonous forward play occapied attention, the Rangers trying to keep the ball as close as possible. At the outset the kick-off was mulled, but Potts atoned for this mistake when be put the finishing touch to clever play by Higham, Bate, and Evans. After the Rangers had con- ceded a minor, Jolley started a movement which should certainly have ended in something tangible, and only a little

Steadiness was Rewired to have effected the score. However, :he opportunity was allowed to slip, and though the county forward again led the way in an attack originating from a free kick taken by Turner, the visitors failed miserably when near the line. The game was well on in this half before Warrington gained the lead, and following some smart play by Bate, Potts again ran in from half-way, and from this point the play became tame and uninteresting if we expect one brilliant movement started by Evans and taken up by Bate,and the final result read—War- rington, three tries (six points) ; Broughton Rangers,one goal (five points). Warrington: Bhscow, back ;C. , Potts, T. Barnes, and F. Heesom, three-quarter backs ; Alines Bate and J. W. Evans, half backs ; H. Ashton I (captain), Fair Turner, J. Jolley, J. Fligham, J. Berry, I Thorniley, T. Davies, W. Handles, and T. Donohue, forwards. Broughton Rangers : G. El. Woods, back ; F. Ashton, H. Chapman, F. Green, and J. Hacking, three-quarter backs ; F. Wild, and X. Hopkins, half barks ; J. M'Oowan (captain), J. Shaw, S. Oman, J'. Fitton, J. Nowell, T. Cleminson, J. Reeves, and W. G. Campbell, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. H. Smith, Wid- nes.

Cup.—ST. HELENS RECREATION V. BROtrali, TON.—The Recs. had one or two notable absentees frnm this match at Broughton on Saturday, but nevertheless had a fairly strong team. Broughton won the toss, and Seddon started, the ball being returned to half-way. Tali exchanges followed, and Bolton made his mark, and , fast following up prevented a return. Seddon got a pass from Dolan, and dropped at goal. The ball fell short. At half time neither side had scored. After the restart , Shepherd gained a try for Broughton. Theßecs. then played up, and Molleneux dropped a goal. B. Fildes got over for the visitors. Final result Helens Re- creatibn 1 goal 1 try, Broteghton 1 try. RUNCORN V. SWINTON.—The Cheshire champions paid their annual visit to the Swinton ground on Satur- day, and notwithstanding many counter attractions, a- large number of people witnessed the match. Runcorn were minus the services of two of their regular three- qoatters, Crompton and Kingaton and one of their halves-, Abrams, was absent also. drompton'e place was not an easy matter to fill. The Runcorn captain, it seems had played football three or four evenings last week,and on Thursday, in a work's match, he hurt one of his arms very badly, whilst Abrams was unable to play on ac- I count of a nasty knock he-had received over the head in a match against Warringtemon Wednesday evening last. Crompton's place was taken by that sterling forward. W. Faulkner, who not only officiated as centre three- quarter, but also undertook the duty of captain. The opening stages ef the contest were much in favour of Swinton, hut the players appeared to go into the fray in a half-hearted manner, and the only things worth mentioning in the first half were- a magnificent run on the part of Houghton,. the Cheshire full back, who snatched the ball cleverly from the toes of Lomax, , and a run by Burnby, who, having only Houghton to dodge gave one the impression that be had no wish to , challsnge the last-named, into whose open arms he fell 1 and received a warm welcome. Two ininors to Swinton represents the scoring capabilities of the two teams up to half time. Then some life seemed to be put into the play. dwinton at once making tracks for the Runeorn quarters, where the auburnhaired Boltonian (lIa: J. Lomax) was seen to gather the ball in a capital and finished way, and then get into his etride, completing a a mastery piece of work by grounding the ball over the line amidst the plaudits of the assemblage. Rumby, however, did nr-t increase the value of the point. Run- corn now woke up, and for the first time in the match did the respective fifteens get to business in a character- istic maftner. The Cheshire men attacked with great determination, and so well did they succeed that only twice after this to the close did the Lancastrians get past the centre line—once by excellent dribbling an the part of Lomax and Murray, and again by a fast and neatly- executed run by the lithesome Lewis. But though Run- corn attacked in such commendable style, they realised when the crucial point arrived that their adversaries defence was a bit too good for them, and when the referee announced the signal for the cessation of hostil- ities, the visitors had to retire defeated, but by no , means disgraced, by a try to nothing. It is seldom that continuous rounds of applause are given a player in an ordinary club match, but Houghton, the Runcorn full back, met with this kind of thing. Clearing cleverly when hard pressed, he ran almost the length of the field, decig.ine the whole of the Swinton men,an almost certain try being spelled by the man he passed to being tackled. It ia no exa,F,teration to say that it was one of the 110e3t runs ever seen at Swinton, and the home supporters were fairly delighted with it. Tteecoßx v. • STOCKTON HEATH V. PARISH CHIIRCH.—This match was decided at Stockton Heath on Saturday. There was very large attendance of spectators. A start was made a little after the advertised time, and the first to show up were Stockton Heath, who took the ball well down the field, only to see the visitors' front division by smart footwork remove play to half vi ay. It was soon seen 1 that the game would be confined to the forwards, all attempts at open play being frustrated by the sharp tackling of both sets of halves. Bolesworth was prom- inent with a neat run and kick to Woods, who had to find relief by punting into touch. Broady was the means of removing the danger, but the visitors would not be denied, and Lawton and Fricth making no mistake in the tackling line the, home quarters were again reached, Three minors were speedily forced, and then the Heath- ens came away with a rush to the other end. Lawless got away with a tricky piece of work, and Barber also put in a lot of pretty play. A pass from Cross to Barber saw 'Welsby grassing his man near the quarter-flag, and then a throw forward spoiled a sequence of transfers which might have been turned to good account. How- ever the visitors came again, and were having slightly tht, best of it when the whistle was blown for half-time. So far the game had been pretty even, but follawing Mason's re-start the Clitirchites with a grand rush forced their way to the line. The bulk of the back work was devolving on Mason, Garrity, and Carey, on the one side, and Gregory, Cross, and Broady on the other ; and the latter trio had all their work cut out to kenp the visitors at bay. Woods, the home custodian, was at fault on several occasions, and, at last Cross took his place in that position. Time was now close at hand, and the visitors still pressed hard. Neat passing by Garrity, Mason and Daniels, saw the latter held a yard from the line, and tlum Garrity knocked the tall forward when he had an easy journey over, but at the cessation of hostilities the game remained drawn, the score read- ing—Parish Church, 0-0-4 ; Stockton Heath, 0-0-0.
SALFORD v. WARRINGTON.

This match (postponed from November last on account of the prevalence of small-pox in Warrington) was played on the Warrington ground, on Monday evening in dull but line weather. The match practically de- cided the Rugby championship in Lancashire, so far as Salford and Swinton am concerned. There was a splen- did attendance of spectators, numbering upwards of 6,000. Both clubs were strongly represented, the only absentees from the home team being John Bate and Donohue. Sudlow (of St. Helens) assisted Warrington as right wing three-quarter. Salford (who had the help of Parlane, Lancashire County and Manchester Rangers) played only fourteen men, the missing man, Whittaker, of IValkden, failing to catch the train, and as a conse- quence the visitors could only muster eight men in the forwards against their opponents' nine. The play was of a very fast description, Warrington habing slightly the advantage in the tight scrimmages, but they re- peatedly lost opportunities of scoring through erratic passing. Fair Turner Started against the Wind, and the kick off being charged, Thorniley gained pos- session and handed over to Higham, who in his eager- ness to rid himself of the oval passed forward. The Warrington forwards heat the opposing eight, and as a consequence Bate and Evans had frequent opportunities. The former got beautifully away from a pack, tricking Parlane, and running to Paul before he handed over to Potts, for the latter to fumble the easy chance of scor- ing. Smith relieved, and following some capital defen- sive.play Ify Walsh and Parlane, the home forwards rushed to the line, where Jolley's over-anxiety lost a certain score. Bate next tricked Walsh, but again was the finishing stroke at fault, for Evans was well held by Barratt, when a pass to Heesom or Sudlow might have been turned to good account. Another effort by Bate and Evans saw the same order of things as previous attempts,and Salford taking advantage of the homesters' weakness in the scoring department, at last found relief when Evans- was penalised. The kick did not aid the Bede much, for the whole nody of home forwards rushed to the line, and Paul and Barrett were just in time to save. Plots the pack which ensued a sequence of passes between Bate, Evans, Beeson), and Sudlow ended in the latter

Racing over at the corner after a fast sprint, but the kick, taken by Fair Turner, was not turned to account. Paul dropped out, and Boscow's reply found touch at half-way. Bate and Evans continued to monopolite the bulk of the work, and five minutes were engaged in seeing the home halves pulled down on the line. Still Salford's defence was grand, and passing by Walsh and Smith gained slight relief. Twice over Salford were awarded free kicics,.but bscow was safe each time. Potts led the way to the line, and Turner was almost in from a line out. Hard luck attended an effort by Nevins, whilst Jolley ridiculously dropped at goal when a pass to Heesom or Sudlow would have augmented the score. So far Warrington had had all the play,, but a couple more [penalty kicks for the first time afforded Salford a chance ;of invading the home twenty-five. Turner, Thorniley, land Holmes led the way nut of danger, but Salford per- sisted in the attack,., and just before We interval Walsh passed splendidly to Miles, who eluded Sudlow, and placed the sides on an Equal footing. Turner's drop out saw play at half way, and a pass from Bate td Potts again saw liiimpulled up on the line. A fine dribble by .Tolley maintained the attack, but the interval was reached with both sides ono try each. Atter an unusually short interval' Kent restarted for Salford,. the home team again attacking; but Smith and litmt relieved finely, as a consequence of which the visitors had slightly the best of the position Salford- were penalized, but Paul made an effec- tive reply, and the home team were forced back to their goal line. Sudlow had an opportunity to run through his opponents, but he nutde a throw forward, and Salford kicked into touch. From a pass by Walsh Barrett got in a drop kick, which enabled Boscow to make a mark, and play in the Salford half followed. The play at this point of the game was very fast and es7zeiting, and the visitors were again severely pressed. Parlane, Walsh. and Miles, relieved at a critical moment, the latter collaring Bate finely when he was making, a strong rush for the Salford goal-line. A minor point fell to Warriwton, and this was the last incident in an extremely hard-fought game. The light was then so bad that the referee called time before it had fully expired, the game ending in a draw, the score standing—one try each. Salford now stand at the top of the competition table, being one point above, Swinton. The following were the

Teams : Salford : A. G. Paul, full back ;:F. Miles (captain), A. Barratt, and J. Smith, threequarter backs ; S. Walsh and W. Parhme, half backs ;:T. Kent, F. King,T. Craven, F. Knowles, A. Knowles, G. Cartwright, S. Haslem, and F. Brierley, forwards. Warrington : J. Boscow, full back ; C. Petts, F. Heesoraond T. Sudlow, threaquarter hacks ; James Bate, and J. W. Evans, half backs, H. Ashton (captain),F. Turner, J. Jolley, W. Nevins. W. Rand'es, J. T. Thorniley, J. Higham, W. Berry, and J. Holmes, forwards. Touch-line judges : Messrs. R. lValrasley (Salford) and W. Povey (Warrington). R&e. feree e. Mr. E. Seddon (Broughton Rangers.) WARRINGTON A V. SALFORD. A.—The meeting of these teams at Salford on Monday night was invested with a great amount of intereet, as the home team had a few weeks previously, been heavily defeated at Warring,ton and a crowd of about 4-,000 were present. Salford played the identical "IS" that did duty in the pyeaious encounter, but unfortunately Warrington hadla poor team. Salford played down bill and after pressirg the visitors on their lines, some weak play by the visitors backs, found Barrett running in, right behind the posts after smart pas.sing,. Oswald kicked an easy goal. With this strong lead tha Sallordians again attaG4ced and in a short space of time, another exhibition of weakness and in decision, allowed Ashton to get in bohind the posts and Oswald placed a second goal. Them Warraeg- ton had a spell of attacking but the forwards receiving little support from the backs, the point of vantage was. quickly lost. Sumo kicks were indulged inlay the War- rington backs, hut so little judgement was. used that no ground was gained, and with the above score ends wive changed. Upon the resumption the Warrington for- wards ctsickly made a raid on the Salfoed citadel but the former weakness was quite, apparent and the inatAity . of the visitors' backs loosing all the. advantage gained by t} front rank. Again the visiting forwards attacked gaining a strong foothold under their opponents goal- posts, but Ow backs were unable to. seize the opportuni- tia which presented theinselvesand danger was. relieved h--y Oswald. Salford then rushed to the other end but . the stay was of short duration for the Warringtonians [again raised the siege, Ashurst intercepting a pass and getting clean in. The point, however, was disallowed for some cause and amidst great jiibilation the New Darns champions retAr4 nztuners by 2 goals to nit,

ST. ELPHIN'S V. BartnacKs.—This.rwatch was played on the Cricket Ground before a gate 0 close upon 2,1100.' The Rector (Rev. F. W. Willis) kicked off. Marsnall staved off the opening danger, and a beautiful cerztro nearly scored. The Saints kept the upper hand; Higgth- bottom made a good attempt, but I&Bride repeatedly showed himself a good custodian. The soldiers then came away with a rush,and scored what look'td,like a goal.Simiu- lar had luck betel the Saints,a fine centre by Taylor being headed over the bar by Higginbottorni From the goal kick, Turner got possessirin, but was robbed by Clayton, who, however, shot too high. Play ruled fast, a pretty run up,the left by Hatton and Taylor resulting in a goal from the latter. Play was now confinedto midfield, but 'Turner getting possession eluded Placeniw and sending across to Spenter, he scored with a magnificent shot, thus equalizing matters. Scarisbrick restarted with the wind at his back, and the Saints were early, to the front, but the Barraairs' backs used their weight to advantage, Hatton then had a chance, but shot wide. The soldiers now took up the attack, Spencer centreing beautifully, but Marshalbrebeved with a huge kick, and J. Colley raced along the right only to be despoiled by Reed. However, the Saints kept up a forcing pme, and Mcßride further showed his capabilities as a goalkeeper., Clayton shot in,„Jones conceding a cerner,..which was quickly followed by another, both being unpreductive. Time was called with the barracks pressing :—St. Elphin's one, Barracks one. It was decided to,play an extra half liourra quarter each way. No goakt,resulted in the first quarter, but in the second, from a Awe kick for hands, Clayton nicely placed the ball. Seariebrick rushed the ball through seemingly with his hands, but the referee ruled a goal. 'This only made the soldiers play with moredeternaination, and Plicenix missing hie kick Turner sent in a long drooping shot whiala, Bates ought to have saved, but he misjudged the ball. Time was called immediately after, the game being a draw of two goals each.

WARRINGTON' Irl 11111131.--This match was play at Penketh,on Saturday,before a fair number of spectators. Warrington, winning the toss, elected to play up-hill and agaicst the wind, and Lymm started the game. The game had not progressed far before the arringtqn for-, wards had the Lymt s. men on the defensive,and Radford gaining possession passed to Ball, who sent in a spiritool shot and the Lvmm custodian in trying to clear turned the ball through the goal. The Lyrnm men new resorted to rough rather than goodplay,and fouls were of frequent occurrence. Howeverowing to a creditable bit of work by Thornton, who dribbled well up the field and finished up with shooting a gnal,the Warrington men were placed two goals ahead of their opponents. Nothing further was scored up to half4time. On re-starting Warrington, forced the. play and found the Lymm backs plenty of work to do. The play was most vigorous, oftitrxs amounting to rough-tglay. Thompson, of Lymm, was cautioned by the referee, and shortly afterwards was ordered off the field. Nothing having been scored in this half, Warrington eventually ran out winners of a hard-fought game by two goals to nil.

ST. ELPHIN'S V. 011 FORD BIRRACKS.—These teams r& - played their semi-final tie on the Cricket Ground, at Arpley, on Tuesday night., There were about 1,500; spectators present. StfElphins kicked off in the direction of the railway, and the soldiers paid a briet visit to their opponent's goal, but shot wide. For about ten minutes. after tli is.the Saintpennect their opponents in their goal: The goalkeeper, however, did splendid work, and saved numerous warm shots, but was at length, compelled to • coneede a corner,which was fruitless. The soldiers then got away and in their turn gained a corner which was well saved by Colley. The Farracks men were now hav- ing the best of it. but Cook, Colley, and Tickle kept them at bay, and Marshall also had to fist out. A splen- did bout of passing ty,the Saint's forwards took opera- tions to the opposite end, but their progress was stopped by Jones, who by a huge kick transferred play again before the Saint's goals and a shotiust grazed the goal post. Marshall had to clear several warm shots, and half time came with A clean. sheet. After the interval' both goals were visited' and Mcßride had to fist out a warm shot from Tayl,lr, Owners fell to both sides,and the game was very exciting, long scrimmages were very frequent before theloal posts. At length, after about twenty minutes play. Hatton got through, amid great excitement, from a scrimmage. The soldiers tried hard to equalise, but Colley, Marshall and Cook, were too good for them, and 'towards the end of the game, St. Elphin's had the upper hand,Claytoa and Taylor sending in warm shots, which Moßride only just saved. After a most exciting game the final result was St. Elphin's, 1 goal ; Orford Barracks, nil.

THE BETTING 'RAID
AT WAARINGTON.
POLICE PROCEEDINGS.-lIEAVY PENAM.

At the Warrington Police Court on Monday be- 'fore Mr. F. Monks (chairman), Alderman Fran- - comb, Councillor Roberts, and Messrs. William Pier- point, mid 8. Wright, Richard Rash aw, of the Big Horse ehoe, Horsemarket-street, Warrington, was chlerged that on the 13th inst.,he unlawfully used the said house for the purpose of betting for persons rescutting thereto. The Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle) appeared for the prosecution, and Mr. Mulholland of Liveepool, instructed by Mr. Arthur Browne, , defended. Before-proceeding with the case, the Town Clerk wished to amendthe summons by adding March 21st in addi- tion to ths-12th and lath inst. This was in connection wth the Lincolushire Handicap. The magistrates allowed tke amendment of the summons. , The Town Clerk said that the prosecution was taken under the Bet- ting Act of 1963;in which aoy person, using his house for the purpose of betting:, shall be Habits to a fine of £lOO or ' six months ireprisonnitert. The facts of the case were as ;follows I—On Wednesday, the IjAily heft. in the evening, a mad named George Mazel came to. the police office, and from what he said, respecter Spinks went to defendant's place cf besinest, and said to him ,"*This man bar made a complaint that he made a bet with you and VOll -refuted. to pay him.," upon whichl defendant said thin it was not true, as- he bed not made a bet for two yew*: Inspeotorepinks then told defend-1 ant that Hazel had" said that he had seen two farmers Snaking bets with him that day. On. the folio-wing day, a warrant was proaUred, and a raid was-made upon de- fenditat's premises t* Idspectors Spinks,Cimound Bowen, andother plice offer. Inspector Wats- told defend- ant'the object of thebt visit and asked himeo give me all things pertaining to betting. He replied that he had no betting books, and had not done any betting since "somebody died." The warrant was then read at de- fendant's request, and the officers then proceeded to searctotho premises. Olsieta defendant were fbund two telegrams to" Paradox, which was defendant's racing narne,• and which undoubtedly referred to. racing. A book was also found in which were entries teethe City and Soburban race run on April 12th: Ofher papers were alsefeeind on defendant's premises and elate& great number of telegrams all ealating to betting; as also rac- ing card*. and calendars. • SoMe of the telegrams' were addressed. to defendant in Ids own name, and others were addressed in his ractsg 'name "Paradox" When defendant' was searched he. 'was told he weird have to go to the pollee station. Be-replied that he had main no bets for over two years. He"only took bets on commis- sion, and pet 5 per cent, on the wins. Be was brought before Mr. 'Garnett, J.P.; on Thursday afternoon, when. he made the same admission. The defence seemed to contend thae defendant was justified in taking bets on commissionti.but he (the Town Clerk) contended that' that WAS no answer to the charge, as the houee had been used betting. On the 12th Aprialazel made two bete with, ; defendant, osier for himself, and another jointlywith'isitne self abd a friend, and while he was there, two farmers also made bete for the came race, the City and SebUrban.. The same witness, Hazel, also stated that he had made a bet on the Lincoln Handicap on March 21st. George Hazet,. who was then called, said that he was an insurance agent. On April 12th he went intedefene- dant'e premisma. to make a bet. He put 2s; 61. ore. Windgall, at the City and Suburban Time, at 5 to.l.and as. fid. for a plafie. The former was fot himself and the, latter was for a friend. Defendant took the bet and booked it. While witness was In the house, two farmers- ' also put somq:money on a horse. Windgall came second in the race, and witness went at night to defend- ant's house for tile: money. Defendant tvplied that he • thought witness lead had some drink and he Must come for it the following day. Witness refused to go, and :another man knocked him over the table, and some 'glasses were broken. He afterwards made a complaint •to the police. With, reference to the Lincolu Handietto , witness could not Mee the exact date. ' Cross-examined by Mr. Mulholland, witness said he was not drunk on. April 12, and had no drink to his dinner. There wenetwo friends present when lie made. the bet, one named Mr. Kirke. He did not know the farmers' names, whansade the bet. ,He came, in the evening to be paid between seven and nine o'clock, .and • ,was not drunk them.end was not put out of the house with the assistance of the police, nor 'by defendant's wife. He was assaulted from behind when talking to ,Mr. Kilseaw. Mr. l'Ufshaw afterwards said he had made no bet, When witness brought Inspector Spinks' defend- ant said that it was untrue that he had made a bet. Witness was not awarethat he was liable to be prosecuted. ,This was the first time he bad demanded money for betn thig, and had claimed' no money from any person upon a i. horse named Wolfe Ciag, and knew nothing whatever about that horse. The bet on the 12th inst. Was only the second bet he had ever made either for hirnstell•br anyone else. Richard Singleton was present when the bet was made, and when the bother took place, .he cleared off, saving hadid not want to get into trouble. -=—lnspector Spinks corroborated the facts concerni n g the taid, detailed by the, Tewn Clerk. Cross-exstnined by Me.. Mulholland: Head not say to Mr. Kilshaw that he ',believed him when he•said he had not made any bets for two years. He knew that Messrs. Greenall had warned defendant about two years since nut to make bets. He was sure that defendant admitted to the magistrate that he made bets on commission in his house. The witness Hazel was not drunk when he carne to the police statitm. 'lnspector Spinks then pointed out the articles he found upon defendant's person, which Mr. Mulholland examined and read from one of the books amid great ' laughter "To be raffia for, a fat goose." Inspector Bowen corroborated last witness. He was present when defendant was brought before Mr. Garnett and eculd corroborate Inspector Spinks' statement as. to defendant saying that he took bets on commission in his house.
Inspector Cox also corroborated Inspector Spinks' evidence. .

Mr. Mulholland, in his speech for the defence, se,d,it 'was not a criminal ofinue to make a bet, it was cot a criminal offence to be w book maker, nor to keep a bet- ting book. The only criminal offence in reference to the matter was to keep ortiee a house for the purpose of bet- ting. Their Worships must he satisfied that the house in question was used and habitually used openly for that ' purpose. Defends nt was not charged under the Licen- sing Act at all. If he were, he could. be examined and give his own account of the case, Imt for some rcason, the police-acted under an earlier Act; the • Betting Act. Under this Act,the person keeping a. house fer the purpose of betting, and the persons resorting thereto were equally lablfs to be prosecuted. Wei of the documents seized in defendant's house were not of the slightest importance, eneept two betting booksv.which were locked up ln the safe. The principal evidence against defendant was-by the man Hazel,who wc.ii liable to be prosecuted, and mile was the prover, he must he corroborated according. to law. This man said that he made bets thc day before the police searched tl.lhouse. Yet after the summons had been amended by adding the , 21sat March, from his information, he could not confirm I what he had said. Htcseid that another perms named Mike was with him at the time that the bet wet taken, and why was Kirke not called ? He mentionedqs person named Singleton, but that person would tell them that he knew of no bet. The facts of the present ease were these. Until about two years agr*, defendant used the house openly and admittedly for betting. He wes Warned by the landlord. He-was net going to deny that-defend- ant still did bet on commission, but he did it, as any licensed victualler might do. He did not uso, his house for that purpose. name " Paradox " had+ been men- tioned, and Inspector Spinks said it war,defendant's- racing address. There was no proof that it was his rac- ing address, and tne•Post Office did not ta:te any notico. of a racing addresso., but only registered the name and I address to which the telegram was to be sent. A man I might also be a bookmaker and yet not break the Betting Act, so long as he did not use his house for the purpose of the bookmaking. A book with a number-43f names had been found in prisoner's possession,and Izspector Spinks seemed to be kindly disposed towards those gentletufn, as he would not tell their names. Why did he not bring some of. them to prove that defendant Kul used his house for the purpose el3etting ? With regard to,what defend- ant said before Mr. Garnett, defendan4 had instructed him that he had- said that he admitted making bets on commission,but hehad never used the house for an illegal purpose. As to the man Hazel, defendant had to put him out for a disturbance,and he would like to ask.,their Worships whether,if defendant had made a bet,he would I not rather hav3 paid the ss. which he owed, than to have the police brought in and have this sezions charge brought against him. Richard Singleton was then called ad said time he was a superannuated member of the police force,,Jind an insurance agent, and had been a Mend of • Zoit. Ho was in thapublic house on the 12th inst., and saw no het mado,. Hewes there also he the evening.and saw the disturbance. • He was sure there was no bet made while he was in the house. Cross-examined by;the Tomb. clerk., Ile went to the publio-house to collect. 113 sometimes went there three times in one weak. He doid• not go there tomake bets, and had never mode any bees in the house. With regard to tit° bother on the night of the 12th inst., he did not know what it N,49 about, and did net notice anything being said about a horse 'race. He had Visited the house for many years aud did not , know it was a betting house. _ _

Albert Kilshaw said he yeas a farmer in Burtonwood, and was brother to the defendant. He-vaas in that house on April 13th, when the polioe came ich He visited the house two or three times a week, but had seenno bett- ing for some years. Martha Walker, domestic servant„ at the Ng Horse Shoe, also said that although there was betting up to about two years ago, there had beea none to her know- ledge since. The magistrates retized to consider the case,and when they returned after about five mutes consultationsthey announced that they had resolved to fine defendant £25, or in default threoatonths' hard labour.

MURDEROUS ASSAULT ON A SISTER AT WIDNES. '

At Widnes ,Police Court. on Monday, before Mr. Deacon, a rough-looking fellow, named Christopher Daley, 9, Caroline-street, was placed in the dock charged with having wounded his sister, Annib Daley, with, intent to do her grievous bodily harm. Superintendent Keighley stated that prisoner went home drunk on Saturday night, and commenced to quarrel with his sister, who went into the front room out of his way.' Prisoner followed her, and it was alleged pulltd her down, struck her with the chair produced, and then kicked and jumped upon her, inflicting a very serious wound. Dr. Allen said he exammedthe injured woman at the police station, and found a wound over the right eye on, the forehead 4 inches long penetrating to the bone. There were numerous bruises on the face. 'She had lost a quantity of blood, and cotnplained of having • been kickea all over the body. The wound was a serious one, and considerable violence must have been used to cause it. The woman would be unable to appear for at least a week. P.O. Reid said he ,apprehended prisoner j at 9, Caroline-street, where he found Annie Daley lying 1 on the fluor, and prisoner standing over her with two men holding him. She was covered with blood. When at the police station prisoner threatened to kill his sister before a month was over, and without saying anything j more he picked up a kettle of boiling wa'.er from the fire in the parade room, and threw it at his sister, but ! did not hit her. The ,prisoner was remanded for a week.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Tuestiay in the Town Ball. There were then present Mr. 11. Wade Deacon (in tht§ chair), Revs. Dean Finegan, G. IL Garrett, Jos. Clarke, and Messrs. It. anaw, S. Quinn, J. C. Barlow, D. Lewis, and G. B. Danby (clerk).

div.head: DISTRICT. .E.DUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: DISTRICT. .E.DUCATION COMMITTEE.

This cormnittee reported that during the, month of March, the number of cases summoned before the co in- mittge were :—Applications for free places, 98 ; for contravention of Education Act, 189 ; free places granted 189 ; number of prosecutions before the magis- trates, 40 ; number of convictions, 39 ; withdrawn tile. —Before the leport was adopted Dean Einegaz drew attentionito the very erratic attendances at the schools, He said that it was common for 20 children who were present at school in the morning to be abteut in the evening.=-11,1r.Quinn : Is it not a fact that there were mea- ls in the vicinity of some of the schools.—Dean Finegan No ; and it there were measels they we,uld not attach children in the afternoon and not in the morning. (Laughter). The report was adopted.
SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this Guinnduce reported that the Corn- mi.tee had let the West Bank Infant School playground to the Tenn ks Club,from six to nine o'clock each evening, until Septemutr 1893, for the sum at 2s. ed. per week and fixed the remuneration of the caretaker fur attending the same, at 4s. per week, the club to pay for any damage done to the property. This report was adopt- ed.

div.head: FINANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: FINANCE COMMITTEE.

The accounts for the month notified by this Committee were :—District education committee £3l 12s. 9d. ; School management committee £461 11s. 4d. ; finance committee £529 17s. sd. The committee also stated that since their last, report the following sums had been paid into the bank,asscht.ol fees tor March :—From Slunn's Cross bchool, £l3 Ms.6J. ; Warrington-road school, £6 15s. 6d. ; West Bank school, £9 18s. ;, £3O 10s. ; hooks sold to children—Simin's Cross schools, £7 Bs. id.
