Fee grants Simm's Cross school £l6l 17s. 6d. ; Warrington-road school, £7O 17s. 6d. ; Wear Bank school, £l2O 7s. 6(11; hire of rooms, £5 us. The offal' receipts amounted to £403 Os. 9d. The report was adopted. Thero was no other business.
PRESENTATION £0 MR. J. S. TIMMIS,

div.head: J.P., OF WIDNEg.
div.p: J.P., OF WIDNEg.

Previous to the transaction of the ordinary business of the meeting of the Widnes School Beard, held on Tuesday afternoon, a testimonial was presented by the members to the former Chair- man, Mr, J. Sutton Timmis, J.P. The testimonial was an artistically designed illuminated address. The. Clerk read the following letter from Dr. °lite& :—" Brendan Ilouse,—Dear Mr. Danhy,-1 regret that 1 cannot be present at the meeting of the richool Board to-morrow in consequence of being subpcened to attend at the Quarter Sessions. My regrets are all the greater for not being able to take part in the preseatation to our late esteemed Chairman, Mr. J. S. Timmis. I should like to bear my testimony to the able and dignified and courteous manner in which he presided over our deliberations for a great number of years, and when he had to rule on order, his ruling was se fair and impartial in my opinion that he might be compared to the celebrated Athenian general and judge, who gained the name of Aristides the Just. I have still I further if not stronger ,reasons for the tribute of esteem and regard 1 entertain for Mr. .1. Sutton Timmis and if I ; only mention one it will suffice for the others. The 'generous and munificent gift which he has lately given to the people of Widnes to promote the superior educa- tion of the rising generation deserves the grateful thanks of the community at large, and ii I had the pleasure of being present at the meeting te-morrow I would have much pleasure in saying to him "sere in corium re- deas.7 I hope you will make my apologies for being absent.—Yours faithfully., J. Mc N. O'Kuirravx." Mr. H. Wade Deacon, who was in the chair, address- ing Mr. Thnmis, said they had invited him there that afternoon to tpresent him with a mark ef their esteem that might serve, in future years, to remind him of the pleasant times he had passed amongst them as Chairman of that Board. The Board was formed in 1874, be believed, and Mr. Tinamis had had the hon- our or being one of their first members, and he had filled the office of chairman for something like 12 years. 'raking everything into consideration he considered that Widnes School Board had fulfilled its duties and much of the credit of that was due to the impartial yet firm and successful manner in which Mr. Timmis had conducted the Board as president.. By his resignation the town had suffered a great loss, and the members of that Board had lost the frrendly presence of one of their most popu- lar and genial and useful colleagues. But although Mr. Timmii had resigned, he had left his work behind. By his generous gift in establishing scholarships in connec- tionwith Yaruworth Grammar School, the Board would be able to continue the grants which had hitherto been made by the Council of Education, and which had proved such great blessings to those who had taken ad- vantage oh them. The Board a,sked Mr. Thannis not to accept the address for its intrinsic value, but as a mark and expression of esteem in which his services to the cause of education were held by them, and he (the chair- man), on their behalf, expressed the wish that ho might have many years of happiness and health before him. The Rev. Father Clarke, in endorsing the tribute of the Chairman, said Mr. Timmis presided over the pro- ceedings of the Board with an impartial but strong hand, for his services bad met the approbation of the whole Board. The public would also know how to appreciate the generous, gift he had given in furtherance of the cause of education in Widnes. v • Mr. Hobert Shaw, the Rev. Dean Finegan and Mr. Lewis also gave their testimony to the benefits con- ferred by Mr. Timmis upon education at Widnes. Mr. Timmis briefly acknowledged the gift and said that although he had ceased to be a member of the Board he should continue to take great interest in its proceedings, and so far as the cause of education was concerned he was always willing to comribute his ser- vices and labours on its behalf.

div.head: Renfro to tin etttor.
div.p: Renfro to tin etttor.
THE "JERUSALEM BAZAAR."

Sir,—l take this the earliest opportunity of thanking on behalf of the Clergy of St. Alban's, all those kind friends who supported and encouraged us by their pre- sence, their gifts, and their monetary help in our last week's sale of work. We are conscious that many gener- ous helpers are not numbered among our parishioners, and, therefore,we appreciate their sympathy the more. In spite of dull trade in the town, and only partial work at several of our large establishments, we are sanguine Df raising a substantial sum, which we hope shortly to publish in your Columns. Everyone who visited the bazaar knows what an at- traction Mr. Down's excellent band was, and to him and his family and bandsinen we are very much indebted for the ,'acrifice they made for us. Besides the lady stall- holders and their assistants who have already had our thanks and recognition, we cannot easily pass over our Executive Committee, viz., Messrs. C. Unsw-irth, L. Voisey, jun., H. Houghton, A. Marsh, A. Brookes, and W. Turner.
Thanking you in anticipation for the insertion of this letter.—Yours, ttc.,

div.head: THOMAS B. FEENY.
div.p: THOMAS B. FEENY.
Saint Alban's, April 18th, 1893.
THANKS TO CONTRIBUTORS.

Sir,—Permit use to offer my thanks (through the VExaminer") "Isoe" end " Flury Esmond " for their able and interesting letters aspublished in the "Examiner" It is, I think,more than probable that many besides my self would, if they had the personal opportunity, also thank them. On the other hand, many would condemn them,—more especially the clerics, inasmuch as they have had the temerity to discuss questions which be- lone exclusively to their "divinely(?) appointed "order thereby rendering themselves fit subjects for that terri- ble place as portrayed by tho late Mr. Spurgeon, and as quoted in Mr. Esmond's last letter. It is cheering to the reasoning mind to know that "we are living in an age remarkable for its independence of thought." The time dizit of our fellow man, separate from cerroborative evidence, will not be accepted as true, however respectable his credentials may be. I need scarcely say, that in the past, both as to the " masses' and the classes," there was an easy-going assent (with few exceptions), to all and everything coming down to us from remote ages through the Bible. to doubt which. incurred pains and penalties of the most painful kind. Happily for us, a!nd for " Isos "and " flarry Estnond," in particuLtr, the burning faggot, and the executioner's axe, are things of the oast, never, let us hope, to return. In the stead of I keet, now, when "heterodox" (?) ideas are published (example of which we have in the letters in question), " they are severely left alone," as in the case of " Isos, " this modern policy of silenct proceeds from the fear, and not from the love of truth.' Lymm, April 21st, 1893..
EX-FARMER.

div.head: REV. tARK GUY PEARSE AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE REV. tARK GUY PEARSE AT WARRINGTON.

The Rev. Mark One -Pearse of the London Vi es- leyan West Central Mission, gave kis popular lec- ture entitled "Some old folks at borne" or "Sketches of Cornish life," at the Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapel on Wednesday night. There was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. R. Garnett. J.P., and he was Supported by the Revs. Mark Guy Pearse, J. Kirtlan, A. Freeman, and T. Ross, Dr. StArkey Smith, J.P., Councillor Shaw Green, and I Messrs. R. Cooke, and William Bennett. The meeting I was opened by a hymn, and the Rev. A. Freeman en- gaged in prayer. Mr. Garnett after a few remarks called upon the lecturer. The Rev. Mark Guy Pearse, who was received with applause, said that his lecture that night would be a sketch of Cornish character. The first suggestion of the present lecture came from some Americans in whose company he was some years ago in the Isle of Wight. They conr.menced talking about the character in his books and suggested that he should give a lecture on them and entitle it " Some old folks at home." Be first gave the lecture in America. The Cornish people were a peculiar people, and their pecu- larities arose from the fact of their remoteness. Corn- wall was the only county in England which only touched one other county, and was almost an island. In his younger days the only connection with the rest of the Country was by a single coach. Although he thought the present times were better than the " good old times," yet he loved to speak of the old times. The re- moteness of Cornwall gave the people a strongly marked originality, and the Celtic blood had also left its mark upon the people. The lecturer then proceeded to sketch out in his characteristic style different characters he had known as a boy, the lecture abounding in pathetic in- cidents interspersed with humour.

div.head: CINTATA AT ST. JAMES' SCHOOL.
div.p: CINTATA AT ST. JAMES' SCHOOL.

A grand cantata, entitled "The Happy Family was performed in the St. James' School, Latchford, on Tuesday and Wednesday eyenings,by the scholars attending the sch ools,bef ore large audiences.Preyious to the performance of the cantata, a miscellaneous programme Consisting of songs, recitations, and musical drill was creditably gone through by the children. An orchestral band under the conductorship of Mr. Smith, played several selections during the even- ing in an excellent manner. The accompanists on the piano, during the evening were, Mr. Frank Booth and Miss Sykes. The platform represented Green Elms Cottage (exterior), residence of the old woman and family who lived in a shoe. The cantata opened with a chorus "A happy family we," which was followed by a solo by the old woman, in which she regrets her removal from the old shoe, but sighs for the return of her chil- dren abroad. It being her birthday she had a strange presentiment that her children would retnrn that day. After another chorus, Aladdin with his wonderful lamp arrives, and gives an account of his adventures, when he is introduced to Miss Muffett, and after a game at " The Captive Maiden " on the stage, Sinbad with his crew of sailors arrives, and after the singing of Oh, we are the crew of the 'Nancy Lee ' " and the chorus "The sailor leadeth a joyous life" Marjory Daw arrives and is introduced to Sin bad. Blue Beard is the next to arrive, and a game of " blind man's buff " is played. Robinson Crusoe next puts in an appearance with his man Friday, and he gives an account of his adventures. A solo follows by Friday, for which he receives a well deserved encore. After a trio by Cinder- ella, Patience and Grace, Ali Baba enters with four of the forty thieves and.after singing " My name is Ali Baba Bold " a "tug of war " ensues between Sinbad's sailors and All Baba's thieves during which the chorus " A long pull, and a strong pull "is sung. The cantata concluded with a procession and march by the children with flags and bells and the singing of" A sweet good-night." All the parts were excellently performed and reflected great credit on the schoolmaster, Mr. Stansfield, who has been ably assisted in the training of the children, by the teachers of the school. The dresses of the principal characters were all that could be desired, and the wigs, etc., lent by Mr. Birch Brown, showed good taste. The role was made up as follows :—The Old Woman who lived in a1h0!3,, Mbss Davies ; Aladdin, James Dobson; Sindtrad, Witham Sheriatt ; Blue Beard, Geo. Daintith ; Robinson Crusoe. Joseph Barlow; All Baba, Thomas Taylor ; Miss Muffett, Lily Marrow; Marjory Dew, Jane Battersby ; Dorothy. Draggletail, Mary Carter ; Cinder- ella, Beatrice Carriage ; „Grace, Margaret Edleston ; Patience, Ada Wright ; troody Two Shoes, Beatrice Wright ;Friday (Robinson Crusoc's Black "Man '') John Edleston ; Crew of the " ;Nancy Lee," Fred Dowd, James Callan, Thos. Ashton, Ernest Leigh, F. Foulkes; Four of the "Forty Thieves," Robert Waugh, John Roberts, Thos. Batton, Percy Forster. A vote of thanks was passed to all who had assisted was passed on the pro- position of Mr. Stansfield.

The ladies of Melbourne have adopted the violet vail craze with much eagerness, to the great annoyance of their male acquaintances, who protest against such an unbecoming addition to the sun-burned faces so much in evidence in Antipodean summers.
NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.

"Moral victories "so far have generally been confined to the realm of politics, and are used soley—so says the P. D.—as healing balsam to the disappointed partizan. But Warrington, in their match on Saturday with Broughton Rangers, introduced the "moral victory" into the world of football. According to the total num- ber of points, they merely" left" the Rangers by one point. But the five points of the Broughton men repre- sented one goal, whilst the six points of Warrington represented three tries, and thus comes ia the moral victory.

John Bate was not present to facilitate the dexterous movemen;s of his name sake; but, nevertheless, Evans blessed James Bate—by his presence at half-hack. The manner in which these two players conducted busine,,s was highly commendable,and assisted the three-quarters to display their respective qualities. Potts, as one of the three quarters made a very good turn out, and the presence of Barnes was welcomed by all. Boscow is considered to have played better than he has done be- fore anytime during the past month. Ameng,st the for- wards Jolley came out conspicuous—and he was con- spicuous chiefly because of the surprising manner he always kept. in the vicinity of the ball.

The Wa*ring,ton spectators--or rather a handful of them—did the premier team a bad service at the match against Salford. If soectators have a grievance against a referee, no matter how well founded it may be, or may seem to be, the last thing they should do is to" mob" him. If the match is allowed to pass ever peacefully there may afterwards be some 'redress for gross unfair- ness, but once there is anything in the nature of vio- lence, the county authorities are bound to put their foot down. They cannot afford to ignore the" mobbing " of referees. Henco a club, all the responsible members of which are quite innocent of any offence, may be made to suffer in prestige and finance. That has followed in the present case for the Warrington ground has been "suspended " for to-day.

It is announced that "owing to the extreme roughness exhibited by Warrington in the recent match " the Run- corn Committee have scratched all future engagements with Warrington Club. How admirably the Runcorn Committee can adopt the tone of injured innocence? But I have been told that in the "recent match" the style of the Runcorn players was not one whit milder than that of their opponents, and I think I have read sometimes of other matches in which Runcorn have been engaged that their play was "vigorous "—and that is a word which occasionally implies a good deal. Runcorn have had their gate out of Warrington • I think it would have looked better if they' had paid the return compli- ment and then—if • they liked—cancelled all future engagements.

There were crest fallen looks, and lnck lustre eves in the ranks of the Broughton A. team, after the Warring- ton A. team played the match with them on Saturday. It does seem funny. The animated suit of ink-bespattered clothes, which goes about under the initials P.D. ,actually placed his money on the Broughton team, and at the end of the game when he went and looked at the scoring board and saw in bold bad—l mean black—letters : Warrington sti GOALS. THREE TRIES, to nil.—he said a word which he would have been fined for in the Latch- ford Swearing Club. This is piling on the agony, any- how. I'm afraid tha A. team is getting very merciless ; it will have the score marker going no strike, if this thing continues without extra remuneration. '

In the junior Cup Competition on Saturday, between Stockton Heath and the Parish Church, distinct pronun- ciation was given to two facts. The first fact was that the Churchmen are going to have the cup; and the second was that last Saturday but one, the Churchmen got knocked severely about. There were four of their men absent in " consecinence of injuries received in the match with Latchford." The game, however, was a very strong and fast, and vigorous cne, and resulted in a draw, in favour of the Parish Church.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

The replayed tie between St. Elphin's and Orford Barracks on Tuesday night, was without doubt, one of the most exciting football matches—and certainly the most exciting under the Asiociation code—ever seen in Warrington, and the closeness of the play is well re- presented by the final score of 1-0. The large crowd of spectators were, from first to last, kept on " tenter- hooks " as the play swayed first for St. Elphin's and then for the Barracks. Among St. Elphin's, Cook, Marshall, and Colley were very prominent, Marshall proving a very reliable goal keeper. The three half backs were very good. Tickle probably being the best, and Taylor was without doubt the best forward. Hatton, however, deserves special mention as it was from his foot that the winning goal came, amid a perfect yell of delight front the St. Elphin's followers. Mcßride kept geal in fine style for the soldiers, and Jones at full back was a terror to the Saints. Tha forwards, however, were rather weals lo r;ont 0 goal.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

On Saturday Mickle Trafford was favoured with a visit of a large number of members of the Warrington C. C., who inaugurated their country quarters at the Shrewsbury Arms. There were thirty of them. When tea had been" partaken of," a fishing competition took place between the Chaplain and the Secretary. The operations of these two august persons were viewed with considerable ame by the members. The two Restrain- ing Ones were hard at work for a long time, persuading the fish, but they wouldn't come. And when the referee called " time," it _was seen the competition was a draw —neither parties having hooked even a " jacky." After this a football match was played both the Association and the Rugby Codes, and a peculiar cyclist code being introduced. They tried a great deal; but even a minor was not scored. The members reached home at 11p.m. after what is expected to be the first of a series of enjoy- able trips to Mickle Trafford.

By the way, I notice that we have amongst us in War- rington a fairly large number of young lady cyclis`s. What I want to know is, why don't they form a club? ("And invite nentlemenfriends to the picnics," says the P.D. sotto voce) Coventry has a large ladies' cycling club, and Mrs. Singer, the Mayoress, is president. The members wear A special uniform neither including crinolines nor" male attire."

div.head: CONGRATULATIONS TO , MR. SPEAKMAN, J.P.
div.p: CONGRATULATIONS TO , MR. SPEAKMAN, J.P.

At a meeting of the Runcorn Improvement Com- missioners held on Monday evening a vote of con- gratulation to Mr. Speakman on his being made a Justice of the Peace was unanimously passed. The Chairman of the Board moved the resolution in felicitous terms. He said that it gave him Areat pleasure to tender the congratulations of the Board to Mr. Speakman on the dignity coaferred on him and that it was a gratification to them to know that this deserved honour had been conferred upon one who had through a long public career obtained, aad held, the confidence of his fellow townsmen and upon one who had been se long associated with the work of that Board. Each of the other nine members present in turn Spoke to the resolution and tendered their congratula- tions in person to Mr. Speakman, and each expressed himself generally on the matter before the Board from their different points of view. They all heartily ex- pressed the hope that Mr. Speakman would long be spared to serve the community in his new capacity and to enjoy the honour so fittingly conferred upon him. Mr. Speakman acknowledged the vote in a feeling man- ner and said that the vete tendered to him by his Coi- leagues on that Board was a valued one, and one which -it was a gratification for him to receive, and that it would be his constant endeavour to deserve the confid- ence of those who had so graciously expressed their sentiments on that occasion.

div.head: CZAR . AND THE- NIHILISTS. A GRIM EASTER GIFT.
div.p: THE CZAR . AND THE- NIHILISTS. A GRIM EASTER GIFT.

As was stated some days ago, the Emperor Alexander found a short time since in a photographic album on his writing table a picture of the famous Nihilish countess, Sophie Pernvskaia, who was hanged with the Murderers of Alexander H. It is now stated that at Easter the Czar received another disagreeable surprise. In his room at Livadia he found an exquisitely-painted Easter egg. Inside it was a small silver dagger, two Ivory- carved death's heads, and a slip of p per on which were these .words :—" Christ is risen. We also shall meet again !” In spite of all endnivours the secret police have not succeeded in firiding•out where either the por- trait or the egg came from.

div.head: EXAMINER, S k TTIMAY, APRIL 22. 1893.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, S k TTIMAY, APRIL 22. 1893.
LIE GROWTH OF STOCKTON HEATH. "A SUBURB OF TIIE FUTURE."
FROM A CORRESPONDENT. _

A great change has taken place at Stockton Heath during the last few months. Frost a com- paratively quiet, sequestered, cluster ef houses, the place has blossomed forth into a fast growing suburb,abounding with popular detached and semi- detached villas. The great change has chiefly been effected in and off the road which leads from the highway opposite the Mulberry Tree Inn, to Bed Lane Bridge. No longer in the spring time can one wakl along this road, and see only scattered resi- dences, each half hidden by the blossoming boughs of fruit trees, and separated from each other by the secluding intervention of orchards. As though the proverbial fairy with her magic wand had been there, the scene has changed." The rickety old gates on the road side have gone; most of the telds to which they were entrances, are na longer pasture land, but sites for the small colony of suburban residences. Several new paths and roads have been constructed, and the total number of houses erected during the last year or two tots up to a total of close upon 100, and there are about 20 houses at present nearing completion. The ordinary growth of Warrington is fast causing people who are able to do so to take up their resi- dences somewhere removed,at least by a few acres of green turf, from the smoke and dirt, and turmoil of "Little London."Latchford for a long time got Its full share of these suburban residents; but during the past three years,the prettier surroundings of Stock- ton Heath have become attractions to those wish- ing to live out of the town. The governing autho- rities of the village, too, are doing what they can to enhance the value of the district as suburban quar- ters. The system of drainage and sewerage has been greatly improved, and for the first time in its long, long history, the village has latterly been lighted by that modern illuminator—the gas lamp. A continually increasing 'bus service is a convenient mode of conveyance to this undoubtedly "future suburb " of Warrington; but I am looking forward to atime not far distant when the'more comfortable tram will be a more acceptable mode of convey- ance. _ . .

But Stockton Heath is very old ; and it has its share of antiquities. The village is a part of the township of Appleton. and according to ancient records the district before the Conquest, was the estate ot a Saxon lord whose name was Dot. He was then the waster of his freedom, and with his people lived as the happy monarch of" all he sur- veyed." But with the Conquest came a certain o..bern Fitz Tezzon ; he seemed to have taken a fancy to the estate, for in the Doomsday Book is recorded this melancholy entry—" The same Osbern holds Epletune. Dot held it and was a free man. There is one hide rateable to the gelt. The land is four carucates. It was and is waste. In King Edward's time it was worth sixteen shillings." Poor Dot had been deposed and with the usurpation of the individual named Osbern commenced the real history of Stockton Heath and Appleton. The great Clock of Time has markiM many memorable events since that, and the estate ha k passed through many hands, until it is now chiefly held by the Egertons and Sir Gilbert Greenall. A great change which must have suddenly appeared by the ascen- dency of Osbern is pointed out by history which tells us " the places of the bearded Saxons became filled with clean shaven Normans." And 3 et there is no trace of one barber's ehop that ever, existed there! . .

All your readers will be aware of the existence of the tree called Appleton Thorn. This was brought by one of Oshern's successors and is said to be an offshoot of the famous thorn planted by St. Augus- tine at Glastonbury ; i.e., according to the valuable history written by the late Mr.Beamont. A Knight who once held these lands was Gilbert Brito, a des- cendant of John Brito one of the Knights who slew Thomas a' Beckett. _ _ _

_ Once an attempt was made to develop an indastry in Stockton Heath. It is a long time ago—in 1609 in fact. King James issued an order that mulberry trees should be planted all over the country for silk worms introduced from France. It is said that a large plantation of mulberry trees was made at Stockton Heath. but the silkworms were never in- troduced, and the only thing which sprung from the attempt was the title of the Mulberry Tree Inn.

Probably the most interesting historical land mark in the locality is the Baptist Chapel at Hill ChM. The records of its history contain in themselves a story,sometimes tragic, other times melancholy,and occasionally bright and hopeful, of the straggle for life which the sect in its early days went through. Rodger Holland, the first notable Bap- tist of the neighbourhood, was burned at the stake by Bonner as an infidel. History says, "His blood tau indeed have been the seed from which sprang the congregation of Hill Cliffs." The chapel which now stands was first built in 1688, and Cromwell is said to have visited it. Thomas Howe was the first minister; he died in 1695. There were some cele- brated men who followed. In 1700 the Hill Cliffs Baptists spread their tenets to Liverpool, and the first minister there was a Dutch exile named " Dr. Daniel Fabius alias Beany." The minister for Hill Cliffe for 1725 was a Stockton Heath man named i9llll McGoWan,whe wee the author of many works which gained contemporary fame. Vne—"The logue of Devils," is well known still. Hill Cliff, too, had some rather remarkable resi- dents. One was the celebrated Italian tragic poet, Vittario. He was a kind of Byron. At 21 he fol- lowed a pretty belle to Warrington. He had great trlent, but gave himself over to bad habits. In his melancholy moments he used to wander about that Fir Thicket, which is the adornment of the hill. In one of these attacks of melancholy musing on his debasement he had a happy thought.... To . . . . . . .

break off his bad habit "be madeahli servant bind him every morning with cords concealed under his 'cloak," and when his friends came for him he did not go out with them because, as he said, he was too busy. He afterwards produced his " Cleopatra" and other works. Another strange character was Admiral Howe, who founded the Reservoir. at 11 Appleton. He built a mansion of wood designed in every detail like a ship, and he had the adjacent ground kept green like a sea. He divided the 24 hours into watches, and for years his household had to take their watches night and day, as though at sea. A popular form of amusement at Stockton Heath used to be horse racing and bull-baiting. The horse races were held on the Heath annually. History I says :—Tbe races did not rival Dondaster or the F.t. Ledger, nor were the horses thorough-bred ' like Marbury Dun, but the races as a home affair doubtless gave much amusement to the company who crowded the Mulberry Tree to witness them. But bull-baiting.was a common pastime and obtained until the beginning of the present century. When the people became good enough to forgo bull-bait- ing their lives became quieter and the history of the village less eventful.

div.head: REPRESENTING HIMSELF TO BE A SOLICITOR • PROSECUTION AT WIDNES.
div.p: REPRESENTING HIMSELF TO BE A SOLICITOR • PROSECUTION AT WIDNES.

On Thursday, at the Widnes Petty Sessions, before Messrs. 11. Wade Deacon and E. Mather, a respec- tably dressed man named Frederick Johnsen, 1, Terrace-road, Widnes, who is agent for Messrs. Fairclough and Sons, flour dealers, was summonad at the instance of the Incorporated Law Society, London, for willfully and falsely representing himself to be a solicitor in the month of March. Mr. G. Norton, solicitor, Liver- pool, supported their:formation on behalf of the Society, and Mr. F. J. Poole represented the defendant. —Mr. Norton stated that the defendant on behalf of Mr. Gidlow of Garston, wrote the following letter to Mr. Eaten, of the same town, who owed Mr. Gidlow £l7B Dear Sir,—Thomas Gidlow has placed 'the enclosed account lute my hands, and I must request you to pay the same on or before this day next week, or otherwise give satisfactory security for the amount which lam aware you possess. You may do this through me or through Mr. Gidlow direct. If you:do not conform to my request I shall serve you with a writ without further delay.—Yours truly, FREDERICA JOrnssois. Mr. A. Eaton, Stanley-st., GarsEon."—lt was the latter part of the letter, Mr. Norton eontinued, that constituted the offence, but as the defendant was not, he believed, a debt collector, and had never done such a thing before, the society in this case were satisfied if the case was made public, so as to act as a warning in the ,future. Taking all the circumstances into consideration, I he would ask the Bench to allow him to withaw the case on the understanding that the defendant paid the costs and expressed regret for what be had done.—Mr. Poole gave this undertaking, and said his client had acted throughout in ignorance of the law. He had no intention whatever of representing himself as a solicitor, but there could be no doubt that he had exceeded his bounds.— The Bench allowed the summons to be withdrawn, and I the defendant paid the costs, which amounted to £1 es. ed.

div.head: PURCII4SE OF RUNCORN WATERWORKS.
div.p: THE PURCII4SE OF RUNCORN WATERWORKS.
THE ItITEPAY6ET DECISION.
A meeting of the ratepayers convened by the Board of Commissioners was held in the Public

- - - - ----- Hall, on Wednesday evening. There was a fair at- tendance. Mr. F'. Wiswall presided and there were on the platform Messrs. P. Speakman, J.P., C.C., E W. Humphreys, J. Meadewcroft, Thos. Lea, D. Bis- brown, J. W. Lightburn, H. J. Grice, J. L. Tunstall, (accountant) ; F. A. Lake, (Law Clerk).; E. Marsh- all, (secretary).-The Chairman said that meeting was held to keep faith with the ratepayers, that before the Board of Commissioners concluded the purchase of the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton waterworks they would submit the terms to the rate- payers. The Board to Committee had adopted a minute that in view of Mr. Tunstall's report dated 'lsth April, and of the rreommendation of the Finance and Parlia- mentary Commissioners the Board is of opinion that it is advisable to conclude the purchase of the Waterworks Company's undertaking upon the terms contained in the agreement of the Ist December 1893. The, Chairman added that the Board had nothing to hide, said Mr. Tunstall, the accountant, in whom they had the great- est confidence, would answer any question that might be asked. Upon this question not one commissioner had voted who had an interest in the Waterworks Company' and in the interests of the ratepayers only the Board appealed to them with every confidence. The Secretary .then read the report of Mr. J. L. Tun- stall, chartered accountant, Warrington. The report waS dated April 15th and stated :-" Gentlemen,-I have, in accordance with the request contained in your Secre- tary's letter of the 30th ulto. examined the profit and loss account of the Runcorn, Weston and Halton Water Works Company for the year ended 31st December, 1892, prepared by Mr. Knight on behalf of the Company. I have compared it with the accounts of the Company and discussed the items with Mr. Knight and, a fter mak- ing certain corrections, we aereed that the Company's accounts show a profit of £2,918 ha. id., available for payment of interest on loans (including Banker's advances) the dividends on share capital. The account showing this result is as follows :-Credit side-By sales of water, £4,096 15s. 7d. ; by meter rents, £l6 184. ; by weighing, transfers, &c., 10s. 3d. ; fittings account, £7O; by Manchester Ship Canal Co. Royalty, £302 15.. 101. ; total £4,486 19L 81. ; less irrecoverable, £72 2s. 11d. On the debtor side was the following items :-To salaries and wages, £713 193. ld. ; fuel and carting, £364 9s. 3d.; rent and way leaves, £2B 193. 3d. ; oil, tallow and pack- ing, ,£l6 123. 61. ; stationery and printing,£26 2s. 4d.; rates and taxes, £220 73. Bd.-Repairs : Machinery, 255 155,; timber for staging in well, £l2 13s. 51. ; cot- tages.£4 Bs. 4d.-£75 16s. 91; trade charges and audit- ing, £45 17s. 61. ; hank commission,£4 ls. 41. ; balance as per Company's books and accounts, availa- ble for payment in interest on loans (includ- ing banker's advances) and dividends on share capital. £2,918 lie. 11. ; total £4,414 16s. 91. The profit shown by the accounts of the Company can- not, however,, be accepted as the true profit, inasmuch as there are no detailed accounts of the stocks at the beginning and the end of the year. whilst the accounts ptesent internal evidence that the stocks, except the stock of fuel, have not been taken on the same basis at the two periods. In order, therefore, to adjust the profit and loss account I think it necessary to deduct the follewiug sums from the apparent profit, viz :-Oil, tallow, packing, &c., ia addition to the amount debited, £37 7s. 61. ; and profit on fittings account apparently arising from inereassd valuation of stock, £7O ; total £1037a. 61.

My estimate of the actual profit earned &ring th: year ' is therefore £2,918 lie. id. less than £lO3 7s. 6.1. -02.815 33 7d, and this woad leave, after payment of £957 103. sd. interest on loans and dividends on prefer- ence share., a net profit of £1,857 13s. 21., as compared with £1,575, the amount assured by your Board as the basis of the negotiations. These are the results of the year under review, but they require further 'modifica- tion in order to ascertain what is the present earning power of the Company, from a purchaser's point of view The estimated actual profit as above is £2,815 3s. 7d. ThA repairs charged during the year amount to £75 16s. 9d., whereas Mr. NEwton estimates the average annual (test of repairs at £lOO. There should therefore ' be deducted on this account £24 33. 3d. ; the Royalty payable by the Manchester Ship Canal Company can only be considered as a temporary source of income and should therefore also be deducted £302 15s. 10d. —£326 193. Id., leaving £2,488 43. Od. On the other hand the Company have found upon close examination that the assessments upon which their rates have been based in the past were in many cases too low. They have now been raised, and show a nominally in- creased further income of more than £2OO, and 1 think it will be safe to assume that £l5O of this will prove recoverable. This amount should therefore be added £l5O. The earning power may accordingly be consi- dered to be £2,638 4s. W. If from this be deducted the interest on loans and dividends on preference shares, £957 108. 5d., there will remain a sum of £1,680 14s. Id., -which exceeds the amount assumed for the purpose of the negotiations, viz. :—£1,575, by £lO5 14s. id. Although owing to the imperfect accounts of the Company, I have been com- pelled in some cases to adopt estimates instead of actual figures, there is little room for error, as only a few items are affected, and I have had the advantage of an exam- ination of several years' accounts. As regards repairs I have, 82 before stated, taken Mr. Newton's estimate, and there can be no reasonable , doubt that when the Company have put the works into a state of thorough repair, as I understand they have undertaken to do, the repairs will for some years to come be light. I have, therefore, no hesitation in saying that your Board may accept the results above set forth with confidence as correct for all practical purposes. The improvement upon .the year. reviewed in my

, . former reports, is accounted for roughly as follows : Repairs have cost less by £l4O ; the coal bill has, by the use of slack instead of burgy, been reduced by £100; the sales of water have increased by £l3O ; the Increase
in assessments will yield further £l5O ; and minor items make up another £3O ; tot al improvement £550,

, In view of the better results shown by the Company, the purchase of their undertaking would appear to be highly desirable, and, as regards the present works, pro- vided the sinking funds are arranged as set forth in my report of the Bth of February last, and the loans are ar- ranged at the rate of 3i per cent, per annum, there will, should the profits even remain stationary, be not only no charge upon the rates, but an immediate annual surplus of £l7O or thereabout. A Ratepayer (Mr. Houghton) asked what was the price to be paid, and the Chairman replied £67,500.— Mr. Houghton : How much in the £ will the improve- ment rate be.—The Chairman : It will be less rather than more according to Mr. Tunstalre report.—Mr. Houghton: You would still charge 6 per cent. on th. ' rent.—The Chairman : Yes.—Mr. Houghton said the Waterwarks Co. might. well make a profit. There were plenty cf houses where they had not sufficient water to wash the floors.—The Chairman : That is why we wish to by the undertaking to put these matters right.—Mr. Roberts, draper, held up a report which he said was pre- pared by Mr. Tunstall, and was about to quote from it when the Chairman said it was not correct. It was pre- pared on imperfect informations but the report presented that night was complete from the fullest information, and was the one upon which they were working.—Mr. Humphreys pointed out that the first report was stepped short at June 30th, whereas the last report was up to the 31st December last.—Mr. Roberts said the report he held showed that the total cost was £70,450 and if the money were borrowed at 34 there would be a deficiency of £4OO. and that said nettling about the capital to be repaid in 55 years. It would be nothing lees than qin the 2 upon the rates.—Mr. Lightburn said £4OO would not be q in the £.—Mr. Bridgewater asked if there was a deficiency on the water account could not this deficiency be charged upon the district rates.—Mr. Lake said any deficiency would fall upon the rates of course.—Mr. Roberts was referring to the first report again, when . . .

. . the Ohs. irrnan told hrm that it wag a private document, and he did not know how he became possessed of it.— Mr. Roberts : lam a large ratepayer and lam entitled to do it as well as you.—The Chairman : It was a pri- vate communication upon the negociations in the Company, and I don't know how you . .

have the audacity- rto refer to it because it is not your property.—Mr. Roberts said since he had been a ratepayer he had paid £l3O in rates and he was as much interested as anybody.—Mr. Speakman said he could vouch notwithstanding anything Mr. Roberts might say that there was no one en that platform directly or indirectly interested in the Water Company. The inter- ests of the gentlemen on the platform and the gentlemen in the flail were identical and he appealed to them not to make the subject a quarrelsome one, because he con- tended that if they did not take the water works now it would be a great pity for Runcorn.-11. Humphreys was about to make a few remarks, when he was inter- rupted by Mr. Roberts saying " Oh, sit down ; we knew what you are.—Mr. Kniveton asked if Mr. Tunstall had taken Vito consideration the increased outlay required to increase the quantity and improve the quality of the water supplv.—Mr.Tunstall said be had taken nothing into account in his report except the present works. He had altogether ignored any extension that might be necessary because he was not an engineer.—Mr. Terrie : Can Mr.Tunstall explain how it is that if the present Com- pany having worked on such -economical lines as they had done they had never been able to show a better return for the capital.—Mr. Tunstall -: I am afraid I cannot answer for the management of the Company. They have managed the Company very much better this year than they have ever done before. and they have made very much more 'money in consequence—Mr. Massey asked whether the Commissioners if they purchased the undertaking cnuld bring water from Norton 'rower at a profit or at a iORS.—The Chairman said ' they had a clause in the Liverpool Act which enabled them to take 11 minimum quantity of 300,000 gallons and a maximum quantity of a million gallons per day. It would cost £2,300 to connect Nor- ton to the reservoir for the purpose of supplyinm the town. They would get the water at ed. per 1,000 gal-- lons and would be able to sell it at 9d. per 1,000 gallons,
so that they ought to make a profit at that price. As be water would pass through a meter they would get a

right que,otity of water. At the pre•ent well there appeared to be an enormous qu tntity pumped in excess ot what was consumed. Mat. was not satisfactory, and they hoped to find out where the leakage was. There were other points. One of the engines had been work- ing with a bad piston and anybody knew that this meant an enormoui consumption of fuel, and that there was I not Ril effective work being done by the steam. They would remedy that. In his opinion they could not do better than go to the Vyrnwy main for their increased supply and as they had great hopes of having a minimum quantity reduced, an J. they would not then incur any serious liabilitv.lo reply to Mr. Bridgewater, the Chairman stated that according to Mr. Tunstalt if the profits of the Company remained stationary, there would be no charge up-n' the rates but a surplus of £l7O.

Mr. Meadowcroft said the question was whether the meeting was prepared to accept on this subject the report of Mr. Tunsta.ll, a gentleman standing high in his profession and whose reputation depended upon the figures he had given or to accept the opinion of Mr. Roberts who was not a professional accountant. (Hear, bear.) He (Mr. Meadowcroft) represented very large ratepayers in the town and he would be no party to any agreement which would be prejudicial 'to their interests, and that made him all the more confident in recommending the ratepayers of Runcorn to purchase the waterworks upon the state- ment which had been presented to them. Mr. Meadow- croft entered into an analysis of the figures of the report, which he said showed a surplus of revenue over expen- diture,and the probability of the ratepayers being called upon to pay anything on district rate account for the waterworks was extremely remote. It was no new thing for commissioners and corporations to be called upon to acquire waterworks.and they did it, not for pre- sent. but for future benefit, and the Commissioners in considering this matter had been looking to the future. Nine out of every ten very much regretted that the old Commissioners did not take steps years ago to purchase the gasworks. (Applause.) The gasworks would have been a profitable concern no*. The Commissioners were acting upon these lines now,and in order that they might not he cluarg,ed with neglecting the interests of the rate- payers,thev had taken this opportunity of endeavouring to make a good bargain.—ln reply to Mr. Kniveton, Mr. Meadowcroft said they had given the worst side of the financial aspect rather than paint the prospects in ten rosy a hue.—Mr: Torrie asked would not the executives' salaries be doubled in a short time after the Commis- sioners obtained the works.—Mr. Meadowcroft laugh- ingly replied that he should not like to say that. Mr. P. Speakman, J.P., C.C., in the course of an ad- dress, showed the apparent difference between Mr. Tun- stall's two reports and pointed out that had the Com- missioners twelve or fourteen years ago succeeded in purchasing the water undertaking they would have saved a very great sum of money. They most re- member that Runcorn was growing, and sea largo rate- payer, he was sprite willing, were it necessary, but he did not think it would be.to tax his pocket for a time for the ! benefit of Runcorn, and if those present would take that ! I view, they would do well for the prosperity of Runcorn. ! I (Applause.) After a reference to the figures, Mr. Speak- man pointed out tho great inducement a plentiful supply of water would be for new industries to settle in their midst, and he appealed to them not to neglect this opportunity of promoting the best interests of the town and district. In reply to a question, Mr. Speakman. said he had sold his interests in the Water Company so that he might do his best for Runcorn. (Applause.) Mr. J. Johnson expressed the hope that there would be a unanimous vote for the purchase of the Water Works and he trusted that the Commissioners as soon as they had completed the purchase would take steps to connect:with the Vvrn wv main and let them have an abundant supply of water. If the ratepayers considered their own in- terests and the interests of tke town, they would strengthen the hands of the Commissioners and t,hank them for the efforts they had madeto carry this matter through—He moved that the iresting approve of the Commissioners purchasing the Water Works. Mr. Humphreys having made a speech in which he showed that the Commissioners were getting the works on easier termsthan several other anthorities, Mr. Kniveton seconded the motion, remarking that he was satisfied that it was a good investment for the ratepayers. Ile pointed out the importance from a sanitary point of view of a plentiful supply of good water, and lie argued that it was one of the first necessities of civilization. The Ship Canal was nearly finished and there was a future before the town. There had been a great deal of building going on during the past few years, and they would want new works from some quarter or another. He stated that last Friday's disaster woold not have taken place at Highfield Tannery if the water supply had been under the control of the Cninmissioners. fie could not see that they were going to be involved in a single penny in the rate by the pur- chase of the waterworks, and even if this were, to go against the purchase would do a serious injury to the prosperity of the town. (Mr. Roberts :) Mr. Knivetow is hike a weathercock. He does not know his own mind.

Mr. Torrie predicted that to purchase the works would be a ruinous step to take, and he announced that should the district rate be increased through the works, he would go to ga.ol before he would pay the money. (Laughter.) The Chairman then put the resolution which was car- ried by a very large majority, only about a dozen vot- ing against.

The Board of Commissioners held a special meeting on Thursday morning when Mr. 11. J. Grice presided and there were present—Messrs. P. Speakman; J.P. C.C., W. Fisher, E. W. Humphreys, W. Hankinson, T. Lea, J. Meadowcroft. D. Bisbrown, J. W. Lightburn, F. A. Lake (Law Clerk). and G. Marshall ksec.)—Mr. Fisher moved the confirmation of the following minute: At a meeting of the Finance and Parliamentary Committee held on the 17th April, 1893, it was resolved that the following minutes bc submitted to the Board for adop- tion. 6, Tnat after considering Mr. Tiinstall's further report. tke Board proceed with the purchase of the undertaking of the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Water- works Company on the terms containcu in the agree- ment with the Water Company,"—Mr. Speakman seconded.—Carried unanimously.
WARRINGTON BANKRUPTCY COURT.
A PECULIAR SYSTEM OF TRADING.

-.- - Yesterday, at the Warrington Bankruptcy Court, before Mr. Registrar Ridgway, William Rhein, of 40. blersey-st,, and Golborue-st., Newton, carter and coal dealer,appeared for his public ext: ipinat ion. The, liabilities amounted to '1272 7s. 6(14 and the assets to £l3l Bs. 10d., leaving a deficiency of £l4O Me. 81. The bankrupt stated that lie commenced business in 1878 with £lOO his own savings, and that he had been the contractor for the disposal of nightsoil for the Newton district. Not having kept proper books ef acounts he was unable to file any accounts explaining his defisciency, but he had lost six horsesin 12 months, which more than - covered his defici- ency. He had also lost heavily on the night. soil contrAcL .He alleged that he only became aware of his insolvency in September last, and admitted that he had contracted debts, still owing with such knowledge. In reply to Mr. A. 13. Potter, the assistant official receiver, the debtor said lie had not filed his position sooner because he had no money to do it with. He took the contract for the disposal of nightsoil for three years at £4OO a year. Latterly he could not sell the manure at all, could hardly give it away. Heind had ths contract twice previous to 1890,and then it proved renumerative. Be only kept a day or memorandum book, but that had been kept so badly that it was impossible to ascertain what was owing, to him. He had no system whatever. Mr. Potter said it appeared that when the debtor received any money he entered it on the first page he opened the book at, and did not put down the name of the person paying it, nor yet the date. He 1, also adopted the game system, or want of system, in ! regard to sales.—The Registrar said it appeared a very loose way of trading.—The debtor said he was unable to furnish any further information than he had already done as to who oi,eed him money or who be owed money to. He did not know that debts were owing, and could not tell from his books. The debtor in reply to other questions varied his statements, the Registrar having frequently to warn him to be more careful in his answers.—Mr. Potter said it was a most unsatisfactory state of affairs. There was no evidence of any of the alleged losses, and for all he knew the debtor might have put the money into his pocket,—The debtor said he had not a farthing.—Mr. Potter said the debtor seemed to know nothing and to care less.—The Registrar : Ile seems perfectly reckless to me. Ultimately the debtor ! promised to attend at the official receiver's office and endeavour to give more information as to his liability and assets.

div.head: pENNP,TII.
div.p: pENNP,TII.

PEKLETIL LIBERAL CLUB.—The annual general meeting of the above was held in the billiard room of the club on Monday night. Mr. J. B. Aitken (president) presided, Mr. F. Hughes (secretary), read the minutes of the previous meeting, which on being put to the meeting were passed. Mr. A. J. White ( treasurer), then laid the financial accounts before the meeting. The accounts showed an income of £4B 133. 111, and an expenditure of £47 Be. 81.0., leaving a balance in hand of Ll 4s. sd. The accounts were passed on the motion of Mr. Aitken. The next business was the election of officers for the ensuing year. Mr. J. B. Aitken was re-elected president the vice-presidents, Messrs. R. Garnett, J.P., B. Gar- nett, 0. H. 13oitow, C. E. Periter, J. Peers, and 11. Hughes. Me'. A. J. White was re-elected treasurer, and Mr. F. Hughes secretary, with Mr. J Lewis as his assis- tant. The following constitute the Committee Messrs. T. Seed, W. Longshaw, Randle, A, Seed,ll. Wilkinson A. Wilkinson. P. Hughes, C. Bartlett, E. Cross, and F. Wilkinson. Resolutions in favour of the Home Rule I Bill, Local Veto, and Parish Councils Bills were read and passed. The rest of the business was of a general nature. Mr. C. E. Parker moved a vote of thanks to the president and committee for their services during the past year. Mr. H. WilkinsonN.S seconded the proposi- tion. Mr. Aitken replied. This terminated the busi- ness.
LATEST NE WS.
-- ALLEM) MURDER OF A POLICEMAN.

At Middleborough, yesterday, John Henry Gould, slaughterman, 30, was chared with wilful murder of P.C. Henderson. A party of four went to arrest him. The prisoner had a loaded rifle, and after the party had spent an hour trying to induce him to lay it down Henderson rushed forward and the prisoner shot him. He was committed for trial for wilful murder.

div.head: SHOCKING SUICIDE IN CHESHIRE.
div.p: SHOCKING SUICIDE IN CHESHIRE.

Yesterday moraing Mary Hannah Houghton, the mother of five children, committed suicide at Ellesmere Port in the most deliberate fashion. She procured a bucket, and placing her I.ead over it, cut her throat and bled to death. She had latterly been in very depressed spirits.

div.head: ILLNESS OF LO RD DERBY.
div.p: THE ILLNESS OF LO RD DERBY.
UNFAVOURABLE SYMPTOMS.

Dr. Bickersteth left Knowsley yesterday morning shortly after ten o'clock after an anxious night. On Thursday evening Lord Derby had a renewal of adverse syentoms, which left him very prostrate, but the skill of his mecUcal advisers successfully warded off tho' critical effec!.s which were feared. In the meanwhile his lordship is in charge of Dr. Warr.

div.head: FATALITY TO A FOOTBALL SPECTATOR.
div.p: FATALITY TO A FOOTBALL SPECTATOR.

At St. Helens Junction, yesterday, Mr. Jones, deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body of Horace Slade, aged fourteen, who on the 18th of February vi,ited a football match on the Railway Recreation field. He climbed up a fence eight feet high to sit and watch the game, but falling on his head was rendered unconscious. Dr. Casey said the fall had set up an abscess or clot on the brain, which caused death. A verdict of " Acciden- tal death" was returned.

div.head: LARGE BEQUEST FOR AGRICULTURAL EDUCATION.
div.p: LARGE BEQUEST FOR AGRICULTURAL EDUCATION.

Probate has been granted of the will of Thomas Harper Adams, of E*lgmond House, Newport, Shrop- shire, who has left his real and personal estate for the purpose of teaching practical and theoretical agriculture to men and youths, and dairying, housekeeping, and other subjects to women and girls, either by iecture4 or by establishing schools in certain places named. It is stated the total amount available will exceed £70,000.
THE DOWAGER DUCHESS'S CONTEMPT.
THE CHANCERY TIPSCAFF AT WINISOR

Mr. Hawkins, the Chancery Tipstaff, after having and interview yesterday morning with Mr. Registrar Ha nnen who drew up the committal order of the Dowager Doc- hess of Sotherlandreturned to Windsor with instructions to wait there until her grace is well enough to be retrieved in custorl!. THE DESTROYED DOCUMENTS.

The "Morning "says the papers which the Dowager- Duchess of Sutherland burned during the inspection of the documents ordered by the court, and which con- stituted the contempt for which she has been sentenced, were three sheets of notepaper covered with the late duke's hand writing. and had reference to the death of her grace's first husband, Major Blair, who was found shot dead in the grounds of Dunrobin Castle.

div.head: SHIP CANAL BILLS.
div.p: SHIP CANAL BILLS.

The Unopposed Bill Committee of the House of Com- mons presided over by Mr. Mellor, yesterday morning, passed the two bills which respectively authorise the Manchester Ship Canal Company to raise £2,000,000 additional capital, and empower the Manchester Cor- poration to advance that sum upon terms that were agreed to when these Bills were before the House of Lords. Subsequently, the petition of the Ship Canal Company for leave to introduce a 'bill dealing with their surplus lands, and to confirm an agreement with the Manchester Racecourse Company, came before one of the examiners of the House of Commons, who decided to report that the petition had not complied with the standing orders, which require that all petitions for Bills must be presented on or before the 30th November preceding the opening of Parliament. This petition will now be cansidered by the Standing Orders Committee, who at their former sitting consented to the petition being presented.

div.head: HULL DOCK STRIKE.
div.p: THE HULL DOCK STRIKE.
EXCITING SCENE AT THE DOCKS.

A special correspondent states that 160 free labourers arrived yesterday morning, and that others would reach the port during the day, from different parts 01 the country. Early- yesterday morning an unusual incident occurred on the Alexandra Dock, and one which but for the prompt action of the constabulary stationed there must have been fraught with serious consequences. A seaman from one of the ships in the deck was excitedly parading the quay and fearfully brandishing a large claspknife. Ile was seen by the police officers, who, after relieving him of his weapon, promptly took him back to his ship, where he was taken chage of by the other men on board. Some of thefree labourers inside the sheds happeneelto be looking out of the window, and seeing this nue in charge the rumour got amongst them that the unionist picket had gained an entrance to the dock- In a very few seconds a general scrimmage ensued, ench man securing the hest weapon of defence he could lay his hands on. Finding that the expected attack never came, the men having worked themselves up to a pitch of excitement, made for the entrance gate, deterinine,d to make their way out and have ago with the pickets outside. The police tip to this time ha dnot the slightest idea of what was going on, and it was with great surprise that Sergt. Rippon and three other constables stationed at the en- trance saw the motley army of free labourere,each armed with either a stout stick or a knife, desperately marching to the gate. Sergeant Rippon immediately erdered the gates to be locked and approached the men They, however, had determined not to listen to any council from the police, and pushed up to the gates. Finding them locked they demanded the key. The atrgeant again appealed to the men, and after a sharp exchange of orders the men began to settle down, not, however, before they had 'explained the whole circumstances. By this time an equal number of police, chiefly pickets, had gathered outside the gates. Sergeant Rippon ultimately prevailed upen the free labourers to return to their sh eds. _ _ _ .

„.-. Yesterday morning about 150 of the free labourers eft Alexandra book for I.,ndon, their period of engagement having terminated. Many of them declared that they would not return, but others hoped to be back soon.

div.head: BATCH OF FACTORY CASES AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: A BATCH OF FACTORY CASES AT ST. HELENS.

Messrs, J. Cook and Co., drapers, the Exchange, St. Helens, were summoned on Monday, under five informations laid ,by Mr. Richmond, Government inspector of factories and workshops, for having ut.lawfully employed certain young people after the hour of four' o'clock in the afternoon of the day fixed for early closing. Mr. R. W. Thomas defended. Mr. Richmond stated that Thursday afternAn had been fixed as the firm's early closing day. On the Thursday before •Good Friday he visited the place at five o'clock, and found about 20 persons at work. The only reason given was that as Good Fri6lay was the next day and they would have a holiday, an extra hour that day, they thpught did not matter.—Mr. Thomas said Mr. Cook did not know the girls were working. The dress- maker had several orders, including a mourning order to complete, and ahe took the responsibility-of keeping them.—The magirrates fined defendants 10s. in the first cafe, and in the others ordered costs to be paid. The St. Helens Printing and Publishing Company were summoned by Mr. Richmond for employing two boys, named Pillingham and Howard, without certificates; also with neglecting tocomply with the 3rd section of the Act by having the printing office of the "St. Helens Chronicle" kept ..in a cleanly, and well- ventilated state ; end further with neglecting to keep an abstract of the Act affixed in the factory. Mr. Swar- brick, the manager, said the lads were errand boys,who sometimes got into the office to amuse themselvEs with type and in other ways.--The magistrates (Messrs. H. Martin and T. Glover) thought the lads might be errand boys and dismissed that case. In the other two cases fines of ss. and costs were imposed.
